The samples were centrifuged at 15,000g for 1 min at 4 °C to pellet chromatin. The supernatants were carefully aspirated, leaving 15 µl above the pellet. Chromatin pellets were washed twice with ice-cold 1× ELB-sucrose (0.25 M). After washing, chromatin pellets were resuspended in SDS loading buffer containing β-mercaptoethanol and boiled. Samples were resolved by SDS–PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes and analysed by western blotting using the indicated primary antibodies.

IP for MS analysis was performed using Protein A Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 10002D). Dynabeads were incubated with the indicated antibodies (mock control or Xenopus PRIMPOL antibodies 1 or 2) and washed with PBS containing 0.02% Tween-20 to remove unbound antibody. Clarified HSS extract was added to the antibody-bound beads and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with rotation to allow IP. After incubation, beads were washed with ELB-sucrose buffer containing 0.02% NP-40 and subsequently washed with PBS.

Samples were trypsin-digested on magnetic beads. The embedded proteins were exchanged into 200 μl of 100 mM triethyl ammonium bicarbonate and reduced with 500 mM of DTT, added to a final concentration of 10 mM. After incubation for 5 min at 55 °C, the beads were mixed head-over-head at room temperature for 25 min on the Barnstead Thermolyne Labquake rotisserie shaker. They were then alkylated with 1 M acrylamide (30 mM final concentration) at room temperature for 30 min. The reduced and alkylated proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C, using 500 ng of MS-grade trypsin/LysC mix (Promega). After digestion, the samples were quenched with formic acid (adjusted to a pH of around 3), eluted from the beads and desalted using the MonoSpin C18 Solid-Phase Extraction (SPE) columns (GL Sciences). Finally, the samples were dried in a SpeedVac SPD 130 DLX vacuum concentrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and exchanged into liquid chromatography (LC)–MS reconstitution buffer (2% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid in water) for instrumental analysis.

Proteolytically digested peptides were separated using an in-house pulled and packed reverse-phase analytical column (~25 cm length, 100 μm inner diameter), with Dr. Maisch 1.9 μm C18 beads as the stationary phase. Separation was performed with an 80 min reverse-phase gradient (2–45% B, followed by a high-B wash) on the Acquity M-Class UPLC system (Waters) at a flow rate of 300 nl min−1. Mobile phase A was 0.2% formic acid in water, while mobile phase B was 0.2% formic acid in acetonitrile. Ions were formed by electrospray ionization and analysed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), operated in a data-dependent mode using HCD fragmentation.

The .raw data were analysed using Byonic v.5.1.1 (Protein Metrics) to identify peptides and infer proteins. A concatenated FASTA file containing UniProt X. Laevis proteins, bait sequences and other likely contaminants and impurities was used to generate an in silico peptide library. Proteolysis with trypsin/LysC was assumed to be fully specific. The precursor and fragment ion tolerances were set to 12 ppm. Cysteine alkylated with propionamide was set as a fixed modification in the search. Variable modifications included oxidation on methionine, dioxidation on tryptophan, N-terminal acetylation, and cyclization of glutamine and glutamic acid. Proteins were held to a false-discovery rate of 1% using the standard reverse-decoy technique69.

Xenopus adult tissues were dissected on ice and washed thoroughly with ice-cold 1× PBS. Tissues collected from female animals included heart, liver, spleen and lung. Ice-cold RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitor was added at a ratio of 50 mg tissue per ml of lysis buffer. Tissues were finely minced using scissors and incubated at 4 °C for 1 h with vigorous vortexing every 10 min. After lysis, the samples were centrifuged at 16,000g for 20 min at 4 °C. The clarified supernatants were collected, and total protein concentrations were determined using a BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein were resolved by SDS–PAGE and analysed by western blotting using a Xenopus PRIMPOL antibody.

Labelling of purified human His6–SNAP–PRIMPOL was performed using SNAP-Surface Alexa Fluor 647 (NEB, S9136S). A 1.5-fold molar excess of dye relative to the protein was added and incubated overnight at 4 °C with gentle end-over-end rotation. The reaction mixture was aliquoted, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Labelled PRIMPOL was used directly in single-molecule assays without further purification.

Purified X. laevis His6–s6–PCNA was fluorescently labelled using in-house purified SFP synthase (surfactin phosphopantetheinyl transferase) and LD655–CoA (purchased from Lumidyne Technologies). S6–PCNA, SFP synthase and LD655–CoA were mixed at a molar ratio of 1:2:10 and incubated at room temperature for 1 h in reaction buffer containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 60 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 10% glycerol. The reaction mixture was further purified using the FPLC-Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 29091596) to separate unreacted fluorophore and SFP from PCNA–LD655. The peak fractions containing PCNA–LD655 were pooled and concentrated.

Protein co-IP assays were performed using anti-Flag M2 Magnetic Beads (Millipore, M8823). Flag-tagged SNAP–hPRIMPOL(1–60) proteins (WT or mutants) were purified as described above and immobilized on Flag beads before incubation with Xenopus egg extracts. For each reaction, 3 µl of beads (binding capacity of around 20 pmol Flag peptide) was incubated with 200 pmol of Flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL(1–60) protein (tenfold molar excess relative to bead capacity). Xenopus egg extracts were prepared by mixing NPE and HSS at a 1:1 ratio and diluting fivefold in 1× ELB-sucrose buffer. Beads were then incubated with Xenopus extract for 1 h at room temperature with gentle rotation to allow co-IP of interacting proteins. After incubation, beads were washed with 1× ELB-sucrose containing 0.05% NP-40. Bound proteins were eluted by resuspending beads in SDS sample buffer and boiled at 98 °C for 5 min. Beads were pelleted by brief centrifugation, and only the supernatants were collected for analysis. Eluted proteins and input samples were resolved by SDS–PAGE and analysed by western blotting with the indicated antibodies.

To measure fork restart after replicative stress, cells were first pulsed with 50 μM 5-chloro-2′-deoxyuridine (CldU; Sigma-Aldrich, C6891) for 20 min, irradiated with UV-C (30 J m−2) and, after a 30 min recovery time, pulse-labelled with 250 μM 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine (IdU; Sigma-Aldrich, I7125) for 20 min. Cells were collected in ice-cold PBS, resuspended at 0.3 × 106 cells per ml and lysed on microscope slides with spreading buffer (0.2 M Tris pH 7.4, 50 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS; 6 min at room temperature). DNA fibre spreads were prepared by tilting the slides 15° after cell lysis. The slides were air-dried and fixed in cold methanol:acetic acid (3:1) for 2 min, and incubated in 3 M HCl (30 min at room temperature) to denature DNA. CldU and IdU tracks were detected by immunofluorescence using anti-BrdU monoclonal antibodies with different specificity (rat monoclonal antibody, Abcam, ab6326, for CldU; BD Biosciences mouse monoclonal antibody, 347580, for IdU). The DNA fibre integrity was assessed using a mouse monoclonal anti-ssDNA antibody (DSHB, AB10805144); all incubations were for 1 h at room temperature in a humidity chamber. Standard secondary antibodies were used (anti-mouse IgG1 AF-488, Invitrogen, A21121; anti-rat IgG AF-594, Invitrogen, A11007; anti-mouse IgG2a AF-647, Invitrogen, A21241; all incubations were 30 min at room temperature). The slides were mounted with ProLong Gold antifade reagent (Invitrogen, P36930). Images were acquired on the DM6000B Leica microscope with an HCX PL APO ×40/0.75 NA objective and analysed with ImageJ. For functional complementation assays, HCT116 PRIMPOL-KO cells were transfected with pcDNA3.1/V5-PRIMPOL plasmids expressing the WT form or the indicated mutant derivative (DED, 3A and 29-35:Linker), using Lipofectamine 2000. n = 4 replicates (WT, PRIMPOL KO, PRIMPOL KO + WT) or n = 3 replicates (PRIMPOL KO + DED, PRIMPOL KO + 3A, PRIMPOL KO + 29-35:Linker). 500 replicative structures were counted in each condition and replicate.

Nikon Elements AR (v.5.20.02) was used to acquire raw microscopy data. ImageJ Fiji (v.2.1.0) was used to stabilize the raw microscopy videos and to quantify signals from autoradiographs and western blots. MATLAB (R2023b) and Origin (2023b) were used to analyse the data. All figures (including cartoons) were created and laid out in Microsoft PowerPoint for Mac (v.16.113.2).

Details of the statistical analyses performed are indicated in the figure legends. As some quantities measured in this study did not have symmetric distributions, we reported the median of the distribution. Unless otherwise specified in the figure captions, error bars represent the 95% CIs for the median. This was calculated using MATLAB’s built in bootstrapping function. The exact meaning of the number ‘n’ reported in each figure is indicated in the figure captions, it usually refers to the number of the number of replication forks or the number of binding events. For single-molecule experiments, we typically used n ≈ 100 events to report. No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample size. No data blinding or randomization was used. P values were computed using the two-sample two-tailed Kolmogorov–Smirnov test function built into MATLAB, and all experiments were repeated at least twice, with independent extract preparations. For the ensemble DNA replication assay, co-IP assays and cell-based fibre assays, we carried out 3 or 4 independent replicates. P values were computed using the two-sample two-tailed Student t-test function built into MATLAB. The data presented in the Figures are derived from one of the replicates. The exact P values for all data presented in the Figures and the Extended Data Figures are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Each replication initiation experiment imaged 4–10 FOVs over the course of 60–90 min with a resolution of 15, 30 or 60 s per frame. Each FOV typically contained 50–200 DNA molecules stretched to 80–90% of their contour length. A suite of MATLAB scripts written in house were used to select and analyse data as described in our recent methods article70. Below we summarize the data analysis pipeline specific for the single-molecule experiments analysed in this study.

Regions of interest corresponding to individual DNA molecules were selected manually based on the previews of DNA stained with SYTOX Orange (these were acquired before the start of the experiment). Only well-separated DNA molecules were used in the analysis.

To measure fork speed before/after the PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we fit the GINS (Fig. 1) or RPA (Fig. 2 and Fig. 4) signals with a linear model (mock + buffer, mock + 10 µM APH, ∆Polα + buffer conditions), a bilinear model (∆Pol α + PRIMPOL, leading-strand DNA lesion + buffer) or a trilinear model (leading-strand DNA lesion + PRIMPOL) in MATLAB and extracted the slope of each linear fit (this has units of pixels per frame). To calculate the fork speed, we multiplied the slope of each linear fit segment to 160 nm per pixel (the size of our camera’s pixel), and divided it by 0.34 nm per bp (to convert nanometres into base pairs), and further divided it by 0.85 (to account for the fact that the DNA template is stretched to around 85% of its contour length).

In Fig. 4, PRIMPOL-mediated CMG-independent fork restart was monitored by FEN1–KikG signal. To measure the speed of DNA synthesis during CMG-independent restart, the raw FEN1 signal was automatically thresholded using OTSU’s method using a built-in MATLAB function. The OTSU threshold binary image was used to fit straight lines to the edges of the growing FEN1 signal, and the fork speed value was extracted from the slope of the line (accounting for pixel size, the time resolution of the experiment and the extent to which DNA was stretched). Note that the efficiency of CMG-dependent and CMG-independent restart can add up to more than 1. This is illustrated in Fig. 4a, which contains two replication forks: both forks restarted in a CMG-dependent manner (white arrows), and there were two additional CMG-independent restart events (white asterisks).

To analyse the binding and dissociation (Δt1) of PRIMPOL–AF647, we used the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) as described in our previously study71. Specifically, we used GLRT to convert single-molecule images into binary images, which were subsequently segmented into binding events. The GLRT algorithm accounts for the intrinsic properties of noise in each experiment—a sliding window (we used a five-pixel window) is used to determine whether the signal at any pixel represents noise or signal. Using GLRT, we determined the time of PRIMPOL binding and PRIMPOL dissociation (and therefore Δt1) before a fork-restart event. To calculate the time delay between PRIMPOL–AF647 dissociation and fork restart (Δt2), we first measured the time of PRIMPOL–AF647 dissociation (as described above for Δt1), and the time of fork restart. The time of fork restart was extracted from the bilinear fit to the edge of the RPA signal (Fig. 2a): fork restart corresponds to the changepoint when the fork suddenly speeds up.

To measure the location and duration of PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events, we used the GLRT method as described above. To determine whether any given PRIMPOL–AF647 binding event is fork-proximal or fork distal, we compared the position of the binding event along the DNA molecule with the position of the replication fork measured by fitting the fluorescent RPA tract (as illustrated in Fig. 2a). Any PRIMPOL–AF647 binding event within 1 pixel of the replication fork was classified as fork-proximal, and all other binding events were classified as fork-distal.

To quantify the frequency of fork-proximal binding events across different conditions (no RS and RS), or for different PRIMPOL constructs (WT, AxA mutant or RPA-interaction mutant), we measured (1) Nproximal, the number of fork-proximal PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events for each fork; and (2) Tfork, the total duration that we observed that replication fork. We divided Nproximal by Tfork to obtain the normalized quantity shown in Fig. 2d.

We chose a different normalization strategy for fork-distal PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events because they can occur anywhere along RPA-coated ssDNA. To this end, for each replication fork we measured (1) Ndistal, the number of fork-distal binding events; (2) LRPA–ssDNA, the extent of the RPA-coated ssDNA; and (3) Tfork, the total duration of time that the fork was monitored. We divided Ndistal by LRPA–ssDNA and Tfork to obtain the normalized quantity shown in Fig. 2e.

All newly generated reagents generated in this study are available on request from the corresponding author.

Raw data and custom analysis code generated for this study have been deposited to the Stanford Digital Repository and are publicly available (https://doi.org/10.25740/hy921dn6469). All other data supporting the findings of this study are available in the Article and its Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.

(a) Representative immunoblots of Xenopus egg extracts used in this study: High Speed Supernatant (HSS) and Nucleo-Plasmic Extract (NPE). Untagged Xenopus PRIMPOL expressed via wheat-germ IVTT (In Vitro Transcription/Translation) was used as a positive control. Two polyclonal antibodies raised against non-overlapping antigens from Xenopus PRIMPOL were used for immunoblotting. Although the predicted molecular weight of Xenopus PRIMPOL is ~77 kDa, IVTT-expressed Xenopus PRIMPOL migrated closer to ~95 kDa. No band of that molecular weight was detected in either HSS or NPE. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (b) A representative immunoblots of egg extracts (HSS and NPE) compared to lysates from adult frog tissues (heart, liver, spleen, and lung) known to express PRIMPOL (according to XenBase). The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (c) Coomassie-stained gel of purified human PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, and PRIMPOLΔRPA (quadruple point mutant D519R, F522A, D551R, I554A). (d) Diagram of in vitro primase-polymerase assay for PRIMPOL. SYBR Green I was used to detect DNA synthesis by recombinant PRIMPOL on a linear ssDNA template. This assay does not contain RPA or any other replication factors. The plot shows the enzymatic activity of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, and PRIMPOLΔRPA measured using this assay, error-bars represent the standard deviation from three independent experiments. Note that 15 μM of aphidicolin (APH) does not impair PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity. (e) Three representative kymograms showing GINSLD655 (orange) and FEN1kikG (blue) dynamics in mock-depleted extract supplemented with 10 µM aphidicolin and 30 nM PRIMPOLWT. No fork restart events were observed under these conditions, likely because aphidicolin inhibited DNA synthesis by replicative polymerases. (f) Biological replicates of fork restart efficiency measured with two different extract preparations. Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of replication forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05 and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (g) Two representative kymograms showing RPAmCherryXL (green), PCNALD655 (red), and wild-type FEN1KikG (blue) binding to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLWT. (h) Two representative kymograms showing RPAmCherryXL (green), PCNALD655 (red), and FFAA-FEN1KikG (blue) binding to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLWT. FFAA is a FEN1 mutant (F343A/F344A) whose interaction with PCNA has been disrupted. (i) Fork restart efficiency calculated from the experiments shown in panels (g) and (h). RPAmCherryXL signal was used to identify fork restart events, defined by a transition in the RPA growth rate from slow to fast. Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test.

(a) Diagram of single-molecule experiments with site-specific leading-strand DNA lesions. Top: a 30-kb DNA molecule containing DNA-Protein Crosslinks (DPCs) positioned ~10 kb away from each end was digested with ProteinaseK, leaving behind small (~4 aa) peptide adducts. If a replication origin fires in the middle of this DNA substrate, both replication forks will encounter the peptide adduct on the leading-strand template, resulting in CMG uncoupling. Bottom: a representative kymogram illustrating CMG uncoupling from both peptide adducts. This experiment was performed in extract supplemented with 30 nM PRIMPOLWT, which promoted fork restart at ~50% of uncoupled CMGs. (b) Biological replicates of CMG speed distributions measured with two different extract preparations. Blue lines indicate median values; shaded boxes represent 95% CI estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of replication forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05 and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (c) A representative immunoblots of samples from the experiment in Fig. 1j. Reaction mixture samples were collected at the 45-min timepoint. A trace amount of endogenous PolA1 (<1% of the total amount) evaded the immunodepletion. (d) A representative immunoblots of chromatin-bound proteins from a chromatin fractionation experiment with mock-depleted and Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with buffer or 30 nM of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, or PRIMPOLΔRPA. (e) A representative immunoblots of chromatin-bound proteins from a chromatin fractionation experiment in undepleted extract supplemented with DMSO or 100 μM of aphidicolin. Reactions were also supplemented with buffer or 30 nM of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, or PRIMPOLΔRPA as indicated. In (d) and (e) chromatin was first licensed in HSS for 30 min, then NPE was added to the reaction, samples were collected at 60 min after NPE addition, and chromatin was fractionated by centrifugation and washed 2 times to remove any unbound proteins. For (c-e), the experiments were repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data.

(a) A representative fluorescence image of recombinant PRIMPOL labelled with increasing amounts of SNAP-Surface® Alexa Fluor® 647 (SNAPAF647) compared to a serial titration of a known standard (GINSAF647, where the PSF3 subunit is fluorescently labelled). A 1.5x molar ratio of SNAPAF647 to PRIMPOL was used to label all protein preps employed in this study. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (b) A representative gel image showing the results of the plasmid replication assay comparing DNA synthesis in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled PRIMPOLWT or 30 nM fluorescently labelled PRIMPOLWT-AF647. #1379. Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history

Eighteen years ago, Bournemouth were minutes away from being liquidated and playing in the fourth tier. On Thursday night, Bournemouth not only welcomed AC Milan in Europe; they did so as favourites, and then pummelled them.

When Amine Adli curled in an 84-minute free-kick with his left foot at the Vitality Stadium, it put the seal on the most extraordinary evening in Bournemouth’s history. On a brutally windy and wet night, Bournemouth trounced AC Milan 3-0.

Amine Adli with a SUPERB free-kick to give Bournemouth a 3-0 lead vs AC Milan 🚀 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/KX5i5oM3TG

Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

Amine Adli with a SUPERB free-kick to give Bournemouth a 3-0 lead vs AC Milan 🚀 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/KX5i5oM3TG

Thirty-one years ago, Patrick Kluivert scored against AC Milan in Europe. If his son Justin’s eighth-minute penalty will not receive the acclaim of Patrick’s winner for Ajax in the 1995 Champions League final, the goal will be etched in Bournemouth’s hearts.

After Evanilson’s header from a corner struck Koni De Winter’s hand, a VAR review led to Bournemouth being awarded a penalty. Kluivert eyed up Mike Maignan, and waited for the goalkeeper to dive before nonchalantly stroking the ball into the unguarded left corner.

Bournemouth lead against AC Milan in a European competition! 🍒 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1BQt3wKSr9

And so Bournemouth were beating AC Milan, a scenario that would have seemed unfathomable for vast swathes of these two clubs’ existence. Even more extraordinary was how deserved the goal was: both Kluivert and Evanilson had already spurned opportunities, with Milan seeming overwhelmed by Bournemouth’s intensity.

Watching his side lack any coherence in their passing, Ruben Amorim rapidly came to look as ghoulish as in his last days at Old Trafford. Or, indeed, Michael Carrick in Como 24 hours earlier.

Amorim swiftly had cause to become more irate. Just as Milan had threatened to regain a semblance of control, Maignan inexplicably pushed Tyler Adams in the face when Bournemouth had a corner. VAR had no reason to give Maignan a reprieve from his red card, and Bournemouth’s ensuing penalty.

Bournemouth were 2-0 and a man up within 32 minutes; AC Milan were collapsing like the Dow Jones Industrial Average in 1929.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1378. Lots to work on but Pocognoli firmly believes Scotland ARE on the right track under his stewardship

Published: 18:44 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 19:02 EST, 13 November 2026

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli admitted his side were far from perfect in their Nations League win over North Macedonia – but he believes they ARE moving in the right direction under his stewardship.

The victory puts the Scots one point behind second-placed Slovenia in Group B1, ahead of Monday’s trip to runaway leaders Switzerland.

John McGinn notched a second-half double to secure a hard-earned second win of this campaign and Pocognoli’s first in front of the Hampden crowd.

‘We knew before the game that it [a win] will help to build a winning culture,’ he said. ‘And would make the work through the week end with a good feeling.

‘In terms of what we produced on the pitch, I know exactly what we worked on this week. I’m quite satisfied about what I see in some moments of the game, about the work on the ball and off the ball.

‘It was not always perfect but we created a lot of chances that we should score and maybe have a better feeling of the game.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his Hampden win as Scots boss after a 2-1 win over North Macedonia

Stalwarts John McGinn (left) and Andy Robertson applaud the Hampden crowd at full-time

‘Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive. We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

‘We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that’s a new approach of the game.

‘We created chances and we had a lot of pressure in the side of Macedonia. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for five minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus. So, it’s something that we need to fix.’

Asked whether his side need to be more clinical, Pocognoli added: ‘Yes, probably. But I prefer to talk about this with creating a lot of chances. We should score two or three. And probably we should have kept a clean sheet. So that’s really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect.

‘But it’s part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.’

Talisman McGinn put the Scots ahead on 54 minutes before Elmin Rastoder headed the visitors level against the run of play shortly after, with McGinn then stepping up to convert what turned out to be the winning penalty after a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak with 16 to play.

The Aston Villa midfielder has now taken his tally to 24 for the international team – just six behind legends Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law.

His manager is confident that it is only a matter of time before the 32-year-old is standing alone as his nation’s top scorer, and believes McGinn will have plenty of opportunities to smash the record playing in his team.

John McGinn scored from the penalty spot to clinch an unconvincing victory

He said: ‘I’m more focused on the collective challenge and goals. And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record.

‘We created a lot of chances through these five [Nations League] games together. The individual record is important, but I always focus on the collective package.’

McGinn admitted that chasing the record is in the back of his mind and stressed his relief that he’s back among the goals after a lean spell at international level.

‘It’s been something that’s been in the back of my head, but obviously the results haven’t been the way we’ve wanted,’ said McGinn.

‘The team come first, but whether it’s myself, Scottie (McTominay), Che (Adams), anyone that’s going on the scoresheet at the minute, we’ll take it.

‘It’s been a bit of a dry patch for me over the past year or two on the goal front, so I’m delighted to get back on that trail and hopefully the same again Monday.

‘I feel good. I’ve still got many years to go, but the first priority is getting Scotland back to another major tournament and we’ll take it from there.’

#1377. Named: Premier League team of the season so far as Erling Haaland, THREE Chelsea players and a surprise addition from Sunderland make the cut

Published: 02:00 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 04:56 EST, 14 November 2026

The international break has rolled back around and with it a chance to take stock of the Premier League season so far.

The first ten games of the new campaign have thrown up a few surprises – none of three  promoted teams find themselves in the drop zone at this stage and the race for Europe is wide open with teams such as Brighton and Everton excelling.

Here is a look at the players who have defined the opening weeks as Daily Mail Sport, in collaboration with stats gurus Sofascore, compile our team of the season so far...

Many will be surprised to see the Argentine's name here instead of Arsenal's David Raya or Brighton's Bart Verbruggen, but despite Chelsea's defensive woes it is their £7million summer signing that makes the cut.

Martinez has been out for the last three games after sustaining a nasty head injury away at Everton but his average match rating remains the highest out of all the division's shot-stoppers.

A look at the stats tells you why. Despite only keeping one clean sheet so far, Chelsea's new No1 has prevented 1.64 goals, had 13 high claims and 0 errors leading to goals.

The big man has also looked extremely competent with the ball at his feet, something that Blues keepers have struggled with in previous years, and has even created three chances from his own box so far this season.

Emiliano Martinez has been out for three weeks with a head injury he sustained at Everton but has still done enough to make our team

There was always going to have to be at least one of this Brighton team in our XI. We all knew they were an excellent outfit coming into the season but perhaps even Fabian Hurzeler  may not have envisaged his side sitting second after ten games.

The linchpin of this side has of course been their skipper, Lewis Dunk. A local boy who came through the ranks at Brighton and has spent virtually his entire career at the club, he continues to impress at 34 years of age.

Dunk has played in nine of Brighton's ten games this season looking solid in each, leading his side to six wins and keeping a clean sheet in each victory. And his personal defensive stats make for excellent reading as well – he has won 22 aerial duels and registered 31 recoveries already this season.

But there are some things that can't be quantified, such as Dunk's impact on the  Brighton dressing room and the guidance he gives such a young squad which must be immense – after all, he is a year older than his own manager.

Next up is another old school English centre-half who has captained his team to an excellent start to the season.

The big man is rolling back the years as the Toffees look to push for Europe

In recent years the Toffees have become far more familiar with the bottom of the table than the top but at present are making a serious push for the European places and are currently in sixth place, level on points with fifth.

And the 33-year-old has been vital to David Moyes's new system, providing stability and strength to a defence that has conceded just ten goals – with only Arsenal (five), Brighton (seven) and Leeds (eight) conceding fewer.

Again similar to Dunk, Tarkowski's stats show the veteran's ability to adapt to the demands of the modern game, having 108 line-breaking passes, creating four chances and one big chance so far this season.

The skipper has also come up trumps in close games, bagging a crucial goal in a 1-1 draw at Bournemouth and getting an assist in the 1-0 win over Ipswich.

Completing the back three is the only one out under 30, but is also the man with the highest average match rating in this team.

Considering Tottenham's defensive record this season, one of their defenders making it in may come as a bit of a shock but anyone that has watched the north Londoners this season will know that 26-year-old Van Hecke is hardly the reason for their woes.

The Dutchman has been magnificent since moving from Brighton and reuniting with his old boss Roberto De Zerbi, playing every single minute of the Premier League season so far.

Van Hecke epitomises the modern centre-half, having the second most one-line breaking passes (162), the most two-line breaking passes (37) and the most passes into the final third (138) out of any player in the league – and has even bagged two goals for Spurs as they have started to pick up some form.

Despite Sunderland's poor start, the Black Cats' skipper anchors our midfield with the highest average match rating in his position this campaign. Most would have been expecting Pascal Gross to take this position in an XI such as this considering his eight goals and assists and all-round stellar showing this season.

Xhaka is a surprise entry considering Sunderland's form but the stats tell us that the skipper is still performing

But the boffins have Xhaka here instead and the numbers show why. The Swiss international has excelled in a number of areas despite Sunderland's faltering start having the second-most passes into the final third (132) and the joint most line-breaking passes into the box (21).

Moving onto the midfield, we have perhaps the most electrifying winger in the league  this season.

Manchester City have tailed off with three defeats on the spin but Jeremy Doku still remains a major source of headaches for the league's full-backs and a full-time entertainer for us viewers.

When he first joined the league the Belgian was criticised for a lack of consistency but recently he appears to have put that all behind him. Doku does only have one goal and one assist this season, but that does not tell the full story.

He has completed the most dribbles in the league this season (27), won nearly 60 per cent of his duels and has created 4.25xG while on the pitch.

He also provided us with arguably the performance of the season so far when he changed the game off the bench away at Liverpool, scoring a goal-of-the-season contender to down the Reds.

The first and only man from the champions and league leaders to get into our team is Bukayo Saka.

Saka appears to be getting back to his best as the champions get off to an excellent start in their title defence

It was always going to be hard for the man the fans call 'Starboy' to keep up his form from last season but in actual fact his desire to bring more silverware to the Emirates appears more prevalent than ever.

We all know what he can do going forward and the Englishman has netted three goals in the league, but this year he has improved his defensive game massively, winning 43 duels, 11 tackles and registering 23 recoveries already.

Saka has struggled with his fitness for the past year or so and although he has played their first seven Premier League games, has been on the sidelines since mid-October with a thigh injury.

Despite a testing start to the season, Chelsea are the team with the most players to make the list – though few will quibble with this man's inclusion.

Morgan Rogers proved himself to be a special talent at Aston Villa and there won't be many Chelsea fans doubting the wisdom of paying £117million for his services after his flying start.

Morgan Rogers has been a revelation at the bridge thus far, scoring six goals in all competitions and assisting five more

The Englishman has lit up Stamford Bridge with six goals and five assists in all competitions and has instantly formed a deadly front three with best friend Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro.

The Blues have struggled for form under new manager Xabi Alonso but no criticism can be laid at the feet of Rogers who will hope his goals can bring some much-needed consistency to west London.

Completing the midfield is a man who is finally getting his flowers after months of quality and consistency. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall is one of the many reasons Everton fans are excited for the first time in a while.

The Englishman became an instant fan favourite at the Hill Dickinson after moving from Chelsea last year but this season has gone up a gear in every way, running  games from start to finish with surgical passing, clever dribbling and an incredible work rate.

Only seven players have covered more ground in the league than his 101km (63 miles), and he has also contributed three goals and an assist – as well as delivering a magnificent 79 defensive contributions. His spot in this team could not be more deserved.

Going into the strike-force these next two names are simply must haves, and the first of the two is the mercurial Joao Pedro.

Joao Pedro has the best goals and assists ratio to games in the league with eight in six games

After an excellent debut season in blue the Brazilian took the risk of taking on the infamously cursed Chelsea No9 shirt. But it appears to have only spurred him on further as he has enjoyed a  stellar start to the campaign in front of goal.

It only took him two minutes to get on the score sheet this season in Chelsea's opening game away to Fulham and he just hasn't stopped scoring since.

Pedro has five goals and three assists in just six Premier League games and has become a menace for opposition defences. Unfortunately for gaffer Xabi Alonso his side have been unable to match that consistency, having won five, drawn one and lost four in the league.

But the Spaniard will hope to have his star man back soon – in the six games Pedro has managed to play this season the Blues have lost just one.

It would not be an elite Premier League XI without this man in it.

Even with all the controversy surrounding Manchester City, Erling Haaland manages to roar on and continue scoring at an alarming rate. It is yet another season where he props up the Premier League goal scoring table with nine in ten games.

For a  City side in transition away from a decade under Pep Guardiola Haaland's goals this season have been so crucial in smoothing the process and getting important wins.

The big Norwegian has bagged winners against rivals Manchester United, Ipswich and Coventry as well as netting the vital opener in their 3-0 win at Anfield. Yet again,  he is proving he is the ultimate goal machine.
