#1366. So much pace and potential, not enough positive impact... surely Scotland must now redefine the role of Ben Gannon-Doak?

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:14 EST, 14 November 2026

In an age where much of the football on show in the English Premier League is so robotic as to be almost unwatchable, flashes of individual brilliance are increasingly becoming things to be cherished.

Across his time at Liverpool and Bournemouth, Ben Gannon-Doak has sporadically distinguished himself as someone who can light up a game by doing something out of the blue and out of the ordinary.

As many a defender will testify, that electric burst of pace across a short distance makes him unplayable at times. He has an X-factor which sets him apart from the crowd.

What a shame that injuries have restricted his number of appearances to this point. Since moving south from Celtic in 2022, including a loan spell with Middlesbrough, Gannon-Doak has played fewer than 50 times.

At the very time in his career when he could have done with smoothing off the rough edges, he’s spent far too long rehabilitating from one setback or another.

In the build-up to Friday’s match with North Macedonia, Sebastien Pocognoli spoke about how encouraged he was that the player was finally seeing more game time on the south coast, partly as a result of the team’s maiden voyage in Europe.

Ben Gannon-Doak started in a right wing-back role and had an energetic yet frustrating night

The hope of all concerned was that the recent run of matches which the winger had so evidently needed would translate into a more accomplished display in a Scotland jersey. Alas, this proved to be wishful thinking.

Even against very ordinary opposition, Gannon-Doak’s display proved to be another frustrating watch for the Tartan Army.

Time and time again, he brought them to the edge of their seats by facing up a white jersey and seemingly disappearing in a puff of smoke towards the line. Rarely, however, did the end product materialise.

For a winger with such blinding speed to continually struggle with the all-important final ball is a difficult thing to repeatedly witness.

We shall never know, of course, if the player’s crossing ability would be better by this stage if he hadn’t endured such wretched luck with injuries. But you suspect it’s now just about as good as it’s ever going to be.

The trouble for Pocognoli is that the quality of the delivery from wing-backs into the penalty box is arguably the most important facet of his preferred 3-4-3 system.

When it breaks down, as it did so often against the group outsiders, the whole thing threatens to grind to a halt.

Gannon-Doak's crossing remains an area of concern for Scotland given his wide position

On his record-equalling 102nd cap, Andy Robertson was also guilty of being wasteful on the other flank. Given we know what the skipper has delivered down the years, though, we can write that off as merely a bad night at the office.

The difference with Gannon-Doak is that we’ve rarely seen him tear it up on the flank in a Scotland jersey. So much pace and potential. Not enough positive outcomes when it comes to delivering crosses. In 21 matches, he has three assists and one goal. Those aren’t great numbers.

Just how long do you persevere with a player who doesn’t look to have the requisite skill set for such a specialised and vital position?

Aaron Hickey clearly doesn’t have the pace of the man who he replaced late on, yet he’s hardly a slouch. He is, though, more switched on defensively. And he does know how to cross a football.

It was telling that Gannon-Doak’s most positive contribution of the night against the group outsiders came when he left his station to move infield and take Oli McBurnie’s pass in his stride with the score standing at one-apiece.

His surge towards the goal initially looked like it had been hampered by a heavy touch only for VAR to correctly identify that he’d been impeded by the goalkeeper. He earned his corn in that moment.

John McGinn’s conversion from 12 yards, his second goal of the night, spared Pocognoli’s blushes after a display which didn’t exactly inspire.

That sequence of play certainly raised the possibility that Gannon-Doak could be utilised to better effect in another role.

Gannon-Doak's forward burst led to the award of a penalty and hinted at an alternative role

If played more centrally, his crossing – undoubtedly his weak spot – would not be such an issue. But the acceleration and driving runs would still be there to cause chaos in and around the penalty box. That will always be his strong suit.

To get the best out of him, maybe the manager needs to redefine him.

Any redeployment would, obviously, create another issue. If Pocognoli remains wedded to the current system, it seems likely that Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson will occupy the two holding berths.

Ahead of them, and behind the main striker, McGinn and Scott McTominay are virtually undroppable. It might be the case then, that Gannon-Doak is eventually utilised as an impact sub. Yet, it would not be a plan without its merits.

He’s got a part to play in this set-up. Probably just not where he’s currently being positioned.

You’d be surprised, frankly, if he started in St Gallen on Monday. Switzerland are a far superior side to North Macedonia, already assured of promotion to League A by topping the section and looking to end this campaign with a flourish against a Scotland side they beat comfortably at Hampden.

They’ll ask far more questions of Pocognoli’s side. It feels like a task more suited to Hickey.

Scotland, collectively, will need to buck up their ideas if they are to stand any chance of emerging with a positive outcome or, at the least, some credit.

Scotland fans are desperate to see Gannon-Doak succeed but a little change might be needed

There was a flatness to Friday’s performance, especially in a first half in which the much-vaunted high-press was conspicuous by its absence.

The passing was too safe and predictable. The tempo was low and the play was unimaginative. By half-time, the visitors had fashioned the better chance when Enis Bardhi smashed the ball into the side net.

Scotland were markedly better after the turnaround. After Billy Gilmour’s scarcely believable miss, they were deserving of the opener which came when McGinn burst into the box and lashed home after fine work from Che Adams.

Stemming straight from a corner, North Macedonia’s equaliser – which ended their eight-game goal drought – asked a serious question of Pocognoli’s players.

To their credit, they stepped up with Gannon-Doak’s foray into the box causing the moment of indecision on which the game swung.

The manner of a first Hampden win for Pocognoli won’t live long in the memory. The fervent hope is that it proves to be the start of something.

#1364. Mauricio Pochettino leaves behind a negligible legacy at USMNT... where raised standards never materialized into results as tearful Argentine bolts for Man United

Published: 13:29 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:42 EST, 14 November 2026

Perhaps it's incredibly cynical, and maybe too harsh, to call the tears that fell down the face of Mauricio Pochettino 'performative.' But it's the first word that came to mind – followed by 'surprising' and 'a bit much.'

It was only four months ago when the Argentine who had been atop the United States' men's national team since 2024 signed a contract extension to stay on board for another four years.

'We want to try to have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field,' Pochettino said when his contract was signed.

Yet, after a few months and one international window, that experiment to make a 'lasting impact' has ended. Pochettino may have cried because he fell in love with the country, but it's not like he got fired. Instead, he's off to lead one of the world's greatest football brands in Manchester United.

So now the question turns to the legacy Pochettino leaves behind. Plenty of American soccer writers and fans point to the spirit the former Chelsea boss created and how he helped to energize a team which had been bogged down by past coaches.

But Pochettino's results don't scream success. The World Cup finish was nothing special compared to his peers, his record against the best nations the USA faced was poor and he'll leave as the first full-time USMNT manager in nearly 30 years to not win at least one trophy.

Mauricio Pochettino cried as he left the United States' top job for Manchester United

Pochettino's USMNT played exciting football, but ultimately didn't progress past the norm

But any potential for further growth evaporated when the Argentine returned to England

By all accounts, the greatest thing Pochettino did was install a hungry, all-in-or-nothing culture in a team bogged down by an earth-rocking scandal and a poor 2024 Copa America run.

But he did so in a way that often left the biggest players of the USMNT system behind. Rather than keep a consistent core of his best players around, he seemed intent on tinkering with the lineup in each window.

The results reflect that instability. Leading to the World Cup, Pochettino played 12 games against sides in the top 30 of the FIFA World Rankings. He won just three fixtures – drawing once and losing the remaining eight.

All the while, he was linked to returns to Europe. Pochettino may have said in his exit press conference that he 'never said I wanted to go back to the Premier League' but the Premier League certainly wanted him – especially Tottenham.

Come World Cup time, Pochettino's team finally seemed to gel with a scintillating style of play never before seen in the USMNT.

But it all crashed down after the Round of 32 game against Bosnia when Folarin Balogun's red card was (as this American will admit) deviously overturned. The noise and controversy led to the Americans' embarrassment at the hands of Belgium on home soil.

A summer of exciting soccer for the USMNT followed years of hard resets and mixed results

It all fell apart with a demolition by Belgium, leaving Pochettino without any success

The Yanks were not expected to go much further than the last 16. But branding Pochettino's time atop the USMNT a 'success' on the back of this World Cup performance is giving him too much credit – especially considering the four prior managers to take the US to the World Cup all made it to that stage of the tournament as well.

With his departure confirmed, Pochettino is the first USMNT manager to leave the post without any silverware since the 1998 departure of Steve Sampson, who hadn't been a professional manager before being appointed to the job.

Even though he achieved little in terms of results, players praised Pochettino's leadership and development skills, which shouldn't be ignored.

Middlesbrough midfielder Sebastian Berhalter said: 'He's meant so much to me and he's helped me develop as a player and as a person. And as a player, that's all you can ask for, to have that trust and have that belief in you.'

But not every player in the system was tripping over themselves to play under Poch. Just ask Christian Pulisic, who took the entire summer off in 2025 to rest before the World Cup – only to put up a goose egg in his home country.

Any hope for further progress under Pochettino evaporated when United came calling

All of this being said, there was reason for hope in the future. By re-signing Pochettino, the chance to cement that work ethic, culture and leadership presented itself.

With his extension, Pochettino had the chance to build a foundation in US Soccer to engender future success for decades to come.

Now, that's all gone. Now, Pochettino's time in charge will be remembered more for unfulfilled potential than culture shifting. After all, how do you expect to keep a culture if its chief architect leaves?

US Soccer now is faced with a quagmire of either hiring the biggest possible name again (Guardiola, if you believe the rumors) or hiring someone who will treat the position less like a stepping stone and more like a cornerstone.

It never seemed like Pochettino fully embraced the US, despite the tears on Friday. He'll be off for Old Trafford and a United squad bogged down by perpetual disappointment, all while leaving behind the biggest "What If" in the still-growing history of the American game.

#1363. Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1,2,3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

The physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions. Fragile or misshapen nuclei are hallmarks of cancer, cardiomyopathy and premature ageing4,5. Nuclei in stem cells gradually stiffen during differentiation4,5,6,7. While these changes are widely recognized as consequences of altered nuclear composition and chromatin dynamics, they also influence genome organization and transcription8,9,10. Despite the importance, the physical state of the nucleus at the earliest stages of mammalian development, when life begins, remains unclear.

During the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program. In mice, this transition occurs within the first approximately 48 h after fertilization and is associated with a surge in new transcript production, known as major zygotic gene activation (ZGA)11,12,13. Major ZGA occurs during the mid-to-late two-cell stage, and embryos that impair ZGA fail in subsequent development. Around the time of ZGA, chromatin exhibits distinct structural and biochemical changes accompanied by histone modifiers and transcription factors14,15. By contrast, whether the nucleus organizing chromatin undergoes any crucial changes that drive ZGA is not known. In somatic cells, nuclear shape and mechanics depend on lamins, which line the inner nuclear membrane16,17. Lamins are long-lived, enriched in eggs and are crucial for mammalian development18,19,20. Previous studies have documented that, of the two major types, A-type lamins exhibit cell-lineage-specific differential expression patterns, whereas B-type lamins are constitutively expressed throughout development16. However, their dynamics and transiency, as well as the underlying core regulatory mechanism, during the earliest embryonic stages are poorly understood. Likewise, how the nuclear lamina, which forms a structural meshwork, controls nuclear mechanics and genome dynamics during this critical transition is unknown. Investigating physical nuclear characteristics necessitates direct quantification and manipulation of their mechanical properties. However, achieving this without compromising cell viability poses a challenge.

To investigate physical nuclear properties, we first performed high-resolution confocal scanning of fertilized mouse eggs during early cleavages (Fig. 1a). Our three-dimensional (3D) images of nuclei with H2B–mCherry, expressed without perturbing development (Extended Data Fig. 1a), revealed their distinct shape features, showing uneven local deformation at the two-cell stage in contrast to their predominantly spherical appearance at the one-cell and four-cell stages (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Timelapse imaging revealed that one-cell nuclei remained spherical during the cell cycle (Fig. 1d). Two-cell nuclei underwent slow, incremental deformation, which started at around 21 h post-insemination (h.p.i.), peaked at 24–26 h.p.i. and then gradually regressed by 32–36 h.p.i. (Fig. 1e). At the four-cell stage, nuclei were again spherical (Fig. 1f) (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Videos 1−3). Before the onset of deformation, two-cell nuclei had fully swollen and reached steady sizes; once deformed, the altered nuclear shapes persisted for hours (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Similar deformation was observed using emerin–eGFP for the nuclear envelope (Fig. 1g) or mCherry–NLS for the nuclear interior (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

a, Schematic of early-stage mouse embryos. b,c, Representative 3D images of nuclei visualized using H2B–mCherry (b) and quantification of nuclear sphericity (c). F, female; M, male. d–f, Time courses of 2D nuclear deformation during the one-cell (d), two-cell (e) and four-cell stages (f). Live imaging was performed at 1 h intervals over around 52 h for n = 9 embryos; the mean (orange) and s.d. (shaded area) of nuclear deformation, calculated as shown in the inset in d, are plotted. g, Nuclear membranes were imaged using emerin–eGFP (green) and analysed for 2D nuclear deformation. The arrowheads indicate prominent deformation sites. h, Schematic of nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement. An embryo is held with a holding pipette, while a pressure-controlled nanocapillary captures and stretches the nucleus to measure nuclear elasticity and stiffness. i, Snapshots of nuclei subjected to the nanocapillary-based measurement (red, H2B–mCherry; overlay with bright field). Representative from four (8 and 24 h.p.i.) and two (48 h.p.i.) independent experiments. j–l, Maximal nuclear deformation (j), nuclear stiffness (k) and the degree of elasticity (l) analysed from experiments as in i. S0, Smax and Sr are as in i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For c, g and j–l, statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s-multiple comparisons test; the thick horizontal bars represent the mean values (red or black). Scale bars, 10 μm (b, g and i).

This finding prompted us to develop a biophysical setup that quantitatively characterizes the mechanical properties of early embryonic nuclei in situ (Fig. 1h). The setup equipped a pressure-controlled nanocapillary, of which the tip was inserted into a fertilized embryo to capture the nuclear surface. A weak, constant suction pressure (2.1 × 101 kPa) pinched the surface, which was then stretched through axial translocation of the nanocapillary. The nuclei could be gradually strained, resulting in tension, and the strain reached a maximum just before the detachment (Fig. 1i). The analysis could be performed from the one-cell to four-cell stages, over which the predominantly fluid-like cytoplasm minimally influenced the measured mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f). Measurements were also insensitive to nuclear markers and were comparable to label-free imaging results (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h).

Our analysis revealed that two-cell nuclei were significantly more deformable than one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1j). The deformable nature persisted throughout the cell cycle (from 21 to 32 h.p.i.) even as DNA doubled at about 24 h.p.i. Nuclear stiffness, as estimated based on the nanocapillary pressure and the extent of nuclear deformation, transiently lowered at the two-cell stage (one-cell, 5.0 ± 1.3 nN µm−1; two-cell, 2.0 ± 0.5 nN µm−1; four-cell, 4.6 ± 1.9 nN µm−1; n = 18, 38 and 13 embryos, respectively) (Fig. 1k). The stiffness values varied between male and female pronuclei (30.7 ± 21.3%, n = 8 pairs) and between blastomeres of each two-cell embryo (23.5 ± 14.5%, n = 16 pairs), while the differences were pronounced among the developmental stages (Extended Data Fig. 2i). Two-cell nuclei also exhibited significant plasticity, in contrast to more elastic one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1l) (shape recovery, 91.0 ± 4.3% for one-cell; 66.9 ± 8.0% for two-cell; and 87.9 ± 4.6% for four-cell). The deformable two-cell nuclear stiffness was consistent when embryos were examined using lower nanocapillary pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). An alternative capillary-based approach, using an incremental suction pressure that aspirated nuclei, yielded consistent results (n ≥ 12 embryos per stage) (Extended Data Fig. 2l–n). These corroborate the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus.

Our nanocapillary-based assay at 1.2 × 101 kPa minimally perturbed development, enabling us to relate two-cell nuclear stiffness with embryos’ developmental competence (Fig. 2a). We found that all fertilized embryos that timely reached the blastocyst stage had soft nuclei (2.0 ± 0.6 nN µm−1; n = 66 of 66 embryos), while nearly half of the embryos that impaired development had stiff nuclei (n = 7 of 15 embryos; defined as more than twice the mean nuclear stiffness of the normal development) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Detecting embryos with stiff nuclei was infrequent (8.6%; n = 7 out of 81 embryos). The outcome was regardless of the fluorescent tag type and marker expression levels (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). A similar mechanical feature was observed for cloned embryos created through somatic cell nuclear transfer (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,d,e) (n = 46 embryos). Thus, deformable two-cell nuclei are a signature of normal preimplantation development.

a, Schematic of the assay. Embryos prepared through in vitro fertilization or through somatic cell nuclear transfer were subjected to the nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement during the two-cell stage using a pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k), after which the embryos resumed standard culture. b, The relationship between two-cell nuclear stiffness and the frequency of development to the blastocyst stage at 96 h.p.i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For b, statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney U-tests (two-sided); the thick horizontal bars (red) represent the mean values.

We next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus. Using immunofluorescence, we first examined four major lamins, A/C, B1 and B2, and found that lamin B1 transiently cleared from the two-cell nuclear envelope, nearly paralleling nuclear softening (Fig. 3a,b). The clearance was rapid and substantial, with an approximately 70% decrease in peripheral signal during the early-to-mid two-cell stage (21 to 24 h.p.i.; Fig. 3b). Lamin A/C and B2 levels also changed, but their trends were gradual and monotonic, with only a minor decline, if any, during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Another nuclear envelope protein, Lap2β, also changed little (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Live-embryo imaging confirmed the clearance of lamin B1 from the two-cell nuclear envelope with a decay time constant of 86 ± 44 min (n = 5 embryos; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). An immunoblotting assay revealed a reduction in lamin B1 during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3d), suggesting degradation.

a, Immunofluorescence images of endogenous lamins in early embryos (h.p.i. are as in Fig. 1j–l). Representative images are shown from six independent experiments. Identical imaging conditions were used. b, Quantification of lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope from assays in a. c, Live-imaging data showing mEGFP–lamin B1 signals at the two-cell nuclear envelope, acquired under conditions that minimized photobleaching and phototoxicity. d, Immunoblotting of lysates from two-cell embryos for lamin B1; β-actin was used as the loading control. Two independent experiments with similar results. e, Diagrams of the lamin B1 constructs used in this study. Representative images are shown from three to five independent experiments. g, Quantification of lamins at the nuclear envelope from assays in f, analysed as in b. h, Developmental rates of embryos expressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ versus the non-injection control. i, Live-imaging analysis was performed to quantify mCherry-fused WT and mutant lamin B1 signals at the two-cell nuclear envelope. j, Colocalization of lamin B1 (red) with lysosomes (green) at 24 h.p.i. The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means (b, g, k and l). For c and i, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 10 μm (a, f and j). Source blot data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. Additional image data are provided in Extended Data Figs. 4c and 5a.

Our pilot assay using wortmannin implicated that autophagy promotes lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Autophagy is active in early embryos and is essential for preimplantation development21. In live-embryo imaging, the autophagy factor LC322 was diffusive at the one-cell stage and accumulated in the two-cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Our antibody microinjection targeting LC3 suppressed lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Cell cycle progression as monitored by EdU was normal (Extended Data Fig. 4g). We therefore designed a construct that interferes with the endogenous interaction between lamin B1 and LC3, using a short fragment of lamin B1 carrying LC3-binding domains and an intrinsic nuclear localization signal23 (hereafter, sfLB1; Fig. 3e). When expressed in embryos, this fragment was predominantly nucleoplasmic (Extended Data Fig. 4h), while a major autophagy substrate p62 maintained stable protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Our analysis revealed that the clearance of lamin B1 was suppressed by sfLB1, whereas lamin A/C and B2 remained largely unperturbed (Fig. 3f,g). An accumulation of lamin B1 was detectable in western blot analysis of lysates (Extended Data Fig. 4j). A sfLB1 variant (sfLB1Δ), which was nucleoplasmic but with abrogated LC3 binding23 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,k), had little influence on lamin B1 clearance (Fig. 3f,g). The development of embryos was impaired by sfLB1, but not by sfLB1Δ (Fig. 3h).

To understand the mechanistic basis of lamin B1 clearance, we constructed fluorescent reporters based on full-length lamin B1 fused to mCherry. Consistent with the results shown in Fig. 3a–c, the wild-type (WT) construct (flLB1wt; Fig. 3e) localized to the nuclear envelope and exhibited rapid lamin B1 clearance (T1/2 = 83 ± 44 min, n = 18) (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). The other three constructs carried mutations near or at an LC3-interacting region core motif (flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A)) or at the major N-terminal CDK1 phosphorylation site for nuclear-envelope breakdown24 (flLB1(S24A)) (Fig. 3e). These constructs also localized to the two-cell nuclear envelope (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Notably, the mutations that abrogated LC3 interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5b) suppressed the lamin B1 clearance, whereas the mutation at the CDK1 site did not prevent the clearance (Fig. 3i). The mutations in flLB1(5A) were at the site targeted for autophagic degradation of lamin B1 during oncogene-induced cell senescence23. The selectivity of lamin B1 over lamin A/C and B2 was also consistent with the phenomenon reported in senescent cells23.

Our assay further suggested that lamin B1 is degraded through an autophagy–lysosome pathway. This was confirmed by tracking the fate of flLB1wt and identifying its predominant lysosomal localization and formation of foci (n = 18 embryos; Fig. 3j,k). flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) localized much less to lysosomes (n = 12 and 14 embryos; Fig. 3j,k), while the numbers of lysosomes remained comparable (Fig. 3l). We did not observe prominent lamin-B1-positive structures bulging from the outer nuclear membrane23 nor an accumulation of lysosomes on the nuclear surface25 within the timescale examined. Collectively, our mechanistic view of lamin B1 clearance is shown in Fig. 3m.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 on two-cell nuclear stiffness. Nanocapillaries indicated that two-cell nuclei of which the envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1 were stiffer and less plastic than controls (4.2 ± 1.3 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (sfLB1; Fig. 4a–d). These nuclei were as stiff as normal one-cell and four-cell nuclei (~5 nN µm−1, Fig. 1k). We next overexpressed lamin B1. As WT lamin B1 rapidly dissociated from the nuclear envelope, we used flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) to compensate for the clearance. Whereas excess loading of these lamins resulted in collapsed nuclei, titrating expression levels preserved the overall nuclear shape, with lamin B1 loaded to the nuclear envelope at a level comparable to that using sfLB1 (Fig. 4a,b). We found that flLB1(F454A/L457A) profoundly increased nuclear elasticity and stiffness (4.0 ± 1.1 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (Fig. 4c,d), while overall autophagic activity as assessed by LC3 signal26 was maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5c). The phenotype quantitatively mirrored the embryos perturbed through sfLB1. By contrast, flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, which lacked the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif for farnesylation16 and remained nucleoplasmic, did not significantly alter nuclear shape and mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 5d). These data indicate that two-cell nuclear stiffness depends on the nuclear envelope localization of lamin B1.

Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) showed nuclei of which the shape remained largely deformed as in normal two-cell embryos (Fig. 4a). These nuclei were soft and plastic (1.6 ± 0.4 nN µm−1, n = 10 embryos), despite their comparable level of nuclear envelope loading to sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4b–d). The minimal mechanical impact of flLB1(5A) was probably due to its poor assembly competency at the nuclear envelope for the following reasons: first, our nuclear isolation assay indicated that flLB1(5A) was more soluble than flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4e). Second, sfLB1(5A) showed comparably slightly higher affinity for LC3 than sfLB1(F454A/L457A) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, our expansion microscopy (ExM) analysis revealed a less-uniform peripheral localization of flLB1(5A) in comparison to endogenous lamin B1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A)27 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–g). The difference in peripheral DNA signals appeared less pronounced between perturbed embryo groups (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Our nanocapillary-based assay further suggested an early reduction in nuclear stiffness before lamin B1 clearance (Figs. 1k and 3a,b). Collectively, our data suggest that lamin B1 controls two-cell nuclear stiffness depending on their assembly stability at the nuclear envelope and that the stability depends on the site to which LC3 binds.

We next examined whether the observed nuclear changes impact the two-cell transcriptional reprogramming. We analysed the above embryos using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 1). The first cleavage and following cell cycle progression were normal in those embryos; the overexpressed protein levels were stable and comparable among conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Our analysis indicated that the transcriptomes of flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos were distinct from those of the flLB1(5A) and non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified more than 3,000 downregulated genes in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos compared with the non-injected controls (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). The downregulation was evident even when compared with flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4g), whereas very few DEGs were detected between flLB1(5A) embryos and the non-injected controls (Fig. 4h). Importantly, the genes downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) overlapped more with major ZGA and two-cell-activated genes than with minor ZGA and one-cell-activated genes28 (972 out of 3,763 (25.8%) versus 251 out of 3,763 (6.7%); P < 0.01, Fisher’s exact test) (Fig. 4i). The overlap was even greater when compared with another major ZGA gene list29 (1,338 out of 2,508, 53.3%) (Fig. 4i,j). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC embryos did not show an appreciably altered transcriptome at comparable expression levels (Extended Data Figs. 5g and 7e). Our analysis also indicated perturbed expression of key transcriptional regulators Obox15 in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos but it was not prominent in flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4k). The profiles of maternal and zygotic Obox genes suggested a failure in minor-to-major ZGA transition15.

We next analysed how ZGA is altered when the nuclear envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1. Analysing embryos overexpressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, along with the non-injected controls, we found that thousands of genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated through sfLB1 (Extended Data Fig. 7f–l and Supplementary Table 3). Many downregulated genes identified as DEGs were shared between sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos (71.1%; Fig. 4i (bottom right)). Developmentally essential genes were enriched among the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7m). Analysing published chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) datasets further indicated sharp H3K4me3 signals around the transcription start sites of the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7n). We therefore performed genome-wide profiling of H3K4me3 through an optimized cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis. By establishing a condition that maintained the nuclear structure, reproducible signals were obtained that agreed with previously published ChIP–seq data14,30 (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e). Our analysis indicated that H3K4me3 is more abundant at transcription start sites in sfLB1 embryos than in the non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 8f). It has been demonstrated that broadly spread noncanonical H3K4me3 is removed by histone demethylation for major ZGA14. Indeed, H3K4me3 remained accumulated in broad-domain H3K4me3 (bdH3K4me3) in sfLB1 embryos, whereas H3K4me3 enrichment in lamina-associated domains unchanged (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Analysing the expression levels of histone methylation-related enzymes, key lysine demethylase (KDM) genes, which are needed to eliminate bdH3K4me314, were downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) and sfLB1, but the changes were not significant through flLB1(5A) and sfLB1Δ (Fig. 4m). These data suggest that the establishment of histone methylation status2 failed in embryos when lamin B1 stiffened the two-cell nuclear envelope.

There was a marked difference in nuclear stiffness between the embryo groups that failed in major ZGA and those that were transcriptionally less perturbed. To test whether nuclear stiffness per se was inhibitory to ZGA, we developed a molecular tether–anchor system that targets the nuclear envelope and stiffens nuclei (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The tether comprised an elastic I27 module of titin31 of which the ends were fused to a pair of GFP nanobodies. The anchor was made based on a minimal KASH domain fused to mEGFP for outer-nuclear-envelope localization32. When co-expressed, the tether was recruited to the anchor-coated nuclear envelope and increased nuclear stiffness by around twofold (4.3 ± 1.5 nN µm−1, n = 20 embryos; Fig. 4n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Nuclear plasticity and deformation decreased accordingly (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Importantly, in the tether-stiffened nuclei, lamin B1 levels were as low as in normal mid two-cell embryos (Fig. 4p). Lamin A/C and B2 also remained largely unperturbed (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Our mRNA microinjection into late zygotes minimally affected pronuclear stiffness, first cleavage and cell cycle progression (Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Moreover, our two mutant tether derivatives, one that weakened its affinity to the anchor (tether LaG16(5A)) and one that impaired its elastic force-generating property (tether titin(W34E)), showed no appreciable impact on nuclear shape and mechanics (Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d,j). In contrast to the WT, neither of the two mutants significantly impaired development (Extended Data Fig. 9k). Thus, our tether–anchor system increases two-cell nuclear stiffness and perturbs embryonic development when it binds to the nuclear envelope and exerts force.

Our RNA-seq analysis revealed that embryos in which the nuclei were stiffened by the tether WT (tWT) exhibited distinct transcriptomes compared with those expressing the LaG16(5A) tether mutant and the non-injected controls (Extended Data Fig. 10a). A total of 634 genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated in the tWT embryos, while much fewer DEGs were identified in tether-mutant embryos (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e; versus the non-injected controls). Furthermore, the expression of the Obox cluster and other major ZGA genes was dampened (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Downregulation of key ZGA genes and transcriptional repression were detectable in quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) and 5-ethynyl-uridine (EU) incorporation analyses (Extended Data Fig. 10g,h). Whereas the impact on ZGA was broader and less variable for flLB1(F454A/L457A) than for tWT (972 versus 168 genes; Fig. 4i versus Extended Data Fig. 10e; Fig. 4j versus Fig. 4q), 82.2% of the downregulated genes in tWT embryos were shared with those perturbed through sfLB1 or flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4r). Together, we conclude that deformable two-cell nuclei are integral to the execution of proper ZGA.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 persistence on early development. As a result, approximately 50% of the embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) did not progress beyond the two-cell stage (Extended Data Fig. 5h), comparable to those perturbed through sfLB1 (Fig. 3h). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC did not significantly affect development, indicating that the effective site of lamin B1 is at the nuclear envelope. Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) also showed impaired development, despite their nearly normal transcriptome (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Our analysis indicated that those embryos accumulated DNA damage as detected through phosphorylated H2A.X (γH2A.X) foci (Extended Data Fig. 5i), a developmental impediment33. By contrast, DNA damage levels in embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) were as low as those of non-injection control. Our results do not exclude the possibility that the suppressed ZGA and basal DNA damage combinatorially impaired development. Nonetheless, our data indicate that embryos with stiff two-cell nuclei are unable to facilitate proper ZGA and early development. Embryos with tether-stiffened nuclei also exhibited a two-cell arrest (Extended Data Fig. 9k), supporting the necessity of nuclear softness for development.

Given the impact of nuclear stiffness on ZGA, we examined chromatin dynamics in deformable and non-deformable nuclei. Our ExM images at 24 h.p.i. showed peripheral layers of DNA and lamins, with the overlap comparable to those analysed using electron microscopy34 (~150 nm; Extended Data Fig. 6i). Our imaging further revealed a preferential localization of DNA near concave regions of the two-cell nuclear envelope (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Lamin B1 signals also exhibited a weak negative correlation with nuclear deformation35 (Fig. 5b,c). However, the biased DNA localization was shared among deformable nuclei regardless of lamin B1 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), suggesting that nuclear deformation is associated with peripheral DNA organization.

(the plots show the mean values; at least 10 foci per embryo). h, DNA mass volume at 21 and 24 h.p.i. i–l, 3D DNA FISH. i–k, The locations of the Kdm5b (i), Obox6 (j) and Gabarapl1 (k, for control) genes (green) in two-cell nuclei at 21 and 28 h.p.i. We next examined how deformable nuclei are linked to gene expression regulation during ZGA. In 3D images, large fluorescent foci positive for elongating RNA polymerase II (Pol II Ser2P) shifted their distribution towards the nuclear periphery, as nuclear deformation increased from 21 to 24 h.p.i. (Fig. 5d,e). Notably, the majority of the Pol II foci became more frequently associated with nuclear concavity (Fig. 5f). The focus sizes increased over time, and their growth was suppressed by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5g). Concomitantly, DNA mass volume decreased by 14.7 ± 6.5% (Fig. 5h). We next performed sequential 3D fluorescence in situ hybridization (3D FISH) analysis36 to examine the link between peripheral transcriptional activity and ZGA (Fig. 5i–l). We analysed the genomic loci of Kdm5b and Obox6, along with Gabarapl1 as a non-ZGA control and found that their distributions were broad and changed from the early to the mid-to-late two-cell stage, but the average distance remained 2–3 µm from the nuclear periphery around the time of major ZGA (2.7 ± 2.0, 2.0 ± 1.6 and 2.1 ± 1.3 µm, respectively; 28 h.p.i.) (Fig. 5i–k). Pol II Ser2P intensities were greater when the Obox6 and Kdm5b loci were positioned >1 µm from the nuclear periphery, while DAPI signals remained unchanged, suggesting that the increased local transcriptional activity was not merely a consequence of higher chromatin density (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j). This trend was not observed in Gabarapl1 (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Our sequential FISH further enabled us to determine the locations of multiple gene loci within the same nucleus (Fig. 5l). Our data indicated a widespread positioning of Obox6 and Kdm5b loci at 21 h.p.i. and a change in the localization of gene loci at 28 h.p.i., with a frequent incidence of their concomitant presence near the nuclear periphery. This locus distribution was disrupted by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5l). Notably, Pol II Ser2P intensities at Obox6 loci depended on the nuclear stiffening, while their changes at Kdm5b loci appeared less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We therefore performed sequential 3D DNA–RNA FISH analysis to detect nascent Kdm5b transcripts and found a surge in the production around 2–4 µm from the nuclear envelope, and it depended on peripheral nuclear stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 10l–n). In summary, our data suggest that soft and plastic two-cell nuclei ensure the formation of active transcription sites a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope and enable the coordinated positioning of key ZGA gene loci around the sites for expression.

Our study reveals physical characteristics of early embryonic nuclei and their distinct changes that facilitate ZGA. Our data show that the autophagy factor LC3 and lamin B1 clearance confer nuclear plasticity and softness, and that deformable nuclei are key to robust zygotic transcription. Extensive studies have profiled epigenetic states of chromatin and provided a genome-centred view of this critical developmental transition. Our study highlights the importance of physical nuclear state for this transition and underscores the need for integration of diverse embryonic parameters, including their subcellular material properties.

Our work identifies a transient phase of nuclear deformability that manifests as cells transition through a totipotent state (Fig. 1). Notably, this nuclear change marks normal preimplantation development and contributes to transcription and gene locus movement (Figs. 2, 4 and 5). Notably, the sites of active DNA transactions appear a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope, often associated with local negative curvature, suggesting the generation of inward forces around these sites (Fig. 5d–h). During ZGA, chromatin undergoes dynamic remodelling and compaction37,38,39, while maintaining contact with the nuclear lamina40. A flexible nuclear envelope may accommodate these internal and peripheral chromatin activities, mediating a mechanical conflict for the consolidation of functional genome architectures. Our analysis also suggests that intense transcriptional activity near the deformable nuclear envelope enables the full activation of key ZGA genes that shape the two-cell epigenome14 (Fig. 4l,m). Such mechanical control may also operate in naive embryonic stem cells, in which soft nuclei are linked to pluripotency and priming for differentiation41.

We find that the embryonic mechanism governing lamin B1 clearance shares similarities with nuclear autophagy activated during oncogene-induced cell senescence23 (Fig. 3). As autophagy is accompanied by an increase in intracellular calcium levels and is independent of mTORC1 in early embryos21,42, the clearance is most likely developmentally programmed. Our data suggest a role of nuclear translocation of LC3 and its distinct effect on nuclear shape and mechanics. Further analysis of its regulated nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling43 should reveal the mechanistic basis behind the physiological and pathological nuclear remodelling.

Our findings also raise several interesting questions for future studies. First, our imaging assay detected diluted lamin B1 at convex regions of the nuclear envelope35 (Fig. 5b,c). It remains to be explored whether the clearance of lamin B1 merely contributes to nuclear softening or controls DNA organization by sensing local nuclear curvature. Second, as lamins influence transcription44,45 and the chromatin–lamina contacts change during development40, understanding the interplay between mechanical cues and biochemical factors that ensures robust transcriptional control will be an essential next step. Third, soft and transcriptionally active nuclei, yet enriched with lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope, were prone to DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). As excess lamin B1 can cause persistent DNA damage46, autophagic clearance of lamin B1 may be necessary to protect against such damage. It would be interesting to dissect nuclear actin in two-cell nuclei47, as per its involvement in DNA damage repair48.

Physical nuclear stability is likely important for early embryos, given the potential mechanical challenges they face during passage through the uterine tube49. Yet this period coincides with a transient state in which nuclei become less mechanically resilient. Early mammalian embryos are also prone to DNA lesions and chromosome missegregation50,51,52. Understanding how embryos navigate the vulnerable state may reveal principles underlying developmental robustness.

Mice (ICR and B6C3F1/Jc1 or slc (BCF1)) aged 5–15 weeks53 were purchased from CLEA Japan, Japan SLC or Kiwa Laboratory Animals, maintained in light-controlled (light: 08:00 to 20:00; dark: 20:00 to 08:00), air-conditioned rooms (ambient temperature: 23 °C ± 1.5 °C, humidity: 50 ± 10%) at each facility and used for experiments. All mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and all efforts were made to minimize suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

To obtain oocytes, female mice were superovulated by intraperitoneal injections of 7.5 IU of pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG; ASKA Animal Health), followed by 7.5 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; ASKA Animal Health) at 48 h after PMSG injection. After the female mice were euthanized at 15–16 h after hCG injection, oocytes were collected from the oviducts by an abdominal operation and transferred to a pre-heated medium of Human Tubal Fluid (HTF; ARK Resource). Sperm were collected from the caudal epididymis of male mice for in vitro fertilization (IVF). For fertilization, freshly prepared or cryopreserved sperm were incubated in HTF medium for 1–1.5 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 to allow for capacitation. Subsequently, the sperm suspension was mixed with the medium containing the oocytes, and fertilized eggs were collected 1–2 h after insemination followed by removal of cumulus cells with 0.1% hyaluronidase. The eggs were then transferred to drops of preheated KSOM medium (ARK Resource) and cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2.

Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) was performed as described previously54. In brief, enucleation of cumulus-free MII oocytes was performed in drops of CZB medium including 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B. One donor cumulus cell in CZB medium with 6% deionized-BSA was transferred to the perivitelline space of an enucleated oocyte together with a small amount of HVJ-E (GenomeONE-CF; Ishihara Sangyo) by tightly attaching the donor cell to the enucleated oocyte. The oocyte was then cultured in KSOM medium for 1 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 for the cell fusion. The reconstructed oocytes were activated in KSOM medium containing 5 mM SrCl2, 2 mM EGTA and 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B (Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. The activated SCNT embryos were cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 in KSOM medium.

Pharmacological inhibition experiments were performed by treating embryos with the following chemicals in KSOM medium containing 0.5% (v/v) DMSO: 10 µM wortmannin (19545-26-7, AdipoGen); and 200 nM bafilomycin A1 (SML1661, Sigma-Aldrich). Wortmannin treatment was started at 12 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 32 h.p.i. Bafilomycin treatment was started at 15 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 28 h.p.i. The mock control also contained 0.5% (v/v) DMSO throughout assays.

For immunoblotting assays, the following antibodies were used: anti-p62 rabbit IgG (PM045MS, MBL), anti-β actin mouse mAb (AC-15, Santa Cruz), anti-GFP chicken IgY (ab13970, Abcam), HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (32460, Thermo Fisher Scientific), HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG antibody (61-6520, Thermo Fisher Scientific), HRP-conjugated goat anti-chicken IgY-HRP (A16054, Thermo Fisher Scientific), anti-lamin B1 mouse IgG (sc-374015, Santa Cruz), anti-HA antibody (51064-2-AP, Proteintech) and HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG antibody (32460, Thermo Fisher Scientific). For immunostaining imaging assays, the following antibodies were used: anti-lamin A/C mouse IgG2a (39287, Active Motif), anti-lamin A/C mouse IgG1k (sc-376248, Santa Cruz), anti-lamin B1 mouse IgG (sc-374015, Santa Cruz; amino acids 559–586 of lamin B1), anti-lamin B1 rabbit IgG (ab16048, Abcam), anti-lamin B2 rabbit IgG (ab151735, Abcam), anti-lamin B2 mouse IgG1 (68475-1-Ig, Proteintech), anti-RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at serine 2 mouse IgM (920203, BioLegend), anti-phospho-histone H2A.X (Ser139) mouse IgG1 (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich), anti-LAP2Β mouse IgG (611000, BD Transduction Laboratories), anti-BrdU mouse IgG1 (sc-32323, Santa Cruz), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (A11001, Thermo Fisher Scientific), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 568 (ab175473, Abcam), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (ab150115, Abcam), goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (A11008, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 594-labelled donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody (A21207, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and goat anti-mouse IgM (Heavy chain) Alexa Fluor 594 (A21044, Thermo Fisher Scientific). For antibody microinjection experiments, the following antibodies were used: anti-LC3 mouse IgG (CTB-LC3-2-IC, Cosmo Bio) and normal mouse IgG (sc-2025, Santa Cruz).

pcDNA-emerin-eGFP-polyA was a gift from Y. Zhang (Addgene, 59747)55. pcDNA-nesprin-TS was a gift from D. Conway (Addgene, 68127)56. pcDNA3.1-H2B-mCherry-polyA, pcDNA3.1-H2B-EGFP-polyA and pcDNA3.1-EGFP-polyA were gifts from K. Yamagata. pcDNA-emerin-eGFP-polyA was used to label the nuclear envelope. pcDNA3.1-EGFP-polyA was used as a backbone or an expression control, while pcDNA3.1-H2B-mCherry-polyA and pcDNA-H2B-EGFP-polyA were used as nuclear markers. Moreover, custom constructs generated in this study for live-embryo imaging and overexpression assays are as follows: pcDNA3.1-sfLB1-polyA, pcDNA3.1-sfLB1Δ-polyA, pcDNA3.1-eGFP-sfLB1-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-sfLB1Δ-polyA, pcDNA3.1-eGFP-LC3-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-flLB1wt-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1wt-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(5A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(F454A/F457A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(S24A)-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1(F454A/F457A)ΔC-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mCherry-NLS-polyA, pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-KASH-TM-polyA, pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry-polyA, pcDNA3.1-LaG16(5A)-titin-LaG16(5A)-mCherry-polyA and pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin(W34E)-LaG16-mCherry-polyA. For generating each of the WT constructs, the corresponding genetic sequences were amplified by PCR from mouse ovary cDNA, which was synthesized using SuperScript VILO Master Mix (11756050, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the following primer pairs: flLB1_fp1 and flLB1_rp1 for lamin B1 and LC3_fp1 and LC3_rp1 for LC3 (sequence information is provided below). Amplified fragments were cloned either into downstream of eGFP in the pcDNA3.1-eGFP-polyA vector to create fusion constructs, or used to replace its eGFP sequence. All cloning procedures were performed using the In-Fusion cloning system (Clontech) unless otherwise noted. For mCherry fusion constructs, the eGFP sequence was replaced with mCherry, and a codon-optimized linker sequence (SGLRSRAQA)57 was inserted in between. The plasmids for full-length lamin B1 mutants were generated by introducing substitutional mutations into pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1wt-polyA using the following primer pairs: flLB1_fp2 and flLB1_rp2, flLB1_fp3 and flLB1_rp3, and flLB1_fp4 and flLB1_rp4, for flLB1(5A), flLB1(F454A/L457A) and flLB1(S24A), respectively. For flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, the corresponding CaaX sequence was removed using flLB1_fp5 and flLB1_rp5 followed by ligation. The plasmids carrying sfLB1 were generated by amplifying the corresponding coding sequence (371–459) from the lamin B1 plasmid using the following PCR primers: sfLB1_fp1 and sfLB1_rp1, sfLB1_fp2 and sfLB1_rp2, sfLB1_fp3 and sfLB1_rp3, and sfLB1_fp4 and sfLB1_rp4, and inserting them into a pcDNA3.1 vector. A codon-optimized linker sequence (RDPPVAT) was inserted between eGFP and sfLB1. pDHFR-3HA-LB1, pDHFR-3HA-LB1Δ, pDHFR-3HA-LB1(5A) and pDHFR-3HA-LB1(F454A/L457A) for pull-down assays were generated by cloning out the corresponding coding sequence from the full-length lamin B1 plasmids and inserted them into the DHFR vector (New England Biolabs). For GST-LC3, the coding sequence of LC3 was inserted into a pGEX vector downstream of GST and the PreScission sequence. pcDNA3.1-mCherry-NLS-polyA for nuclear imaging was generated by inserting a codon-optimized SV40 large T antigen NLS downstream of mCherry in pcDNA3.1-mCherry-flLB1-polyA (inverse PCR primers: NLS_fp1 and NLS_rp1). To generate pcDNA3.1-mEGFP-KASH-TM-polyA for nuclear envelope tethering, the KASH-TM sequence (amino acids 6525–6874 of nesprin 2G) was amplified by PCR from the pcDNA nesprin TS vector (Addgene, 68127, gift from D. Conway) using primers KASH-TM_fp1 and KASH-TM_rp1. The amplified fragment was then inserted into a pcDNA3.1-mEGFP vector. pcDNA3.1-LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry-polyA was generated as a fusion of titin immunoglobulin domain (I27(V11P))31 flanked by a pair of GFP-nanobody (LaG16)58. First, the coding sequences of LaG16 and I27(V11P) codon-optimized for mouse were synthesized by Eurofins Genetics. The first LaG16, I27(V11P), and the second LaG16 comprising the tether were each amplified by PCR using primer pairs LaG16_fp1 and LaG16_rp1, Titin_fp1 and Titin_rp1, and LaG16_fp2 and LaG16_rp2, respectively, and then inserted in order into a pcDNA3.1-mCherry vector using restriction enzyme digestion (ClaI and HpaI) and sticky/blunt-end ligation with a Ligation Mix kit (6023, Takara). Codon-optimized linker sequences (GGGGS and RDPPVAT) were inserted between the first LaG16 and titin I27 and between the second LaG16 and mCherry, respectively. The DNA fragment of LaG16 mutant (S32A/T56A/V57A/R103A/V106A), designed according to a previous study59, was also synthesized by Eurofins Genetics and used to generate the plasmid in the same way as above. The mutation in titin (W34E)60 was introduced using the primers Titin_W34E_fp1&rp1. All the plasmids were verified by DNA sequencing (Eurofins Genetics).

The primers used were as follows: sfLB1_fp1 (5′-TGGTGGAATTCGCCACCATGCTGGACATGGAGATCAGC-3′); sfLB1_rp1 (5′-CATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCAGTTCTTCAAGCGAATAAACTTCCCATC-3′); sfLB1_fp2 (5′-TGGTGGAATTCGCCACCATGCTCTCTCCAAGCCCTTCTTCCC-3′); sfLB1_rp2 (5′-GCCCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCAGGCTGAGGCAGAGTGGGA A-3′); sfLB1_fp3 (5′-GGGATCCACCGGTCGCCACCATGCTGGACATGGAGATCAG-3′); sfLB1_rp3 (5′-CATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCAGTTCTTCAAGCGAATAAACTTCCCATC-3′); sfLB1_fp4 (5′-ATCCACCGGTCGCCACCATGCTCTCTCCAAGC-3′); sfLB1_rp4 (5′-GCCCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCAGGCTGAGGCAGAGTGGGA A-3′); LC3_fp1 (5′-CGGCCTGAGAAGCAGAATGCCGTCCGAGAAGACC-3′); LC3_rp1 (5′-GCCCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTTACACAGCCATTGCTGTCCCG-3′); flLB1_fp1 (5′-ACTCAGATCTCGAGCTCAAGCTTCGATGGCGACCGCGAC-3′); flLB1_rp1 (5′-GCCCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCACATAATGGCACAGCTTTTATTGGATG-3′); flLB1_fp2 (5′-CAGCCCCTGCCGCCGCCGCCACCGTGTCCAGAGCGTCC-3′); flLB1_rp2 (5′-GGCGGCGGCGGCAGGGGCTGGAGAGAGCTTTAACCGCTCTTC-3′); flLB1_fp3 (5′-GGCTATTCGCGCGAAGAACACTTCTGAGCAGG-3′); flLB1_rp3 (5′-CGCGCGAATAGCCTTCCCATCAACATCTATCTCT-3′); flLB1_fp4 (5′-ACGCCGCTCGCCCCCACGCGCCTGTCGC-3′); flLB1_rp4 (5′-GCGCGTGGGGGCGAGCGGCGTGGCGGG-3′); flLB1_fp5 (5′-GCGGCCGCTCGACTATG-3′); flLB1_rp5 (5′-CCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCTCAGCTTTTATTGGATGCTCT-3′); NLS_fp1 (5′-GGGCCGCCTAAGAAAAAGCG-3′); NLS_rp1 (5′-CGCTTTTTCTTAGGCGGCCCCTTGTACAGCTCGTCCATGCC-3′); KASH-TM_fp1 (5′-GATCTCGAGCTCAAGCTTCGCAGGAGCTTCACAGCAAGCT-3′); KASH-TM_rp1 (5′-GCCCATAGTCGAGCGGCCGCCTAGGTGGGAGGTGGCCC-3′); LaG16_fp1 (5′-GTGTGGTGGAATTCGCCACCATGGCACAAGTG-3′); LaG16_rp1 (5′-CCCATCGATGGACACAGTCACTTGTGTTCC-3′); LaG16_fp2 (5′-TGGCTCTGTTAACATGGCACAAGTGCAGCTG-3′); LaG16_rp2 (5′-CCGTTAACGGACACAGTCACTTGTGTTCC-3′); Titin_fp1 (5′-GTGTCCATCGATGGGGGCGGGGGCTCTCTGATCGAGGTGGAGAAGC-3′); Titin_rp1 (5′-AGAGCCACCTCCCCCCAGCTCCTTCACCTTCAG-3′); Titin_W34E_fp1 (5′-CAGGAGAAGCTGAAGGGCCAGC-3′); Titin_W34E_rp1 (5′-CTTCTCCTGGCCGTGCACGT-3′).

After insemination, fertilized embryos were collected at 12–14 h.p.i. and subjected to mRNA injection unless otherwise noted. Cumulus-free embryos were transferred to drops of M2 medium (ARK Resource) and mRNAs were injected using a piezo manipulator (Prime Tech). The final concentrations of injected mRNA were as follows: 500 ng μl−1 of sfLB1, 500 ng μl−1 of sfLB1Δ, 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(5A), 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(F454A/L457A), 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, 20 ng µl−1 of mCherry-NLS, 100 ng µl−1 of eGFP-LC3 or eGFP, 300 ng μl−1 of mEGFP-KASH-TM, 125 ng μl−1 of LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry (WT, LaG16(5A) and titin(W34E), respectively). In some experiments, mRNA of eGFP (25 ng μl−1) or histone H2B-eGFP (20 ng μl−1) were co-injected to confirm successful injection or to visualize nuclei. After mRNA injection, embryos were cultured in KSOM medium at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. For assays with flLB1, flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A), post-injected embryos were inspected at 24 h.p.i. using a fluorescence microscope and those displaying collapsed nuclei were excluded from analyses. mRNAs synthesis was performed using mMESSAGE mMACHINE T7 Transcription Kit (AM1344, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after linearization of plasmid vectors by restriction enzyme digestion. The synthesized mRNAs were purified using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (74034, Qiagen) and subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis and spectrophotometry to verify the purity (criteria: optical density at 260 nm/280 nm ratio of >2.0). The purified mRNAs were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, stored at –80 °C and used within 6 months.

Fertilized embryos were collected at 12–14 h.p.i. and subjected to injection of the following antibodies in M2 medium (ARK Resource): anti-LC3 mouse IgG (100 µg ml−1); normal mouse IgG (100 µg ml−1). After the antibody injection, the embryos were cultured in KSOM medium until 24 h.p.i. and then analysed.

After mRNA injection, embryos were cultured in KSOM medium at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. The developmental stages of the embryos were monitored at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h.p.i. The frequency of development to the blastocyst stage for non-injected embryos at 96 h.p.i. was 85.5 ± 7.6% (mean ± s.d. among five biological replicates).

Live-embryo imaging was performed using an inverted fluorescence microscope (Ti-U, Nikon) equipped with a motorized sample stage (MS-2000, Applied Scientific Instruments), a piezo-driven objective scanner (PIFOC, Physics Instruments) with a piezo controller (E-665, Physics Instruments), a stage-top incubator (TIZ, Tokai Hit), a spinning-disk confocal unit (CSU-X1, Yokogawa) with two excitation lasers (488 nm and 561 nm; OBIS LS, Coherent), a silicone-immersion objective lens (UPlanSApo ×60/1.30 NA, Olympus) and a sCMOS camera (Neo4.1, Andor). After injection of mRNA, embryos were placed in drops of KSOM medium (10 µl each), which was supplemented with 0.00025% (w/v) polyvinyl alcohol (PVA; P8136-250G, Sigma-Aldrich) and placed onto a glass-bottom culture dish (P35G-1.5-14-C, MatTek) filled with paraffin oil (26137-85, Nacalai Tesque). The embryos were maintained in a cell culture incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2 before being transferred to the microscope’s stage-top incubator, which was pre-conditioned at 37 °C and filled with humidified air containing 5% CO2. For acquisition of long-term timelapse data (Fig. 1), fertilized embryos were injected with mRNA (20 ng µl−1 of histone H2B-mCherry) at 1–2 h.p.i. and imaging was started at 8 h.p.i. Optical sections were acquired across individual nuclei (step size: 5 µm; total scan width: 60 µm) at 1 h intervals. Imaging with emerin–eGFP and mCherry–NLS (300 ng µl−1 and 20 ng µl−1 mRNA, respectively) was performed in the same manner but at 8, 24 and 48 h.p.i. The exposure of embryos to the excitation lasers was minimized by shuttering the illumination using image acquisition software (NIS elements v.5.0, Nikon) (exposure time, 200 ms). The laser power at the objective’s focus was set to 0.3 mW and 50 mW for the imaging of H2B–mCherry and emerin–eGFP, respectively. For acquisition of timelapse data with flLB1 constructs (Fig. 3), embryos were injected with mRNA (20 ng µl−1 of mCherry-flLB1 or 20 ng µl−1 of mCherry-flLB1 mutants) at 12–14 h.p.i. and the imaging was started at 21 h.p.i. (interval, 1 h; laser power, 9 mW). Under these conditions, the development of embryos to the blastocyst stage was 80.7 ± 3.9% (n = 4–11 embryos per preparation; versus 83.6% for non-injected embryos cultured in an incubator, n = 55 embryos). For lysosome imaging, embryos were incubated in KSOM medium containing LysoPrime Green (1:2,000, 345-09903, Dojindo) for 1 h, followed by washing with KSOM before acquisition of confocal slices at 1 µm intervals. Photobleaching was negligible as varying the exposure time or imaging time intervals did not significantly affect the observed dynamics. For the analysis of the first cleavage events (Extended Data Fig. 9g,h), embryos at 12–14 h.p.i. were injected with mRNA (20 ng μl−1 of histone H2B-mCherry) for nuclear visualization and subjected to timelapse imaging at 30 min intervals, starting at 15 h.p.i. (objective lens: Plan Apo ×20/0.75 NA, Nikon, z-step size: 2 µm; total scan width, 40 µm).

IVF embryos were fixed in 4% PFA/PBS at room temperature for 20 min. Fixation was started at 8 h.p.i. for one-cell, 21 h.p.i. for early-two-cell, 24 h.p.i. for mid-two-cell, 32 h.p.i. for late-two-cell, and 48 h.p.i. for four-cell embryos. The fixed embryos were washed three times with 0.01% PVA/PBS. To quantitatively compare lamin signals among embryos at different developmental stages, embryos of all stages were simultaneously treated for the following immunofluorescence (IF) steps and observed by a confocal microscope under the same conditions. The samples were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich)/PBS at room temperature for 20 min, followed by incubation three times with 3% BSA/PBS for 10 min each at room temperature. The samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (anti-Lamin B1 mouse IgG, 1:100, sc-374015, Santa Cruz; anti-lamin B2 rabbit IgG, 1:100, ab151735, Abcam; anti-lamin B2 mouse IgG1, 1:100, 68475-1-Ig, Proteintech; anti-Lamin A/C mouse IgG, 1:200, 39087, Active Motif; anti-lamin A/C mouse IgG1k, 1:100, sc-376248, Santa Cruz; and anti-Lap2β mouse IgG, 1:100, 611000, BD Transduction Laboratories) at 4 °C overnight. After three washes with 3% BSA/PBS, the samples were further incubated in the dark with goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) cross-adsorbed secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (1:2,000; A11001, Thermo Fisher Scientific), goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) cross-adsorbed secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (1:2,000; A11008, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 594-labelled donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:2,000; A21207, Thermo Fisher Scientific), goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) cross-adsorbed secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 568 (1:2,000; ab175473, Abcam) and goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) cross-adsorbed secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 647 (1:2,000; ab150115, Abcam) at room temperature for 1 h. For DNA damage assay, the embryos were fixed at 34 h.p.i. and were immunostained with anti-phospho-histone H2A.X (Ser139) mouse IgG1 (1:250; 05-636, Sigma-Aldrich) followed by Alexa 488-labelled anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (1:500, A11001, Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the same protocol as above. The samples were washed three times with 3% BSA/PBS and then mounted onto slides using VECTASHIELD mounting medium containing DAPI. Fluorescence signals were observed using the LSM800 microscope (Zeiss), equipped with a laser module (405/488/561/640 nm) and GaAsP detector, using the same contrast, brightness and exposure settings across each set of experiments. z-slice thickness was determined using the optimal interval function in ZEN software. The fluorescence signals of phospho-histone H2A.X were observed using a Nikon microscope equipped with a mercury vapour lamp (Nikon, C-HGFI Intensilight) and GFP and DAPI filters. For 3D nuclear imaging with RNA pol II, embryos were immunostained with anti-RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at serine 2 mouse IgM (1:100, 920203, BioLegend) followed by Alexa 568-labelled anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (1:2,000; ab175473, Abcam) using the same protocol as above and then stained with 1 µM SYTOX Green nucleic acid stain (S7020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min. The embryos were then placed into a glass-bottom dish containing VECTASHIELD (H-1000, VEC) without coverslip mounting to minimize sample compression. The confocal slices were acquired at 1-µm steps using the spinning-disc confocal Nikon microscope above.

RNA synthesis was measured by EU incorporation. The embryos that were microinjected with mRNA and remained viable at 15 h.p.i. were incubated in KSOM medium containing 2 mM EU (C10329, Thermo Fisher Scientific) from 15 h.p.i. The embryos were fixed at 28 h.p.i. and permeabilized according to the above immunostaining protocol, and then the incorporated EU was detected using Click-iT RNA Alexa Fluor 488 Imaging Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (C10329, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Alexa Fluor 647 azide (A10277, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used at a concentration of 25 µM. The samples were mounted onto the slides using VECTASHIELD Mounting Medium containing DAPI. The fluorescence signals were observed using an LSM900 microscope (ZEISS).

Cell cycle progression was examined by 5-ethynyl-2±-deoxyuridine (EdU) or 5-bromo-2′-deoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation. For autophagy inhibition experiments, embryos were cultured in KSOM medium containing 10 µM wortmannin (DMSO as a vehicle control) during 12–22 h.p.i. As a positive control, the embryos were cultured in KSOM medium containing 3 µg ml−1 aphidicolin (A0781-1MG, Sigma-Aldrich) during 18–22 h.p.i.; these timings were determined based on a previous publication61. The embryos were then cultured in KSOM medium containing 10 µM EdU with wortmannin, DMSO or aphidicolin during 22–24 h.p.i. These EdU-treated embryos were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min, and then permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 20 min at room temperature. After permeabilization, the embryos were washed and incubated in the Click-iT reaction cocktail for 30 min according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C10637). After the wash steps, the samples were mounted on glass slides in VECTASHIELD mounting medium containing DAPI. The fluorescence signals were observed using a confocal microscope (LSM800, Carl Zeiss), equipped with a laser module (405/488/561/640 nm) and GaAsP detector. BrdU incorporation assays were performed as above except for the use of 100 µM instead of 10 µM, a 10 min treatment with 4 N HCl (37313-25, Nacalai Tesque) followed by neutralization in 100 mM Tris-HCl solution (pH 8.0) after permeabilization and staining with anti-BrdU antibody (1:100; sc-32323, Santa Cruz) at 4 °C overnight followed by goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (1:1,000; ab150115, Abcam) at room temperature for 1 h along with DNA counterstain with Hoechst 33342 (1:1,000; C10637, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

The mechanical properties of nuclei at each cleavage stage in living embryos were measured using single glass nanocapillaries, which were held with a three-axis, low-drift hydraulic micromanipulator (MHW-3, Narishige) attached to the microscope’s body. The nanocapillaries were prepared by fabricating borosilicate glass tubes (B100-75-10, Sutter Instruments) using a capillary puller (PD-10, Narishige) such that the tip formed a nearly uniform taper with an inner diameter of around 1 μm (1.06 ± 0.02 µm, n = 5). To begin with, embryos injected with mRNAs (20 ng µl−1 of H2B-mCherry or 300 ng µl−1 of emerin-eGFP) were transferred to drops of M2 medium, which was placed in a glass-bottom, open-top culture chamber covered with paraffin oil (26137-85, Nacalai Tesque). The chamber was then placed onto the microscope’s sample stage and a single embryo was captured by using a large holding pipette (inner diameter, ~10 µm), which approached from one side of the embryo. A nanocapillary was then inserted from the opposite side of the embryo and its tip was contacted to the nuclear surface; the nucleus was then captured at its surface by applying a weak suction pressure to the nanocapillary. The level of the suction pressure was controlled using a syringe pump (PHD ULTRA, Harvard apparatus) and a digital manometer (PPA101-M, SMC), which were connected to the distal end of the nanocapillary through a vacuum tube. The pressure level (1.2–2.1 × 101 kPa) was such that the nuclear surface could sustain its attachment to the nanocapillary tip but could not be aspirated. Finally, the nucleus was stretched by moving the nanocapillary position away from the embryo’s centre at a velocity with which the viscous resistance from the cytoplasm could be low. At a typical movement speed of 0.25 µm s−1, the viscous resistance on the nucleus as estimated according to the Stokes–Einstein equation62 was 0.05–0.16 nN (see the ‘Image analyses’ section). This value was over 100 times smaller than the force generated at the nanocapillary tip (~17 nN), as estimated from the product of the applied pressure and the nanocapillary’s aperture size (0.8 ± 0.1 µm2; nanocapillary aperture size = π(d/2)2, where d is the nanocapillary’s inner diameter; n = 5). Internal nuclear pressure was disregarded as different nanocapillary pressure levels yielded similar results. Associated with the nanocapillary’s movement, the nucleus gradually deformed and then detached from the nanocapillary before reaching the embryo’s edge. The extent of the maximal extension that nuclei had exhibited was used to determine effective nuclear stiffness. The measurement was performed for nuclei at the one-cell, two-cell and four-cell stages using approximately the same micromanipulation parameters (that is, pressure level, nanocapillary size and nanocapillary movement speed). Embryos of which nuclei were properly captured, as assessed by (1) a sealed contact surface with no aspiration of nuclear material and (2) translocation of the nuclear surface in response to nanocapillary movement, were subjected to subsequent analyses. Individual nuclei were not subjected to repeated measurements. Where feasible, the order of the measurement for control and treatment groups was randomized. The measurements were highly consistent across experiments (mean two-cell nuclear stiffness of non-injected controls: 2.07 ± 0.20 nN µm−1, mean ± s.d., across four independent experiments). These control data were pooled across experiments and used as a reference, mitigating the limitation in the number of samples that could be analysed within the narrow time window per experiment (1 − 2 h for each developmental stage). The label-free measurement (Extended Data Fig. 2h) was performed using differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy. For the analysis of nuclear stiffness and embryonic development (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3), the above-described micromanipulation procedure was used but with a pressure level of 1.2 × 101 kPa.

The mechanical properties of nuclei were also examined using an alternative micromanipulation technique (Extended Data. Fig. 2l–n), which was based on glass capillaries but eliminated of the nuclear translocation within the cytoplasm. This was achieved by using the same microscopy setup as above but with capillaries of wider bore size (inner diameter, 2.09 ± 0.12 µm, n = 13). Moreover, the pressure level was increased linearly instead of being maintained constant, such that the tension above which the nuclear periphery was aspirated inside a glass capillary could be measured. Specifically, after the physical contact of the capillary tip with the nuclear surface, the suction pressure was raised at a constant rate of 6 × 103 Pa min−1. The capillary’s position was fixed throughout this procedure. The nucleus could withstand the applied aspiration pressure and maintain its overall shape until it yielded to the pressure. The pressure level was constantly monitored using a digital manometer (Testo 521, Testo) and the value at which the nuclear surface started to be aspirated inside the capillary (>1 µm displacement from the tip) was determined by examining the fluorescence image acquired simultaneously. The measurements were performed at 22 ± 1 °C and completed within 60 min, over which no noticeable change in the nuclear mechanics was observed. The objective lens of ×40 (Plan Apo, 0.95 NA; Nikon) was used for the imaging.

p62 and lamin B1 were immunoblotted on embryonic lysates. For p62 and lamin B1 blotting of eGFP−sfLB1, embryos were first injected with mRNA (500 ng µl−1 of the eGFP-sfLB1 and mEGFP–sfLB1Δ as a negative control) at 12–14 h.p.i. and then collected at the two-cell stage (at 24 h.p.i. and 32 h.p.i. for eGFP–sfLB1). Before lysis, the zona pellucida was removed by acidified Tyrode’s (T1788, Sigma-Aldrich) and washed three times in PBS containing 0.01% PVA. Sixty embryos were then soaked with Tris-glycine SDS sample buffer (LC2676, Novex) containing 2-mercaptoethanol (161-0710, Bio-Rad) and 500 ng BSA (Albumin Standard, 23209, Thermo Fisher Scientific) as a loading control and heated at 90 °C for 5 min. For lamin B1 blotting, 34 IVF embryos were collected at 21 and 32 h.p.i. and lysed in SDS sample buffer (Wako). The lysis was done by heating at 90 °C for 3 min. Proteins were separated on 10% or 5–20% (80-12-278, Bioimprove) polyacrylamide gel or e-PAGEL HR (5-20%) gel (HER-T520L, ATTO) and then transferred to PVDF membrane (1704272, Bio-Rad) using Transblot SD (Bio-Rad) or a Trans Blot-Turbo transfer system (1704150J1, Bio-Rad). After blocking with 3% BSA-containing PBS with 0.2% Tween-20 or SuperBlock blocking buffer (37535, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 0.05% Tween-20 (161-0781, Bio-Rad), the membrane was blotted sequentially with the following primary antibodies: anti-lamin B1(B-10) mouse IgG (1:1,000, sc-374015, Santa Cruz) or anti-p62 rabbit IgG (1:1,000, PM045MS, MBL), anti-actin rabbit IgG (1:1,000, A2066, Merck), anti-GFP chicken IgY (1:5,000, ab13970, Abcam; for p62 assays). Each blotting was carried out overnight at 4 °C, followed by 1 h staining with the secondary antibody at room temperature; HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:3,000, 32460, Thermo Fisher Scientific), HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody (1:5,000, 32430, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and HRP-conjugated goat anti-chicken IgY-HRP (1:5,000, A16054, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The membrane was stripped off using Restore western blot stripping buffer (21059, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after each blot. For p62 blotting, the membrane was pre-stained with Ponceau S (P7170, Sigma-Aldrich) and then washed with TBST after image acquisition. Blotting was performed using the ECL Prime Western Blotting System (Amersham, RPN2232), SuperSignal West Femto or West Dura (34094 and 34075, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Images were acquired using the Gel Doc ZE imager (Bio-Rad) or ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad).

Samples were prepared through the bacterial expression of GST-tagged LC3 (GST–LC3) and HA-tagged lamin B1 fragment (HA–LB1). For GST–LC3 expression, E. coli Rosetta (DE3) pLysS (Merck) were transformed with the pGEX-LC3 plasmid and grown in LB at 37 °C. Protein expression was induced at an optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.6 by adding 0.25 mM IPTG, followed by incubation for 20 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation and resuspended in lysis/bind/wash buffer (10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4, 140 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 0.05% Tween-20, pH 7.4). For HA–LB1 expression, bacterial cultures transformed with pDHFR-3HA-LB1(WT, Δ, 5A or F454A/L457A) were grown under the same conditions, with induction at OD600 = 0.3 using 0.25 mM IPTG, followed by 24 h of incubation at 18 °C. Cells were collected and resuspended in lysis/bind/wash buffer. The cell suspensions were then lysed by one freeze–thaw cycle followed by sonication. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 40,000 rpm for 30 min at 4 °C (SW-55, Beckman). For GST pull-down preparation, the cleared GST–LC3 lysates were incubated with glutathione Sepharose 4B resin (Cytiva), which was pre-washed with PBS and equilibrated with Lysis/bind/wash buffer for 1 h at 23 °C. The resin was then loaded into MicroSpin columns (Cytiva) and washed with lysis/bind/wash buffer to remove unbound proteins. GST-only control samples were prepared by treating GST–LC3 lysates with PreScission Protease (Cytiva) overnight at 4 °C to remove LC3. Cleared HA–LB1 lysates were loaded onto the columns containing either GST–LC3 or GST alone and incubated for 3 h at 4 °C.
