Finally, we use equation (2) to generate regression-adjusted predictions for annual probabilities of birth by maternal age and parity necessary to build sequential multi-decrement fertility life tables (Methods), which we then use to derive decrements in China’s TFR over time due to the OVV policy (Supplementary Table 7 shows these calculations in detail).

Extended Data Fig. 7 presents these results, with TFR declines that generally match the pattern of births over time in Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2. To convert these event-year TFR estimates to calendar years, we match each provincial event year with its corresponding calendar year, weight each provincial calendar year estimate by the provincial female population in our survey data, and compute a weighted average for the corresponding Chinese population included in our sample. Figure 5 shows these results, both for the actual TFR and the counterfactual TFR without the OVV policy (generated using regression predictions with OVV indicators set to 1 and 0). China’s TFR declined by 0.98 births per woman between 1987 and 1999, and we calculate that about 48% of this decline (0.48 births per woman) is attributable to the OVV policy (Supplementary Note 24). Although other independent background forces were also at work, this fertility decline under the OVV represents the first time that China’s TFR fell below the replacement rate. Extended Data Fig. 8 shows comparable figures for actual and counterfactual (that is, without the OVV) age-specific fertility rates (ASFRs), suggesting that the TFR reductions in Fig. 5 are largely driven by reductions in ASFRs among women aged 20–24 and 25–29.

The observed TFR (blue line with square markers) and the counterfactual TFR (pink line with circle markers), calculated by subtracting the policy-driven change in TFR implied by estimates in the TFR section from observed TFR in each event year, derived from the event-study sample (n = 1,906,333 stacked woman-year observations; 36,375 unique women). Data are from the 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Changes in TFRs simultaneously capture both changes in the number of births and changes in the timing of births. To consider these TFR components separately, we first estimate discrete-time hazard models to predict the implied density functions of maternal age at childbirth with and without the OVV policy at different parities (following Babiarz and colleagues9). Extended Data Fig. 9 shows these results; the distributions of maternal age at childbirth are similar across all parities with and without the policy, suggesting little effect on the timing of births. We then also conduct a Bongaarts–Feeney quantum-tempo decomposition32. The results from this decomposition, shown in Extended Data Fig. 10, also suggest that China’s TFR decline due to the OVV is predominantly a quantum rather than tempo effect (that is, fewer lifetime births rather than delayed childbearing). Overall, these results suggest that China’s TFR decline under OVV was largely a reduction in completed fertility rather than a change in birth timing.

In this section we assess the robustness of our main results to alternative specifications and estimation samples, conduct a falsification exercise, and probe the sensitivity of our findings to the possibility of undetected pre-existing trends and to multiple hypothesis testing.

First, focusing on our primary estimates for the annual probability of birth, we evaluate the robustness of our results to alternative model specifications: (1) Supplementary Fig. 6a,b presents estimates that include controls for provincial characteristics (GDP per capita, urban population share, health care facilities per capita and the under-five mortality rate), as well as region-by-year fixed effects; (2) Supplementary Fig. 7 presents estimates that include controls for women’s rural or urban residency; (3) Supplementary Fig. 8 reports estimates controlling for five-year age group fixed effects; (4) Supplementary Fig. 9 shows estimates conditioning on maternal fixed effects (that is, a fixed effect for each mother), even though doing so effectively excludes women with only one child; (5) Supplementary Fig. 10 examines the extent to which our results are sensitive to changes in sample composition across event years. As later-adopting provinces have fewer post-treatment observations (as Supplementary Table 8 shows), we re-estimate our primary event study model using progressively restrictive samples that include only provinces observed through event year +k (k = 1, … , 8). (6) Supplementary Fig. 11 also assesses the robustness of our results to sample restrictions through a leave-one-out exercise, re-estimating equation (1) excluding each province sequentially (one-by-one) to test for the undue influence of any single province. In all cases, the resulting estimates for the annual probability of birth are similar to those presented in Fig. 2.

Second, we conduct a falsification exercise by randomizing the timing of OVV implementation across provinces. Specifically, for each province, we randomly assign a false year of OVV implementation between 1988 and 2000 (the first and last years of OVV in our sample), excluding each province’s actual year of implementation. When repeating this reassignment and then re-estimating a variant of equation (1) 1,000 times (Supplementary Note 25), Supplementary Fig. 12 shows the empirical probability density function of the resulting estimates, which is centered around zero (Supplementary Note 26). The vertical red line represents our actual estimate for the effect of the OVV policy (–0.015), which falls below the fifth percentile of the empirical distribution of false estimates, allowing us to reject the hypothesis that the actual treatment effect is statistically equivalent to the expectation of the false estimates at the 1% significance level.

Third, although Fig. 2 suggests that OVV implementation is not correlated with pre-existing fertility trends, we consider how well-powered our assessment of this possibility is (following Roth33). To do so, we first establish the magnitude of the minimum linear pre-OVV trend that we are powered to detect. Sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. 13) suggests that our event study design has 80% power to detect a downward linear pre-trend with a slope as small as 0.146 percentage points per year. If such a trend were to persist after the implementation of OVV, it would accumulate to a bias of 1.02 percentage points by event year 6 (the event year point estimate largest in magnitude). However, even accounting for this potential undetected bias, our peak event year estimate of 2.88 percentage points (in event year 6) remains nearly three times as large, suggesting that our results are not primarily driven by secular trends (Supplementary Note 27). In addition to accounting for linear pre-trends, we also address the possibility of non-linear secular trends correlated with the timing of OVV implementation by applying the approach of Rambachan and Roth34, which bounds the extent to which the slope of any unobserved differential trend can evolve after OVV implementation. As Supplementary Fig. 14 shows, the decline in fertility by event year 6 remains statistically significant, even allowing an unobserved confounding trend to accelerate or decelerate its slope by 0.06 percentage points each year (Supplementary Note 28).

Finally, to address potential concerns about serial correlation and multiple hypothesis testing in our event-study estimates, we construct simultaneous (uniform) 95% confidence bands following appendix B of Marcus and Sant’Anna35 using a cluster-level multiplier bootstrap. These uniform bands control for the family-wise error rate across all event year estimates after the implementation of OVV. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 15, our primary results remain robust.

An extensive literature demonstrates that family planning programmes and population policies influence fertility, but the strongest evidence suggests that these programmes and policies do not explain a large share of fertility decline across many environments1,2,3,4,5,6. Although population policy in China is often considered to be an outlier in global experience8,11,12, a large body of quantitative evidence has not generally supported the view that policy was central in China’s fertility decline7,8,9,10. By contrast, an important contribution of this paper is showing that the OCP was in fact central in China’s more recent fertility decline, pushing fertility below the replacement rate—albeit not when it was first introduced, but rather when it was enforced more forcefully under the OVV policy more than a decade later. Notably, this new evidence confirms arguments long made by demographers on the basis of qualitative and administrative evidence11,12,19,20, quantifying their magnitude. By strengthening bureaucratic incentives, OVV produced a delayed impact of the OCP on fertility in China, accounting for about half of the decline during the 1990s.

Our paper also makes a new contribution to research regarding the personnel economics of the state and the study of state capacity36,37. A central issue in this literature is that high-powered incentives are challenging to implement in bureaucracies, especially given the multiple responsibilities of bureaucrats and well-known concerns about multitasking37,38,39,40,41. Nonetheless, performance incentives for bureaucrats are used in many countries in sectors such as education and health42,43,44, as well as in efforts to stimulate local economic growth15,16,45, but they have been applied much less to population policy (at times in India and South Korea, for example), and, as in China, applications to population policy have been linked to concerns about coercion11,19,20,46,47,48,49,50,51 (Supplementary Note 29). Both India and South Korea introduced incentives for reproductive outcomes among government officials (promotion incentives in India during the Emergency period and financial bonuses for contraceptive service provision in South Korea), but to our knowledge, their effects on demographic outcomes have not been isolated and quantified. In the context of a broader literature on political economy and fertility52,53,54,55,56,57, our paper shows that by linking performance incentives with career concerns58,59,60,61, China’s OVV policy induced substantial increases in bureaucratic effort, helping to explain the effectiveness of a centrally mandated but unpopular policy. More generally, our findings provide new evidence on the importance of intensity of bureaucratic incentives, not simply the existence of policy targets (even in a system with China’s administrative reach).

Chinese policymakers now confront the challenge of persistently low fertility rates—far below the replacement rate—and accompanying population decline. Although relaxing the OCP has not reversed this trend, our research suggests that population policy contributed more to fertility decline in China than it has in other countries around the world, with strength of its bureaucratic incentives playing a critical role.

China’s national population control policies date back to the ‘later, longer, fewer’ campaign launched in the early 1970s, and they became increasingly stringent over time, ultimately culminating in the OCP in 1979–198069 (Supplementary Note 30). In principle, households violating the OCP faced serious consequences such as fines, loss of social benefits, and prohibition of job promotion (or even demotion)7. There was variation across provinces in the magnitude of these fines, although we find little evidence that fine rates changed with the implementation of the OVV (Supplementary Fig. 16). In some cases, women who exceeded birth quotas underwent coerced abortion or sterilization70,71,72. However, implementation of the OCP was also heterogeneous and, particularly in rural areas, it was unpopular and difficult in practice to enforce. In the aggregate, China’s TFR ultimately declined very little following its initial implementation in 1979–1980 (Fig. 1).

To address enforcement challenges, the OVV policy then greatly strengthened cadre evaluation system incentives to adhere to OCP targets, strictly prohibiting the career advancement of government officials for adherence failure73. As with many implementation-focused policies, the OVV was initially introduced and developed through local government experimentation before it was embraced by higher government authorities. Specifically, it was first conceived and introduced in the Changde prefecture of Hunan province across five counties in 1982, and within a year, all other counties in Changde prefecture had adopted it. The Changde government viewed the OVV as successful by 1988. The Hunan provincial government then embraced the OVV, implementing it across the province; several other provinces (including Hebei, Liaoning, Jiangxi and Shandong) followed, adopting the OVV before 1990. Following the release of a central government report in 1991, other provinces then revised their policies on OCP enforcement as well, gradually adopting the OVV, albeit at varying points in time. Refer to Supplementary Section B for more details on China’s birth control policies and the OVV.

Figure 1 shows that more widespread implementation of the OVV policy during the early 1990s coincided with a sharp decline in China’s TFR. Throughout most of the 1980s, China’s TFR was relatively stable and consistently above 2.5 children per woman despite the OCP. However, as the OVV was implemented across provinces early in the 1990s, China’s TFR declined rapidly, dropping below replacement fertility (Supplementary Note 31). By the end of the 1990s, the TFR had fallen to about 1.6 children per woman, plateauing at that rate for almost two decades (the OCP was in effect until 2015). Although period TFR was relatively stable through the 1980s, cohort fertility had been declining for some time as successive cohorts of Chinese women born at least as early as 1950 had progressively lower completed fertility. Supplementary Fig. 17 illustrates this point, showing women’s cumulative fertility by birth cohort, measured at ages 30, 35 and 40. Note that a sharp decline in the period TFR during the 1990s would appear as a gradual decline across cohorts—each cohort is exposed to the OVV only during childbearing years under the policy (Supplementary Note 32).

We first estimate the effect of the OVV policy on women’s annual probability of birth. To do so, we exploit the staggered implementation of the OVV policy across provinces. Specifically, we use a generalized DiD event study framework to estimate:

where \({{\mathsf{Birth}}}_{ipt}\) is an indicator for whether or not woman i in province p gave birth in calendar year t; k denotes event year (relative to the year of OVV implementation in woman i’s province, defined as event year 0); \({D}_{pt}^{k}\) is an event year dummy variable for the kth year before or after province p adopted the OVV policy; Xi is a vector of individual characteristics of woman i (highest level of education and ethnicity); and μp and νt are province and calendar-year fixed effects, respectively. Our primary coefficient of interest (βk) measures the dynamic effect of the OVV policy on the annual probability of birth over time, before and after its implementation. The lead term βk(k < 0) allows us to test for the presence of pre-existing birth trends correlated with the timing of the implementation of the OVV.

To address concerns about traditional two-way fixed effects estimation with heterogeneous treatment effects and staggered treatment timing, we use the approach proposed by Cengiz et al.26 and also report results using alternative approaches65,66,67,68 (Supplementary Note 33). We cluster our standard errors at the provincial level, or at the treatment cohort × province level when using Cengiz and colleagues’ procedure26 (Supplementary Note 34 and Supplementary Fig. 18).

We also re-estimate equation (1) separately by maternal parity (first, second, third and fourth or above), restricting the sample to women at risk of a birth of each parity. Furthermore, to explore the mechanisms underlying changes in annual probabilities of birth, we then re-estimate equation (1), replacing \({{\mathsf{Birth}}}_{ipt}\) with other outcomes including induced abortion, pregnancy, and contraceptive use (by type, and also degree of consent for IUD use and female sterilization).

To assess how changes in the annual probability of birth translate into changes in the TFR, we then use a discrete-time hazard framework analogous to equation (1), estimating the following probit model:

where \({M}_{it}^{g}={\mathbb{1}}({\mathrm{Age}}_{it}=g)\) is an indicator for maternal age group g (15–19, 20–24, … , 45–49). The coefficient θg captures baseline fertility differences across age groups, whereas \({\delta }_{g}^{k}\) captures the effect of the OVV policy in event year k specific to age group g. All other variables are defined as in equation (1). We estimate equation (2) separately by parity and use the resulting coefficient estimates to generate regression-adjusted predictions of birth probabilities for women at risk of first-, second-, third- and fourth-or-higher-order births (by maternal age group) in each event year. We then use these predicted probabilities of birth (qx) to construct sequential multi-decrement fertility life tables by event year, following the approach of Van Hook and Altman22, and Babiarz and colleagues9. By allowing the coefficients for event-year indicators and their interactions with maternal age groups to vary flexibly, this specification captures time-varying and age-by-parity effects of the OVV policy9. With predicted probabilities, we compute survival probabilities (lx, that is, the probabilities of not having a parity-specific birth by age x) and then maternal age-by-parity birth rates (dx). Aggregating the dx values across all parities yields ASFRs, and summing these ASFRs produces the TFR for a given event year (Supplementary Note 35).

This study is based on secondary analysis of de-identified data from the 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey. The survey was designed and administered under the supervision of the National Family Planning Commission of China. Informed consent was obtained from all participants at the time of the survey.

The OVV implementation year varies by province (n = 30 provinces), and the coverage rate is weighted by provincial population to reflect the national population exposure over time. Data: China Population Statistics Yearbook.

Notes: The figure shows DiD estimates for the annual probability of birth from Equation (1) using the Cengiz et al.26 approach, estimated separately by birth parity for (a) first, (b) second, (c) third, and (d) fourth-or-higher-order births. Standard errors are clustered at the treatment cohort  × province level. The sample used includes women ages 15-49 in 2001, and their births between years 1980 and 2001 (n = 1,906,333 woman-year observations; 36,375 unique women). Data are presented as estimated DiD event-study coefficients (point estimates) with 95% confidence intervals. Solid lines with markers show the coefficient estimates, and dashed lines show the corresponding 95% confidence intervals, which are two-sided and pointwise (not adjusted for multiple comparisons). The red vertical line represents the time of OVV policy implementation. Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: The figure shows DiD estimates for the annual probability of birth from Equation (1) using the Cengiz et al.26 approach, estimated separately for (a) provinces with high (above-median) baseline fertility (n = 873,819) and (b) provinces with low (below-median) baseline fertility (n = 429,672). Standard errors are clustered at the treatment cohort  × province level. The sample used includes women ages 15-49 in 2001, and their births between years 1980 and 2001. Data are presented as estimated DiD event-study coefficients (point estimates) with 95% confidence intervals. Solid lines with markers show the coefficient estimates, and dashed lines show the corresponding 95% confidence intervals, which are two-sided and pointwise (not adjusted for multiple comparisons). The red vertical line represents the time of OVV policy implementation. Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: The figure shows DiD estimates for the annual probability of birth from Equation (1) using the Cengiz et al.26 approach, where each event-year indicator is fully interacted with a group dummy, allowing the event-time coefficients to vary by group. Panels present event-time coefficients separately for mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive groups: (a) Han majority women, (b) ethnic minority women, (c) rural residents, (d) urban residents, (e) women with less than a high school education, and (f) women with a high school education or above. Standard errors are clustered at the treatment cohort  × province level. The sample is the full stacked DiD dataset (n = 1,906,333 woman-year observations; 36,375 unique women). Data are presented as group-specific estimated DiD event-study coefficients (point estimates) with 95% confidence intervals. Solid lines with markers show the coefficient estimates, and dashed lines show the corresponding 95% confidence intervals, which are two-sided and pointwise (not adjusted for multiple comparisons across groups or event years). Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: The figure shows event study estimates of the effect of the OVV policy on province-year fertility rates, constructed from two alternative data sources as described in the main text: (a) the 2000 Population Census and (b) the 2005 Population Survey (‘Mini-Census’). Standard errors are clustered at the treatment cohort  × provincial level, following the Cengiz et al.26 approach. Data are presented as estimated event-study coefficients for the effect of OVV on province-year fertility rates (point estimates) with 95% confidence intervals. Solid lines with markers show the coefficient estimates, and dashed lines show the corresponding 95% confidence intervals, which are two-sided and pointwise (not adjusted for multiple comparisons). The red vertical line represents the time of OVV policy implementation. The estimation sample is 1,819 stacked province-year observations. Data: 2000 Population Census; 2005 Population Survey (Mini-Census).

Notes: The figure shows DiD estimates for IUD use from Equation (1) using the Cengiz et al.26 approach, estimated separately by maternal parity, where parity denotes the number of previous births: (a) parity 0, (b) parity 1, (c) parity 2, and (d) parity 3 or higher. Standard errors are clustered at the treatment cohort  × province level. The sample used includes women ages 15-49 in 2001, and their use of IUD between years 1980 and 2001, with 896,381 (parity 0), 484,669 (parity 1), 347,759 (parity 2), and 177,489 (parity 3 or higher) woman-year observations. Data are presented as estimated DiD event-study coefficients (point estimates) with 95% confidence intervals. Solid lines with markers show the coefficient estimates, and dashed lines show the corresponding 95% confidence intervals, which are two-sided and pointwise (not adjusted for multiple comparisons). The red vertical line represents the time of OVV policy implementation. Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: The figure shows the total fertility rate (TFR) for each event year, derived from fertility life tables constructed using microdata from the 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey (the event-study sample: 36,375 women). The red vertical line represents the time of OVV policy implementation. For more details, see Methods.

Notes: The figure shows the observed age-specific fertility rate (ASFR) (in blue with square markers) and the counterfactual ASFR without the OVV policy (in pink with circle markers), by maternal age group: (a) ages 15–19, (b) ages 20–24, (c) ages 25–29, (d) ages 30–34, and (e) ages 35–49. The counterfactual ASFR is calculated by subtracting the policy-driven change in TFR implied by estimates in the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) section from the observed ASFR in each event year (see Methods). Estimates are derived from the event-study sample (n = 1,906,333 woman-year observations). Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: This figure shows the implied density functions of maternal age at childbirth before and after the OVV policy (solid lines, before OVV; dashed lines, after OVV), by maternal parity: (a) first, (b) second, (c) third, and (d) fourth-or-higher-order births. In each panel, we analyze a sample of women-years, limited to mothers who are at risk of, and eventually achieve, a higher parity within the sample period. Sample sizes are 606,452 (parity 1), 373,926 (parity 2), 271,597 (parity 3), and 100,088 (parity 4 or higher) woman-year observations. We estimate a discrete-time hazard model using a probit specification in which the dependent variable is whether or not a woman advances in parity. The independent variables include an OVV policy indicator, age dummies, and their interactions. Using the model estimates, we first predict the likelihood of childbirth at each age, both with and without OVV. Then, we apply a single decrement life table approach to map changes in age-specific annual probabilities of birth, allowing us to predict shifts in the distribution of age at childbirth. Data: 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey.

Notes: Total fertility rate (TFR) by event year, estimated from fertility life tables using 2001 National Family Planning and Reproductive Health Survey microdata (the event-study sample: 36,375 women). The tempo-adjusted TFR’ (light navy) corrects for shifts in childbearing timing to isolate changes in quantum (completed) fertility32. The red vertical line marks the implementation of the OVV policy. See Methods for further details.

#1311. Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

Then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI

The other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi

In truth it was more pantomime than meaningful and Henderson, like another former, Champions League-winning Liverpool midfielder Xabi Alonso – now Chelsea’s head coach – did not celebrate as Morgan Rogers scored. The penalty came after a rash challenge by Gravenberch, who crashed into Moisés Caicedo as the Chelsea captain ran on to Malo Gusto’s shrewd reverse pass inside the area.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. Despite injury to João Pedro and Cole Palmer’s suspension, there was only a place on the Chelsea bench for the 19-year-old Brazilian. And he stayed there even though Alonso used all five substitutions. Estêvão has made just two starts under Alonso, both in this competition. “The season is long and there will be moments for everyone,” Alonso said.

It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. The 23-year-old striker’s contributions amounted to having his shoot-out penalty saved and then bizarrely and violently charging at Virgil van Dijk – his fellow Dutchman, is there an issue there? – long after the ball had gone, pushing the Liverpool captain over.

Virgil van Dijk was NOT HAPPY with Emmanuel Emegha 😒 https://t.co/UEtoJ7n5va

Alonso said the exit was a “small set-back,” and maybe it was, even if he started with a stronger side than Iraola. But with Chelsea not in European competition and unlikely to win the Premier League, it means he is already down to the FA Cup should silverware be won this season.

There is no VAR at this stage of the competition but referee Darren England appeared to get all the big calls right. Rogers claimed a penalty before Chelsea’s one was awarded, but Ronald Araújo was probably just too strong.

Morgan Rogers wants a penalty but he won't be getting one 🙅‍♂️ The referee waves it away and there's no VAR to step in... https://t.co/VR6yhBrx0I

And Liverpool’s penalty? Just what was Fofana thinking? Only three minutes after the lead was gained, Chelsea relinquished it as Van Dijk rose to win a header and Fofana had his arm outstretched. The ball struck it and Cody Gakpo beat Penders from the spot.

SEVEN League Cup games at Anfield - EIGHT goals for the Dutchman 👏 Cody Gakpo is the Carabao Cup king 👑 https://t.co/KaysZedwYr

Little did we know then it would be the first of 17 penalties, 12 of them successful, in front of the Kop with the last being Fofana’s.

"We are really happy with the performance!" Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola on his side's win over Chelsea in the Carabao Cup 👏 https://t.co/kW9DFXG5Iy

🗣️ "I had this paper but everything was wrong" 😆 Giorgi Mamardashvili's penalty notes weren't very helpful but that didn't stop the Georgian becoming Liverpool's shootout hero 🇬🇪 https://t.co/ckU9TOJoY3

🗣️ "[Gomez] was very confident, he was ready to shoot in the first five and I knew he was going to score" 😁 Andoni Iraola on Joe Gomez, Mamardashvili and Liverpool's newer players. 🎙️ @gabrielclarke05 https://t.co/mNLkTbCpOw

🗣️ "We want to show that fight and grit. It's mentality and I think that's what we're known for" 💪 Joe Gomez after Liverpool's victory over Chelsea in the Carabao Cup 🎙️ @gabrielclarke05 https://t.co/fjrbXp0L96

Fleetwood vs Everton/NewcastleManchester City vs BradfordCrystal Palace vs SunderlandLiverpool vs Bournemouth

Fixtures to be played the week commencing December 14.

We are just getting under way to find out the four ties in the quarter-finals.

BradfordFleetwoodManchester CityBournemouthCrystal PalaceSunderlandLiverpool

There is one more spot up for grabs when Everton host Newcastle tomorrow night. The draw is about to take place.

Manchester City 2 Brighton 2 (Manchester City won 4-3 on penalties)Bournemouth 3 Aston Villa 0 Fulham 0 Crystal Palace 1Sunderland 3 Brentford 2Liverpool 1 Chelsea 1 (Liverpool won 6-5 on penalties)

Possession: Liverpool 52%-48% ChelseaShots: 10-11Shots on target: 4-4Corners: 7-5Touches in opposition box: 20-21

Fofana blazes into The Kop and Liverpool take their place in the League Cup quarter-finals. Liverpool have now won all five shootouts against Chelsea.

Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties to reach the Carabao Cup quarter-finals! 🔴 https://t.co/pnCYwRrYzi

The Englishman has never scored a senior goal for Liverpool but emphatically smashes this into the top right corner.

Mamardashvili guesses correctly and makes the save to his right.

Penders makes the save and Chelsea, who now have the chance to go through.

The Englishman lifts it high into the net and we go on.

An emphatic penalty from the Frenchman right into the top left corner.

The former Liverpool captain has to score and he does, sending it down the middle. To sudden death we go...

The Greek defender has a chance to seal Liverpool’s place in the final eight but sends it over the bar.

The Argentine strikes the left post and Liverpool will have the chance to book their place in the quarter-finals with their next penalty.

The German makes no mistake, sending Penders the wrong way and putting it into the bottom right corner.

The Belgian calmly steps up and sends Mamardashvili the wrong way, putting into the right corner of the net.

The Dutchman scored Liverpool’s equaliser from the spot and smashes this one into the bottom left corner, with Penders going the wrong way.

He scored during the game and finds the net again. Mamardashvili goes the right way but the penalty from Rogers is very good, going right into the bottom left corner.

Again, Penders guesses the right way but, like Mac Allister, Isak lifts it brilliantly into the top of the net.

The Portuguese finds the net and we are all square after one penalty each.

Penders went the right way but Mac Allister lifts it over the Chelsea keeper.

They will be taken at The Kop. Chelsea goalkeeper Penders disappeared down the tunnel after the full-time whistle and re-emerges with a towel, potentially some penalty-saving notes as well?

Liverpool will take first and it will be Mac Allister who steps up first...

The final whistle is blown so we go to penalties at Anfield.

Looks like we are heading for penalties and if you are looking for omens... Liverpool and Chelsea have had four shootouts in the past: Liverpool won them all - the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 European Super Cup final, the 2022 League Cup final and the 2022 FA Cup Final.

A word on VAR (again). Watching this competition without the presence of the joy-killing invention is liberating. An occassional decision might get missed but, in the long term, you could live with that if meant you didn’t hear the words “it’s being checked by Stockley Park”. The decision just before, when Florian Wirtz’s shot touched Levi Colwill’s hand, was a case in point. It wasn’t a penalty but VAR being brought into play might convince you it was. Let’s get rid of it, please.

Double change for Liverpool as Isak and Mac Allister replace Ngumoha and Nyoni.

Huge double block from Chelsea and how have Liverpool not scored? Tsimikas’ cross to the back post is headed back across the six-yard box to find Wirtz, who you think is going to score but Colwill makes the block. Then Barcola has a shot blocked by Acheampong.

It is full time at both Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light, where Crystal Palace and Sunderland have booked their places in the League Cup quarter-finals.

Tsimikas gives it away inside his own half and Chelsea counter. Neto drives inside and finds Rogers, who skips past Gomez. Rogers then finds the overlapping Palestra on the left side of the box and the Italian is denied by Mamardashvili at his near post.

Manchester City have just beaten Brighton 4-3 on penalties whilst on the south coast Bournemouth have comfortably beaten Aston Villa 3-0. Both sides are into the hat for tonight’s quarter-final draw.

Lavia cynically brings down Ngumoha as the Liverpool forward drove through the Chelsea half and is correctly booked.

Liverpool are taking off Van Dijk and Jacquet is coming on in his place. No injury for Van Dijk.

What a terrific cup tie this has been. It helps when there is an edge between the sides and you can feel the tension in the air. What has been noticeable in the last three games at Anfield, though, is the change in the atmosphere. Slowly but surely the locals are buying into what Andoni Iraola is trying to achieve. Liverpool could lose this game tonight by going all out to win it but there is a clearly identity developing that makes you think they are starting to get on the right lines.

After Gakpo fouls Lavia, Chelsea have a free-kick just over 25 yards out. Rogers lines it up but his effort is terrible, flying into The Kop.

Chelsea are going to make a triple change. Palestra, Barco and Emegha come on, with the latter on for his Chelsea debut. Gusto, Caicedo and Welbeck head off.

Good save from Penders. The ball comes to Barcola outside the Chelsea penalty area. The Frenchman drives inside before getting his shot away from the edge of the box. The shot takes a small deflection and Penders does well to make the save down to his left.

The game between Manchester City and Brighton at The Etihad has ended 2-2, therefore it has now gone to penalties.

Chances at both ends. Gomez whips in a cross from the right and picks out Araujo in the centre of the box but the Uruguayan’s powerful header is straight at Penders. He probably should have scored.

Then Chelsea counter and Rogers is in acres of space. His shot from just outside the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner, which comes to nothing.

Gusto’s behaviour in recent minutes has been appalling. First he went down after virtually no contact from Van Dijk and now goes down again, once more not a foul. He shows his boot to the linesman as if it came off in a challenge from Barcola but the replays show that his boot did not come off and he was attempting to con the officials.

Andoni Iraola is turning to his bench for the first time tonight and makes a double substitution as Wirtz and Barcola replace McConnell and Koumas. Some double change that for Liverpool!

Fascinating to watchg Trey Nyoni and the responsibility he has taken on his shoulders. He’s only 19 but those who have worked with him since he arrived at Liverpool as a 16-year-old will tell you he has a maturity of someone in their mid-twenties. He has tried to get on the ball and play, he’s been strong when it’s been required and always been in the right place to get a foot in. He’s going to play a lot of games for Liverpool if he maintains this trajectory.

Achemapong scythes Ngumoha down as the latter cut inside and the former is correctly booked.

Down on the south coast, Bournemouth appear to be cruising into the quarter-finals as Alvaro Rodriguez has put them 3-0 up against Aston Villa.

Should Rogers have done better there? In fortuitous circumstances, he is played through but he does not show the conviction to drive towards the Liverpool penalty area. His touch lets him and the ball rolls through to Mamardashvili.

Moments later, Rogers forces Mamadrashvili into a save to his left and the Liverpool players are furious that a handball was not given. It clearly hit Rogers’ arm before he shot but Chelsea do have the corner. Chelsea play it short before eventually Henderson swings it in before Araujo heads away.

We are back under way at Anfield. No changes from either side at the break.

Manchester City have equalised at home against Brighton, with Rayan Cherki’s free-kick from just outside the box taking a big deflection off his teammate Vitor Reis and ending up in the back ot the Brighton net.

Manchester City 1 Brighton 2 (70’)Bournemouth 2 Aston Villa 0 (58’)Fulham 0 Crystal Palace 1 (56’)Sunderland 3 Brentford 1 (56’)Liverpool 1 Chelsea 1 HT

Bournemouth have doubled their advantage against Aston Villa through Lewis Cook just over five minutes into the second half.

Possession: Liverpool 50%-50% ChelseaShots: 6-2Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 5-0Touches in opposition box: 5-9

The first half is brought to an end at Anfield and the game is level at 1-1 going into the break. Rogers put Chelsea in front from the spot only for Gakpo to also score a penalty moments later to equalise for Liverpool.

The outswinging corner is sent in from the left but Araujo’s header goes over the bar. Meanwhile, Lacroix is slowly limping his way around the pitch to the tunnel and is moving very gingerly, which could suggest an extended period on the sidelines.

As we enter three minutes of added time, Colwill replaces the injured Lacroix.

Liverpool can sense a second goal. First, Gakpo has a shot saved by Penders before Ngumoha wins the hosts a corner. Before that is taken, play has been stopped as Lacroix is down clutching at his left hamstring.

Not a murmur from Xabi Alonso as his side take the lead. The penalty Morgan Rogers dispatched went in the same corner as Alonso picked in the 2007 Champions League semi-final and perhaps he had a sense of what was coming as Liverpool are now level and it’s a fair reflection of how an intriguing opening 45 minutes has played out. It really wouldn’t be a surprise if we need spot-kicks to separate these teams at 90 minutes.

Like Rogers moments ago, Gakpo sends the goalkeeper the wrong way and puts the penalty away to equalise. Gakpo slots into the bottom left corner in front of The Kop and the Dutchman continues his fine scoring record in this competition. Both sides have been gifted penalties and both teams take advantage.

Cody Gakpo slots home a penalty to equalise for Liverpool against Chelsea! 💪 https://t.co/rS775LH0Gb

Like London buses, two penalties come in quick succession. From a Liverpool corner out on the left, Fofana is penalised for a handball and the referee has no choice but to point to the spot. The Chelsea players protest but it clearly hit Fofana’s arm, which was above his head.

Rogers sends Mamardashvili the wrong way and puts Chelsea 1-0 up in front of their travelling supporters. It was a quality penalty from Rogers, who deposited it into the right corner of the goal. It is a gift for Chelsea, who did not look like scoring but are gifted a chance to score through that silly Gravenberch challenge.

Morgan Rogers puts Chelsea in front against Liverpool from the spot! 🎯 https://t.co/ocMXFNCW9F

Caicedo goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area and the referee points to the spot. It is a silly and needless challenge from Gravenberch, who slides into the back of Caicedo and gives the referee no choice but to give a penalty. Not that it would be overturned but there is no VAR anyway.

Ex-Liverpool man Henderson was holding the ball for a while but now hands over to Rogers to take...

They are into the second half at Manchester and Brighton have retaken the lead through Georginio Rutter. Brighton now lead Manchester City 2-1.

That is a gift from Chelsea. The communication at the back between Gusto and Fofana is poor, with the former playing a poor pass backwards looking for Fofana, who cannot reach it and the ball rolls behind for the easiest of corners for Liverpool in front of The Kop.

Gakpo takes an outswinging corner but Welbeck is on hand to head away at the front post.

We are yet to see the first goal of the night at Anfield but they are flying in at the Stadium of Light. Brentford have pulled a goal back against Sunderland through Callum Wilson and it is now 3-1 in the north east.

Chelsea want a penalty. Rogers goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area under a challenge from Araujo but it was a fair shoulder-to-shoulder challenge and that is not a penalty.

At the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in dreamland. Malick Fofana has put them 3-0 up against Brentford closing in on half-time.

A wasted free kick from Chelsea, and goodness, Austin McPhee is not happy. Chelsea’s set piece coach was up on the touchline, remonstrating to nobody in particular but it was obvious to see the frustration that the plan he has worked on - a chip to the side, a cutback into the middle - has fallen down at the first attempt. To compound his fury, McPhee just blew a gasket after Chelsea were not awarded a penalty following a coming together between Ronald Araujo and Morgan Rogers.

Tsimikas has let Ngumoha down there. Ngumoha does brilliantly to dribble through two Chelsea defenders around the halfway line and drives down the left. He then plays the ball outside to Tsimikas, who should do so much better with his cross but picks out the front-post defender Lacroix.

Meanwhile at Craven Cottage, Crystal Palace have taken the lead at Fulham thanks to Eddie Nketiah.

McConnell becomes the second Liverpool player to be booked tonight for handball. He lost the ball on halfway and cynically handled the ball as Rogers attempted to counter. A fairly clear-cut booking for McConnell there.

A reminder that there is no VAR tonight and if the game is level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. Referee Darren England has summoned Chelsea captain Caicedo and former Liverpool midfielder Henderson over for a word.

Caicedo puts Tsimikas’ cross from the left behind for the first corner of the night. Gakpo sends in the inswinger but the whistle goes as Chelsea are awarded a free-kick for a foul from Tsimikas on Gusto.

There has yet to be a goal at Anfield but at the Stadium of Light Sunderland have doubled their lead over Brentford courtesy of Tymur Tutierov’s goal.

The first booking of the night at Anfield goes the way of the home side. Koumas slides in to try and block a clearance from Lacroix and is booked. Koumas barely touched Lacroix and that is never a yellow card.

Meanwhile, in the north east, Sunderland have taken the lead against Brentford through Chemsdine Talbi.

Brighton had led in Manchester but the home side have just equalised. Mateo Kovacic has scored from range to bring Manchester City level with five minutes to go in the first half.

Clear to see in these early exchanges that Cody Gakpo has been deployed as Liverpool’s main “striker” with Lewis Koumas, James McConnell - who played in the 2024 final when Liverpool beat Chelsea 1-0 - and Rio Ngumoha operating in behind him. Jordan Henderson seems to be the man whom Xabi Alonso wants to trigger Chelsea’s press. They are playing a rigid 4-5-1 formation but, this being Alonso, the system is always flexible. His ethos is to be able to play two or three systems in a game if needed.

Ngumoha drives at Neto down Liverpool’s left and is felled by the Portuguese forward. It is an obvious free-kick and Neto is a touch fortunate not to be booked for that blatant foul. Ngumoha, who was fantastic for Liverpool against Villarreal in the Champions League just over a week ago, already into the action.

Tsimikas clips in the delivery but it is headed away by Lacroix.

The second goal in the League Cup this evening has come in Manchester and has gone the way of the away side. Malick Yalcouye has put Brighton in front against Manchester City on the half-hour mark.

We are under way at Anfield. Who will book their place in the League Cup quarter-finals; Liverpool or Chelsea?

Jordan Henderson is busily going around geeing up Chelsea’s players, in exactly the same fashion as he did when he played in this stadium for 12 years. He got an ovation here in May, when Brentford drew 1-1, that left him extremely emotional but it remains to be seen what will happen when he gets his first touch this evening. There has been no acknowledgement - yet - from The Kop and the same is true for Xabi Alonso. But, then again, why would there be when there is such lingering enmity between these clubs?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at Anfield. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Has come on the south coast, where Bournemouth have taken the lead against Aston Villa courtesy of Amine Adli’s goal inside the opening 10 minutes.

“The cups are important for us this year. For sure, we face today a good challenge, coming to Anfield, and we want to be in the next round. It is another competition. We know it is another format, it is make-or-break, so we want to make it happen today with a great performance.

“From the beginning we have taken it seriously. We have a tough game and we want to have a good feeling that we are competing. We have to do many great things. In one game there can be many little games with the energy created. These players have played here before. We have practiced penalties but sometimes it is about the feeling of the day.”

The games at the Vitality Stadium, Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light have just begun. That means four of the five ties tonight have started, with just the game at Anfield to begin in just over 10 minutes.

At The Etihad, Manchester City have kicked off against Brighton. Then, there are three 7.45pm kick-offs before Liverpool begin against Chelsea at Anfield at 8pm.

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

Manchester City vs Brighton 7.30pmBournemouth vs Aston Villa 7.45pmFulham vs Crystal Palace 7.45pmSunderland vs Brentford 7.45pmLiverpool vs Chelsea 8pm

Come on you Reds ✊🔴 https://t.co/o9Rc2yjV7c

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

Arsenal have been handed a fresh fitness concern after Martin Zubimendi was forced off during Spain’s dramatic 3-2 Nations League defeat to England in Madrid.

The midfielder appeared to suffer a hamstring problem during the second half at the Metropolitano Stadium and was unable to continue, giving Mikel Arteta another issue to monitor before Premier League football resumes.

Zubimendi has not been a guaranteed starter this season following the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes and the continued form of Declan Rice, but Arsenal’s demanding schedule means losing another experienced midfielder would still be a significant blow.

The Evening Standard reports that Zubimendi hobbled off against England after appearing to hurt his hamstring.

Luis de la Fuente replaced him with Nico Williams during the second half, with Zubimendi pictured grimacing and holding the back of his leg after leaving the pitch.

There has not yet been confirmation over the seriousness of the problem, leaving Arsenal waiting for a clearer medical assessment.

The timing is far from ideal. Arteta’s side return from the international break with a trip to Newcastle United before facing Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League and Manchester City in the Premier League before the end of November.

Zubimendi may currently find himself behind Rice, Guimaraes and other midfield options, but that does not reduce his importance over a long season.

In fact, his potential absence highlights why Arsenal should be extremely cautious about entertaining transfer interest in January.

A recent CaughtOffside report on Zubimendi’s Arsenal future noted that the Spaniard remains patient despite his reduced role and that Arsenal could still need him when injuries and suspensions begin to accumulate.

That argument suddenly looks even more relevant.

Arteta is managing a squad competing for the Premier League and Champions League, and midfield depth could become crucial during the winter months.

The encouraging part is that there is currently no confirmation of a serious injury. Arsenal will hope the substitution was precautionary rather than the beginning of a lengthy absence.

But until the medical picture becomes clearer, Zubimendi’s fitness will be another concern for Arteta heading into a crucial run of fixtures.

Manchester United are expected to back Mauricio Pochettino in the January transfer window, with a new centre-back and striker emerging as the club’s two priority positions.

Pochettino is preparing to begin work at Old Trafford after replacing Michael Carrick, and strengthening a squad that has badly underperformed this season will be one of his first major tasks.

United invested heavily in midfield during the summer, but Benjamin Sesko’s injury problems and questions over their defensive options have forced the club to reconsider where resources should be directed next.

According to Fabrizio Romano, senior figures at Manchester United have already made it clear that they intend to be active when the window opens.

Romano said: “Pochettino will be part of the conversations in terms of transfers. The message coming from Man United’s people is, ‘In January, we will do things.’

“So I expect at least a signing, but there could be even more — there could be two or more.”

Romano continued: “My understanding is that the two key areas they want to cover at United are centre-back, because United believe they could do something in that position in the January transfer window, and a striker.

”To add one more striker to the team [is the aim], considering the physical issues of Benjamin Sesko, it’s a serious possibility. So striker, centre-back — let’s see what happens.”

Football365’s report on Romano’s Man United transfer update also notes that left-back could still be assessed once Pochettino holds detailed recruitment discussions with the club.

Prioritising another striker makes obvious sense.

Sesko’s prolonged absence has left United without a reliable natural No.9, while Joshua Zirkzee has struggled for opportunities. Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo can operate centrally, but neither offers the profile of a conventional centre-forward.

CaughtOffside reported that United are expected to support Pochettino with both attacking and defensive reinforcements, reinforcing the belief that at least two deals could be explored.

Centre-back is a little more debatable. United already have Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt, Lisandro Martinez, Harry Maguire and Ayden Heaven, although age, injuries and inconsistent performances mean another long-term option could still be justified.

The key for Pochettino will be quality rather than quantity. United have repeatedly spent heavily without building a balanced squad.

January should therefore be about fixing clear weaknesses with players who suit the new manager, rather than simply making signings to create an immediate reaction.

#1308. Mancini: ‘Italy will learn from this, but Belgium were better on the night’

Roberto Mancini admits Belgium ‘were better on the night’ to beat Italy 4-1, but believes it can ‘help us going forward’ in the growth process.

The Azzurri went into Brussels knowing a point would suffice to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals, and had the perfect start when taking the lead through Francesco Pio Esposito.

However, they were trailing 3-1 within 15 minutes as Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy and Jeremy Doku turned it all around.

Although Pio Esposito saw his late penalty parried by Senne Lammens, the Red Devils added a fourth on the counter-attack through Milan winger Diego Moreira.

“They were better, we suffered too much on a physical level, in one on one situations. We started well, but they were better on the night,” Mancini told RAI Sport.

“When the ball got to the wings, we struggled to have the right pressing, they caused us problems, we felt some fatigue from the France match, but they deserved the victory, there’s nothing more to say.”

Considering Italy had lost the first match 2-0 at home to Belgium on September 25 and they went into Matchday 6 top of the group, it was still a remarkable Nations League run with plenty to build on going forward.

“These nights can happen in the growth process, you need to learn from these experiences. Considering the way we got here, we had the chance to qualify, but we knew it would be tough, as Belgium are a strong team,” added Mancini.

“We are sad, but this night will help us going forward.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma was booked and will therefore be suspended for the next Italy match, but it won’t be in the Nations League quarter-finals.

Instead, France go through as group winners, with Belgium in second place.

If you would have told me that Italy would get 10 points in this group I would have said no way. So all in all we’ve got to be happy. Great to see all the youth on the field. I am sure Mancini learned a lot

Still a work in progress; no need to panic. Got the qualifiers. Look tired this evening, we will bounce back.

The endeavour was there, but not the quality! Going to gave bumps in the road going forwards, so best to identify and learn from those mistakes now! However, overall, a very positive Nations League campaign with lots of positives to build on!

cambiaghi and fratesi missed..pissili and kealosho very poor…figioli also fint help….than mancini took out tonali for fear of red card and became even more worse… …..the substitutes were poor….I could see only kayode and barella working hard till the end …. bastoni and scalvini were bad today….lack of communication between players felt……

Mancini says Italy will learn from this but honestly i don’t think they will. These crop of players are not good enough. We are light years away from even being contenders to win any major tournaments. Football is finished in Italy, i’m sorry to say. Italy is living on past glories and nostalgia, it’s over. They’ll never win anything again. Going forward now, just be grateful that they might qualify for tournaments and enjoy early round exits. That’s Italy of today, tomorrow and the future.
