#1299. Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nic Fleming is a science writer in Bristol, UK.

Container ships were forced to dock at ports in the United Arab Emirates and other Middle Eastern nations after the Iranian government announced that it would close the Strait of Hormuz in July.Credit: AFP via Getty Images

Protesters burnt tyres and blocked roads in Syria over fuel prices. French fishers blockaded a fuel depot and clashed with police. Government and household budgets were squeezed around the world as interest rates rose and the sales of electric vehicles roughly doubled year-on-year in several countries, including Australia, Brazil and India.

These were just some of the many knock-on effects of the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran that began in February. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 25% of the world’s oil trade and 20% of exported liquefied natural gas previously passed, caused what the International Energy Agency (IEA) called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”, as fuel prices spiked worldwide.

The resulting strain has exacerbated the economic pressures already felt from previous shocks, including the Russia–Ukraine war, the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2008 global financial crash, as well as from the continuing effects of climate change. The current global energy-security picture is “really bad on all fronts”, says Dan Marks, an energy-security researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London. “It’s something of a perfect storm.”

Governments seeking to improve national energy security are taking a variety of approaches — from measures to reduce demand and increase electrification to infrastructure updates and incentive programmes to encourage renewable-energy investment. Researchers, meanwhile, are doing their bit, driving scientific and technological advances that have the potential to deliver a stable and sustainable future energy mix.

Human energy consumption is both growing and changing (see ‘Powering the planet’). Use of global primary energy — naturally occurring energy sources that have not undergone any processing by humans — more than doubled between 1980 and 2025. Over that period, consumption increased from around 85,000 terawatt hours (TWh) annually to 178,000 TWh. That’s approximately 71 times the yearly primary-energy consumption of France.

Electrification — the replacement of technologies that burn fossil fuels with alternatives powered by electricity — is advancing in many countries as various industries look into switching to renewables. Worldwide, electricity demand is predicted to increase by around 40% by 2035, compared with current levels (see ‘The road ahead’). Despite this, many industries are still reliant on fossil fuels. Close to 99% of aviation and more than 90% of shipping relies on fossil fuels, for example. One-quarter of extracted natural gas is used to heat industrial buildings, and around 21% is used for heating and cooking in homes worldwide. Most of the rest (40%) is used to generate electricity. Although the share of primary energy generated by renewables is growing, oil, coal and gas still account for about 80% of energy production.

The IEA defines energy security as reliable, affordable access to all fuels and energy sources. Marks and others highlight that priorities vary internationally, with reliability often seen as of primary importance in high-income countries and affordability taking precedence in low-income nations. The impacts of global shocks to fuel supplies and prices also vary according to how reliant countries are on imported fossil fuels. “There isn’t one global energy-security picture, but many different context-dependent pictures,” says Severin Borenstein, an energy economist at the University of California, Berkeley.

Economies that rely on imported oil products are particularly vulnerable to the current shocks. The World Food Programme, part of the United Nations, estimated in March that the US–Iran war could push an extra 45 million people into acute hunger, taking this year’s total to 363 million, as increasing oil and gas costs push up the prices of fuel, food and other crucial products such as fertilizer. “If, like in a lot of African countries, people are dependent on travelling long distances in vehicles and on other imported oil products, large oil-price increases can be existentially problematic,” says Marks. Some high-income nations have also been hit hard. In Japan — which was importing more than 90% of its crude oil from the Middle East before the conflict — household electricity bills have risen to their highest levels in three years, and government borrowing costs have risen to a 30-year high.

By contrast, nations with domestic fuel supplies have been partially insulated. Although car users in the United States have seen big fuel-price increases, the country’s ample supplies of natural gas have shielded the nation from severe economic hardships. “In most developed free-market economies, there isn’t an energy-security issue in the sense of availability,” says Borenstein. “There are price and macro-economic issues. Some countries, like the United States, are better protected than others.”

Global oil prices have jumped since the US–Iran war broke out. Brent Crude futures contracts, a global oil-price benchmark, hit US$126 a barrel in April — up from around $70 before the conflict. This has affected consumers and businesses, but not as much as some previous energy crises. During the Yom Kippur War, coordinated action by oil-producing countries caused prices to more than triple between October 1973 and January 1974. And oil prices more than doubled after the 1978–79 Iranian revolution.

Many economists think that the global economy is better placed to avoid the soaring inflation, unemployment and recessions seen in many industrialized nations after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks. The ‘oil intensity’ of the global economy, that is, how much oil is needed to generate a unit of gross domestic product (GDP) in the form of goods and services, has fallen by more than 50% since the 1970s. And the IEA, established after the 1973 oil crisis, also requires its 32 member countries to keep reserves of at least 90 days’ worth of crude oil to guard against supply shocks. “For most of the developed world, it’s a big inconvenience, and, for some, a substantial budget squeeze, but it’s not the complete disruption of the economy seen in the 1970s,” says Borenstein.

But economic and energy-security challenges are also expected to grow owing to climate change. Droughts are becoming more frequent and severe, resulting in big reductions in hydropower generation in nations such as China, Brazil, the United States, Spain and Zambia. Low water levels in rivers, including the Rhine and Danube in Europe, the Amazon in South America and the Yangtze in China, have caused freight delivery problems. The other effects of climate change include reduced wind-energy generation and increased demand for power to run air-conditioning units.

Governments, policymakers and others who are working to tackle energy-security challenges have various options. Reducing energy demand, especially for oil and gas, by electrifying industrial processes and home heating, for example, helps with these issues, especially in nations that are heavily reliant on imported fossil fuels. Managing demand volatility through improved energy storage and ensuring that power grids can transition towards greater energy generation from renewables are also part of the picture, Marks says.

Although governments and business leaders have parts to play in energy-demand management, electrification and infrastructure investments, researchers are driving scientific and technical innovations that support energy security. Tapping underground heat to produce geothermal energy, for example, emits only small amounts of greenhouse gases and can be used to generate electricity or to heat buildings. However, at present, geothermal energy produces less than 1% of electricity globally because few locations have the right combination of accessible underground heat, water and permeable rock.

That could change thanks to advances in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), in which underground fractures are expanded or created in hot areas, and then fluids are pumped down, heated up and transferred back to the surface, usually to drive turbines and generate electricity.

Russia has been experiencing a fuel crisis since mid-June caused by increased Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries. Credit: Contributor/Getty Images News

There have been small-scale EGS research operations since the 1970s, but drilling times and costs have fallen substantially in the decades since thanks to techniques adapted from the oil and gas industries. These include the fracturing of rock with pressurized fluids, known as fracking, horizontal drilling to increase the exposure of fluid to heat reservoirs and the use of tougher, faster polycrystalline diamond compact drill bits. “It’s hard to overestimate how much of a game changer the new techniques have been,” says Roland Horne, a geothermal-energy engineer at Stanford University in California.

These innovations are driving investments in large commercial plants. One of the biggest of these is the Cape Station project operated by Fervo Energy near Milford in Utah, which began delivering power in September and plans to build the capacity to generate 500 megawatts (MW) by 2028 — enough electricity to power around 500,000 US homes.

However, there are obstacles to overcome. A number of EGS projects have been halted owing to earthquakes that geologists linked to increased underground forces generated by the EGS process. A magnitude-5.5 earthquake that injured 90 people was probably triggered by hydraulic fracturing at an EGS plant in Pohang, South Korea, in 2017. Lessons have been learnt from this and other incidents. For example, EGS developers are deploying networks of sensors to better predict seismic risks and using multistage stimulation. This involves the use of pressurised fluids or chemical agents to fracture rock sequentially and more gently at several points rather than at fewer locations.

Horne says that he expects the levelized cost of electricity — the average cost of generating a unit of electricity across a power plant’s lifetime — for EGS to drop to a commercially competitive $80 per megawatt hour (MWh) by 2027. The IEA says that this could drop to $50 by 2035 and that geothermal energy could generate 8% of global electricity supplies by 2050.

Efforts to develop more efficient solar cells could also help countries to improve their energy security by increasing sustainable domestic electricity supplies. In 2025, 9% of the world’s electricity came from solar, up from 3% in 2020. Today’s solar cells are mostly silicon-based and can typically convert light into electricity with efficiencies of around 20–24%.

A worker inspects newly installed solar panels at the Fuendetodos II solar park near Zaragoza, Spain.Credit: Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images

When sunlight hits a solar, or photovoltaic, cell, electrons inside the semiconductor material that it is made from are knocked loose, creating an electrical imbalance that produces a voltage and generates electricity. Researchers are now developing next-generation solar cells that use metal halide perovskites, a family of crystalline compounds with high light absorption and charge-transport capabilities.

#1298. Why Italy will be top seeds in EURO 2028 qualifying draw

Italy did not reach the Nations League quarter-finals, but there is still some good news, as they will be top seeds in the EURO 2028 qualifying campaign draw as one of the best third-placed teams.

Roberto Mancini said when he first took the job over the summer that his primary focus was getting the Nazionale ready for the European Championships.

The Nations League was a rollercoaster, going from a 2-0 opening home defeat to Belgium, through victories over Turkiye, a 1-1 draw in Paris, and historic 3-1 home win against Zinedine Zidane’s France on Thursday.

They only needed a point in Brussels to go through to the quarter-finals, but were crushed 4-1 by the Red Devils.

The good news is, although Italy finished third in Group A1, they are one of the best to miss out on the quarter-finals with 10 points.

That means they will be they will certainly avoid the play-offs for Nations League relegation, and will be among the 12 top seeds for the EURO 2028 qualifying draw.

That is going to be held on December 6 in Belfast.

What does remain to be seen is whether the Azzurri will be in a group with four or five nations.

Those qualifiers will be played between March and November 2027.

#1297. Super Mario! Dons hand rebuild job to Swiss success story Frick

Published: 14:14 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 14:45 EST, 15 November 2026

Aberdeen have appointed former Liechtenstein international Mario Frick as their new head coach.

The 52-year-old will take charge at Pittodrie, subject to the completion of UK visa formalities, following a successful spell with Swiss side FC Luzern.

Frick arrives in the north-east after five years in charge of Luzern, where he transformed the club’s fortunes after taking over in December 2021 with the team rooted to the bottom of the Swiss Super League. He guided them away from relegation trouble before leading them to a fourth-place finish and qualification for European football.

Announcing the appointment, Aberdeen chief executive Adrian Bevington said the club had undertaken an extensive recruitment process before selecting Frick as the man to lead the Dons forward.

Bevington said: 'We are delighted to welcome Mario Frick and his assistant coach Roman Matter to Aberdeen Football Club.

'Mario has significant experience as a head coach and has delivered impressive results with both Vaduz and Luzern. He has a proven track record of building competitive teams and developing young players.

'Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team.'

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel also welcomed the appointment and believes Frick has the qualities to make a major impact at Pittodrie.

Pfannenstiel said: 'Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play. He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment.

Aberdeen have appointed Mario Frick as their new manager

'We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I’m convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact.'

Before his spell with Luzern, Frick managed FC Balzers and FC Vaduz, winning promotion to the Swiss Super League with the latter. Across almost 290 senior matches as a head coach, he built a reputation for developing young talent, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players.

As a player, Frick represented clubs including FC Basel, FC Zürich, St Gallen, Grasshopper, Siena and Ternana. A striker who could also operate in defence, he won 125 caps for Liechtenstein between 1993 and 2016 and remains his country’s record goalscorer with 16 international goals.

Frick said: 'I’m excited to be joining Aberdeen FC. It’s a club with a proud history, passionate supporters and big ambitions.

'Together with the staff, my aim is to create an environment where the players can thrive, develop and perform at their very best, while working towards our goals as a team.'

Frick and assistant coach Matter are expected to arrive in Aberdeen at the start of the week and will begin preparations for next weekend’s Premiership clash with Kilmarnock.

Manchester United reportedly made an approach to Brighton over the possibility of appointing Fabian Hurzeler before ultimately turning to Mauricio Pochettino.

According to a detailed report from The Athletic, senior figures at Old Trafford initiated direct, high-level discussions with Brighton to explore the feasibility of recruiting the 33-year-old U.S.-born German tactician.

However, Brighton owner Tony Bloom made it clear that United would have to pay at least £15 million in compensation to secure Hurzeler’s services.

The report adds that as per other sources familiar with the discussions, an even greater sum might have been required to convince Brighton to release their manager.

The financial demands were not the only obstacle, with Hurzeler himself determined to remain at Brighton until the end of the campaign.

Having publicly insisted he would not “throw away” the foundation built with his players, Hurzeler’s commitment forced United to pivot toward Pochettino.

United subsequently appointed Pochettino as Michael Carrick’s successor who has now been tasked with the job to save Man United’s season.

United’s admiration for the youngest permanent head coach in Premier League history is easy to understand given Brighton’s extraordinary start to the 2026/27 season.

Under Hurzeler’s aggressive, possession-based pressing system, Brighton have move to second place in the Premier League table, sitting just five points behind reigning champions Arsenal while outperforming traditional heavyweights like Manchester City and Liverpool.

His side famously dismantled Arsenal 3-0 earlier in the campaign, handed out 5-0 thrashings to Crystal Palace and Coventry City, and even knocked Manchester United out of the Carabao Cup with a thrilling 3-2 comeback win at Old Trafford.

Brighton’s impressive domestic form has been accompanied by their run in the UEFA Conference League, firmly cementin his reputation as one of Europe’s brightest managerial minds.

#1295. Donnarumma: ‘Italy paid for exhilarating France win, nobody expected this run’

Gianluigi Donnarumma feels Italy were carrying a hangover from the ‘exhilarating’ victory over France, but the 4-1 defeat to Belgium mustn’t wipe out their other Nations League performances.

The Manchester City goalkeeper was one of the best Azzurri performers on the night in Brussels, managing to keep the scoreline down to only 4-1, especially with some incredible saves on Kevin De Bruyne.

Pio Esposito had opened the scoring, yet Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy, Jeremy Doku and Diego Moreira turned it all around, with Senne Lammens saving the late Esposito spot-kick too.

“Unfortunately, this is part of the learning process, we started a new era, so you can have these ups and downs,” Donnarumma told RAI Sport.

It was hard to see this performance just days after the 3-1 comeback victory over France at San Siro, which put Italy temporarily top of the Nations League group.

“We weren’t phenomenal then and we’re not a disaster now. It was a wonderful night with France, and perhaps we used up too much energy to achieve that result, so were a little tired just three days later.

“When you play a match that is so exhilarating, it’s not easy to plug straight back in at the same level. It’s not an excuse, but we were certainly less sharp than the other day,” continued Donnarumma.

“Let’s be honest, nobody expected us to have such a good Nations League campaign, we had some really impressive matches, but Belgium were superior tonight, and we know that we must improve.”

Italy only needed a point in Brussels to secure qualification for the quarter-finals, so Belgium expected them to take a defensive approach and play for the draw, but that certainly was not the case.

“What we need to reflect on is that we allowed so many counter-attacks, so we must do better with the preventative marking,” noted Donnarumma.

“This defeat can and will be a valuable learning experience, the coach already said we need to lift our heads. It was painful, we all wanted to keep going in this tournament.”

Roberto Mancini is certainly trying to widen the group of players he can call upon for Italy, as this evening Milan winger Alphadjo Cisse received his senior debut, while Roma’s Niccolò Pisilli got his first competitive start.

“The coach is special, he can give us a big hand. We too have to help the younger players, and we know there isn’t much time because the European Championship qualifiers are coming up, but they need to play and gain experience.

“There are many interesting young players out there, but they need to play more often.”

#1294. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. But he will also have wondered how United could again have found themselves in such a position after an enterprising first half when they attacked with pace and purpose and looked a very different team to the one that had been ransacked by Como and Bournemouth.

Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

We didn’t really get going in the second half. We should have been up in the first half. It was as positive as we could have hoped for. We looked really dangerous.

I don’t think the heads dropped, there’s no hiding from the fact we haven’t won enough games.

The boys were in a good place in the first half. [Chelsea] made the first blow in the second half and that made the difference.

I’ve not looked at it, I’ve not seen it [the incident that led to Martínez’s red card].

[Do you think the fans who booed them at the end feel let down by the players?] There’s a lot of emotion. We’re a great football club. We want to win football matches. Supporters pay a lot of money and have a lot of commitment to come and see us play. You could see from today that the boys had the game in the right place but things have gone against us in a big way. It unravelled quickly and there’s a lot of emotion around right now.

We’ve got to move forward. Take the things we believe worked well for us today forward with a bit of confidence. A lot of the good things in the firts half we need to use to move forward.

[Do you expect to be in charge (vs Roma) on Wednesday?] Yes.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

We know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

If there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

Young players who left after feeling they were not given a chance and went on to flourish elsewhere. Even if Lukaku was re-signed – for almost £90m more than he was sold for – and failed.

The concern is about Estêvão. The Brazilian has barely featured under Xabi Alonso, who kept him on the bench – despite being without Cole Palmer and João Pedro – during the Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool on Wednesday and afterwards gave the 19-year-old the most lukewarm of endorsements.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

Tottenham are actively scouting Middlesbrough star Will Lankshear, just months after selling the striker to the Championship club.

According to The Sun, scouts representing Newcastle, Spurs and Leeds have watched the Middlesbrough striker this season.

The 21-year-old has rapidly established himself as one of the Championship’s most exciting young forwards following his summer move from Spurs.

Middlesbrough are understood to be determined to retain their prized asset, particularly given his importance to their attacking plans.

As per the report, the Championship club have placed a £70 million price tag on Lankshear to deter potential January approaches.

That would represent an extraordinary increase on the initial £10 million fee Middlesbrough paid Tottenham just a few months ago.

However, Spurs did insert matching rights, allowing them to match any accepted future bid—alongside a 20 per cent sell-on clause.

Furthermore, Tottenham are owed up to £10 million in performance-related add-ons, with the report further revealing those triggers include Lankshear playing and scoring for the England senior national team.

Tottenham’s decision to cash in rather than hand Lankshear a first-team opportunity looks increasingly costly given his extraordinary scoring form.

The 6ft 2in center-forward has scored an incredible 15 goals in 16 appearances across all competitions this campaign, including 13 goals in 13 Championship outings, averaging a strike every 81 minutes with a clinical 27 per cent shot conversion rate.

Remarkably, Lankshear has scored just one fewer goal on his own than Tottenham’s entire squad combined this term.

Following earlier EFL loan spells at West Brom and Oxford United, his physical presence, penalty-box instincts, and rapid development have sparked widespread comparisons to former Spurs icon Harry Kane.

His excellent form is attracting widespread interest, with Arsenal among the clubs tracking the striker.

#1292. Van Bommel: ‘Belgium would score six without Donnarumma, my advice to De Bruyne’

Mark van Bommel insists Belgium ‘would’ve scored six if not for Gianluigi Donnarumma’ in goal for Italy, and clarifies he never advised Kevin De Bruyne to quit Napoli for PSV Eindhoven.

This was an incredibly tight Nations League group, and going into the final match the Azzurri were on top with 10 points, ahead of France on goal difference and head-to-head record, with Belgium following on nine.

By the end of the night, Italy had dropped to third place following a 4-1 defeat in Brussels, despite taking the early lead through Pio Esposito.

The hosts had turned it around within 15 minutes to lead 3-1 with Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy and Jeremy Doku, then Diego Moreira added a fourth on the classic counter-attack, while Senne Lammens saved Pio Esposito’s late penalty.

“If Donnarumma had not been in goal, then we would’ve scored six,” insisted Van Bommel to Sky Sport Italia.

It was a dominant performance, far more than the 2-0 victory at the Stadio Olimpico in the opening round of this Nations League group.

Curiously, Italy lost both matches with Belgium, while the Red Devils lost both meetings with France, yet the only team Les Bleus were unable to beat was the Azzurri.

“I’ll be honest, I didn’t expect this when we started two months ago, but even before that first match with Italy, I could tell this was a really intelligent group of players. That makes it a pleasure for a coach to work with them.”

De Bruyne’s performance this evening made him look a completely different player to the one seen regularly in Serie A and the Champions League at Napoli.

Considering the rumours that he is looking for a January transfer to PSV Eindhoven, has the Belgium coach given him any advice on the next step in his career?

“I was asked a question by a Belgian reporter about whether De Bruyne would fit in with the PSV Eindhoven style of play, and seeing as I know the club well, I said yes he would, but he also fits in at Napoli,” insisted Van Bommel.

“So I answered a specific question, but I did not advise him to do anything. The decision is entirely his, and I leave that to him.”

Former Napoli striker Romelu Lukaku remained on the bench throughout and was never deployed.

“He was injured for a few days and didn’t even make the trip to Turkiye, so tonight we said that we would use him in case of emergency. It was a bit cold as well, so we decided together not to bring him on.”

#1291. Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jia Yu is at the Center for Social Research, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China.

China’s one-child policy is probably the best-known population-control programme in history, yet in its first decade it barely changed the country’s fertility rate. Writing in Nature, Meng et al.1 show that the biggest drop in fertility after the policy’s introduction was driven by a change in how officials were incentivized to enforce it. This change accounts for about half of the fall in the country’s fertility rate during the 1990s.

Argentine goalkeeper Ezequiel Bacher scored perhaps the most bizarre own goal ever during his side's recent Primera B play-off game.

Comunicaciones were taking on Arsenal Sarandi at the weekend with the score 0-0, and the goalkeeper had caught the ball from a cross with the aim of getting the game back under way.

As he tried to throw the ball out, though, he got it all wrong and ended up launching the ball into his own net.

Bacher, 30, essentially failed to let go of the ball at the right time, leaving his team-mates stunned.

The player himself covered his face with his hand before retrieving the ball to get play started again.

Arsenal players wheeled off in celebration, only for Comunicaciones to level things up in the game soon after. Arsenal, though, scored again, and eventually won 3-2 in the first leg of the tie.

#1286. Striker Che Adams says Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli is big on the small details... 'he loves his FaceTime calls'

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026

No matter how history judges his time in charge of Scotland, no one will ever accuse Sebastien Pocognoli of leaving a single stone unturned.

Intense, intelligent and highly demanding, the Belgian has already shown himself to be big on the small things which can combine to make a significant difference.

Che Adams discovered this for himself in September, even though an injury prevented him from being part of the new man’s first get together in La Manga.

‘I heard from the manager the last time when I wasn’t in the camp,’ he revealed.

‘He loves a FaceTime call. I think he’s taken a few of the boys by surprise when they’ve been out walking their dogs and stuff. I think KT (Kieran Tierney) was out for a walk when he phoned him.

‘He just calls out of the blue and has done it to a few of the boys. It’s unexpected and it’s different because we’ve never experienced something like that. But it’s good.

Che Adams' appearance against North Macedonia was his first under Sebastien Pocognoli

Striker Adams says Pocognoli is more intense than his predecessor and is 'with the times'

John McGinn is within six goals of the scoring record shared by Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law

‘In the last camp when I was out injured, he was on asking how my injury was, how long I’d be out for and if I still wanted to be part of it.

‘The camps haven’t changed much, but the manager is definitely more intense. I think it’s the European style of play and thinking. It’s going to take time for him to understand the boys, understand us as players and understand us as a squad.

‘But he’s really bought into it and wants to help us do well.’

Hang on a minute. A manager who’s more intense than Steve Clarke? You could be forgiven for thinking that’s simply not possible. But Adams feels it is very much the case.

‘With Steve you could have a laugh and you can do that with this gaffer as well,’ he explained.

‘But he’s a lot more intense in terms of detail off the pitch telling you where to be and what to do.

‘This gaffer has good ideas, a good approach to the game.

‘He is with the times, really. Everyone’s buying into it and I definitely think we’ll see the benefits.’

John McGinn believes it could be as long as 18 months before it all comes up roses. But, in football, you rarely get that long.

Starting in St Gallen tomorrow, the Belgian could do with some green shoots emerging.

‘He’s a few years younger (than Clarke) and has a different philosophy on how he wants his team to play,’ added Adams.

‘It just takes time to click, but it’s up to us as players now to show we can do what he wants.

‘We have been together for a number of years now, so we know each other’s games.

‘You could see on Friday us starting to put the manager’s things in practice. We won a lot of balls high with our pressing.

‘He said to us after the game that it’s about the killer moments and we probably didn’t capitalise on them enough. But it was a win and the first one for the gaffer at Hampden.

‘For every manager they need time, but you saw spells there where the movements and patterns of play were very good.

‘It was very important to get the win and build up the confidence.

‘You’ve also got to keep in context things like that it was Luke Graham’s first start for us, but he had the confidence to play those passes in the build-up.

‘So, you have to credit the manager for putting the belief in the young players who have come in as well.’

The comfort for Pocognoli throughout a time of transition is that he can still depend on the old stagers who were central to the success under his predecessor.

On the night when Andy Robertson joined Kenny Dalglish on 102 caps, McGinn claimed a double to put himself within six goals of the scoring record jointly held by Dalglish and Denis Law.

Having just turned 32, there is every chance that the Aston Villa captain can soon claim his own slice of history.

‘It’s amazing for John, he’s such a great person and he deserves it,’ said Adams.

‘Everyone can see what he’s done for club and country, he puts his heart on his sleeve and gives everything.

‘It’s a pleasure to play with him. I really hope he does do it - and I think he will.

‘Everyone is so pleased for him, he’s the best person I’ve met in football. When I came into the squad I didn’t think we’d have people who would achieve these kind of things.

‘I have loved every single minute of it. We have done some great things here.

‘We have been to three major tournaments now, people are making personal achievements as well. But as a team and as a squad it’s about taking that next step now in tournaments.

‘It’s a pleasure to play with these boys. They’re legends of football.’

#1285. Newspapers deliver mixed verdicts after Italy’s Nations League collapse against Belgium

Newspapers in Italy have delivered mixed verdicts following the national team’s 4-1 defeat against Belgium on Sunday evening, which saw the Azzurri knocked out of the Nations League despite starting the evening at the top of the group.

Italy had started Sunday in first place in their Nations League group following an impressive 3-1 win at home against France on Thursday night, but ended up in third place after losing 4-1 to Belgium and seeing France claim a 2-1 victory over Turkey.

The in-form Pio Esposito opened the scoring with his 10th goal for the Nazionale, but Italy would go on to concede three goals within 11 minutes from Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy and Jeremy Doku in the first half. Milan’s Diego Moreira added a fourth towards the end and Esposito missed a penalty to make the scores 4-2.

The reactions in the Italian press on Monday morning have brought mixed reviews.

La Gazzetta dello Sport criticised Mancini’s decisions on the night, particularly his personnel choices with an untested front three of Esposito, Luca Koleosho and out-of-position central midfielder Niccolo Pisilli starting across the front three together for the first time.

The Pink Paper felt that Italy had a strong opening 10 minutes, resulting in Esposito’s 10th Azzurri goal, but that they simply stopped playing from that point onwards. They suggest that on another night, Italy could have conceded twice as many goals as they did.

However, La Gazzetta dello Sport admits that it is better for this sort of result and performance to have happened now rather than later down the line.

The Corriere dello Sport agreed that Italy could have conceded several more had it not been for a solid performance between the sticks from Gianluigi Donnarumma and that Italy’s first-half collapse was a major disappointment after all the hard work they had put in in their previous Nations League outings.

Pisilli and Nicolo Fagioli were singled out for individual criticism after being hooked at half-time, but there was praise for Esposito, who is now up to 10 goals from his first 15 national team caps.

The Corriere dello Sport concludes that ‘you can’t ask youngsters to learn and grow and then demolish them for their mistakes, we must support them’.

Tuttosport agrees that there have still been plenty of positives from Italy’s Nations League campaign and insists that the Azzurri have ‘come a long way’ since their first game against Belgium back in September.

Tuttosport pointed out that Italy did well to pick up 10 points from a group that contained France, Belgium and Turkey, who all went to the 2026 World Cup that the Azzurri infamously missed out on.

They praised Mancini for bringing Italy back to modern European standards by deploying a 4-3-3 and praised his confidence in young players and his ability to get the best out of Esposito at centre-forward.

The major issue that Tuttosport pointed to was with Italy’s defence, given that they failed to keep a clean sheet in any of their six Nations League group stage fixtures, even conceding twice against Turkey, who finished the group stage with six straight defeats.

Still, Tuttosport urges Italy to look to the future and to focus on the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifiers, which are more important than the Nations League campaign anyway.

According to Fussball Europa, Liverpool have dispatched scouts to watch the Athletico Paranaense centre-back in action as they assess potential defensive reinforcements.

Since graduating from the Brazilian club’s youth academy and breaking into the senior setup in 2025, Dias has rapidly established himself as a regular starter, racking up 55 senior appearances, including 37 outings this year alone.

As per the report, Andoni Iraola’s side continue to monitor his development closely, though they face competition from Barcelona, who have also joined the race for the teenager, alongside Bundesliga outfits Bayer Leverkusen and RB Leipzig.

Tottenham are also understood to remain interested in Dias, having reportedly seen a €20 million offer rejected during the summer transfer window.

Athletico Paranaense are now demanding €30 million for the Brazilian youngster, whose contract runs until December 2028.

Tottenham remain interested but now face competition from Barcelona and Liverpool

Tottenham retain strong interest in revisiting the deal, but they will need to raise their previous bid by €10 million if they hope to secure his signature in January.

Complicating matters further for Spurs is the arrival of heavyweights like Liverpool and Barcelona in the race, alongside Leverkusen and Leipzig weighing up winter moves.

With Athletico Paranaense holding firm on their €30 million valuation ahead of the New Year window, an intense transfer battle is brewing for one of South America’s brightest young defensive prospects.

Originally developed as a center-forward in youth football before transitioning into defense, the left-footed center-back combines imposing physical strength and aerial command with exceptional composure in build-up play.

Operating predominantly as a left-sided central defender, Dias has the ability to break opposition lines with progressive passes and diagonal long balls, completing nearly 86% of his passes in Série A this season.

Idolizing Thiago Silva, his background as a former striker gives him natural comfort under pressure, making him an ideal modern ball-playing defender.

His qualities suits the style of football of all three clubs showing interest in him.

The player himself in a recent interview admitted that he “dreams of playing in the Champions League and in a huge league”.

It remains to be seen whether Spurs make another offer big enough to see it accepted or if the player opts for a club like Liverpool or Barcelona if they make an offer.

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.

Appointed Steve Clarke’s successor in the summer, the Belgian’s attempts to bring in fresh faces and a new style of play has produced mixed results in his opening five Nations League games.

Following Friday’s win over North Macedonia, John McGinn warned the Tartan Army that it could take as long as 18 months for everything to click into place.

But ahead of the final group match in St Gallen tomorrow evening, the manager acknowledged it’s incumbent on him to accelerate that time frame.

Asked if he felt he had to deliver sooner, he said: ‘Yeah, for sure, but we’re only talking about 18 months because John said that. He could have said 15 months. I don’t know. But, for sure, it needs to be quicker.

‘In 18 months, it will be the time of the Euros and that is what he meant. We have to go there and be prepared for this in 18 months’ time.

Sebastien Pocognoli  says his Scotland team need to show progress 'game after game'

‘For sure, game after game, we need to see improvement.

‘Some new faces will come back in March. So, step by step we will have more ideas and in one month’s time a lot can change also.’

McGinn also said that the players were fully behind the manager, reiterating the point previously made by Andy Robertson and Scott McTominay.

‘I can tell you that in the time we have had together the players have been doing well in terms of replicating what I ask them to do,’ the manager stressed.

‘They know that and that’s the most important part.

‘They buy in. They like it. I think they enjoy it too. You can see when players don’t enjoy it.

‘For sure, when you win it’s more enjoyable, but it would be very bad if they weren’t enjoying it and we were also not winning games.

‘So, right now I think we are working well. We give special attention to the collective.

‘In all the camps, I am very clear about what I expect on the pitch. The players wanted this when I arrived. They wanted clarity. And I think that’s what I have tried to bring.’

To claim second place in the group, Scotland need to defeat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t win in North Macedonia.

That outcome would ensure that Pocognoli’s men would be a pot two side in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Asked what it would take to pull off what would be a stunning win in St Gallen, the manager said: ‘Let’s be brave, but be intelligent.

‘It’s about mentality. They (Switzerland) are a very good team, so we need to be smart. Sometimes they will go through our lines with a low block or a high block as they have the quality.

‘We will try to be intense and strong in the duel because I think that’s the first piece to have a good game.’

Pocognoli’s side were booed off at half-time on Friday with criticism of the performance persisting despite them going on to win the game.

But the manager claims he’s oblivious to wider concerns about the performances to date, saying: ‘No, I’m not aware of this. That’s why I was surprised (at the question).

John McGinn suggested that it could take 18 months for Scotland to click under Pocognoli

‘Yes, there were some boos at half-time. I think that’s part of it, it’s been like this for years.

‘I know we are colleagues, but I’m not reading the press.

‘So, I’m not aware of the criticism. I just want to make the supporters happy.

‘If they aren’t yet happy, we will try to do better.

‘There’s pressure in all the jobs with a club. It can be external, it can be internal. It is part of the job.

‘I’m very self-critical about myself. So, that’s the first thing. Try to be stable when we win, when we lose.

‘I’m always thinking what we can do better. If there’s some criticism, that’s fine.

‘But there there were also a lot of positives after the North Macedonia game.

‘I was the first one to say calm down as we need to see more.’

#1280. Three winners and three losers of Mancini’s new crop of Italy internationals

Italy’s Nations League journey has come to a premature end after Sunday’s 4-1 defeat away against Belgium, and though the campaign finished in disappointment, the last few weeks have brought opportunities for a number of new, young faces in the Nazionale squad: Here are three who impressed when given the opportunity and three who still have room for improvement.

Italy were defeated 4-1 by Belgium in Brussels on Sunday evening, despite a 10th-minute opener from Inter’s Pio Esposito. Three goals within 11 minutes from Maxim De Cuyper Nathan Ngoy and Jeremy Doku shifted the balance of the game and a late fourth from Diego Moreira put the game beyond any doubt.

Despite starting the night at the top of the group, Sunday’s defeat against Belgium saw Italy overtaken both by their opponents and by France, who claimed a 2-1 victory over Turkey in their final group stage fixture.

Still, many outlets have urged Italy to look for the positive in spite of Sunday’s defeat against Belgium. Roberto Mancini and his players had picked up 10 points from their last five matches in a tough group and showed plenty of promise and character after a miserable year that had seen them miss out on qualification to the 2026 World Cup.

Though Mancini did not get his selections right against Belgium, he has largely been praised for his willingness to put faith in youth: Only three of Italy’s starters on Sunday were born before the year 2000 and five of them were aged 22 or below.

Mancini also gave opportunities to several players who had previously been overlooked, including Brentford right-back Michael Kayode, who now looks a nailed-on first-choice on the right of Italy’s back four for the foreseeable future. Of all the new faces that Mancini has introduced over the last few weeks, his emergence has arguably been the most encouraging.

Sporting CP midfielder Issa Doumbia has also earned praise in the Italian press on Monday: TMW credited his physical qualities but admitted that he still has room for improvement in terms of game management, but assessed his performances as generally positive when given the opportunity.

Napoli’s Antonio Vergara was also impressive on Italy’s right flank during this international break and has handled the step up to international football comfortably. TMW argues that he should be the go-to starter in that position for the time being.

There are, however, a few of the new Italy faces that may still need a bit more time, including two of the front three that started against Belgium on Sunday night. This was perhaps a touch too soon for Luca Koleosho, who remains untested at the highest levels, while Niccolo Pisilli also struggled to impress, albeit out of position on the right wing instead of his usual position in central midfield.

Sebastiano Esposito, who was dropped from the Italy squad on Sunday, will also be hoping for a touch more consistency in his performances, despite some encouraging moments during this Nations League campaign.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1277. 15 Greatest Belgian Players in Football History [Ranked]

For a sustained period, Belgium boasted one of the most talented squads on the planet. It was a golden generation that were consistently among the favourites to win any major tournament they showed up to but ultimately left every trip to the World Cup and European Championships empty-handed.

With much of the squad that finished third at the 2018 World Cup either retired or coming to the end of their careers, the peak of that particular cycle appears to have passed.

But the country's contribution to the game stretches further than one generation of players. The Belgian sides of the 1980s were no less formidable in their own right, reaching the semi-finals of the 1986 World Cup and finishing as runners-up at Euro 1980.

Some incredible talents have pulled on the nation's shirt for the Red Devils, a lot of them coming over the span of the last decade or so. It begs the question: who are the greatest Belgian players of all time?

Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Karim Benzema feature as the greatest Champions League players of all time are ranked in order.

Axel Witsel was the glue that held Belgium's midfield together for the best part of a decade. While many of the names on this list tended to grab the headlines ahead of him, Witsel quietly got on with the job, providing the balance that allowed his more attack-minded teammates to flourish.

His career saw him play for some of Europe's big boys, spending four years at Borussia Dortmund before a three-year stint at Atletico Madrid. He earned well over 100 international caps and was rarely the first name opposition fans feared, but he was almost always the first name on the team sheet.

After 33 combined goals and assists in a single Eredivise season, Dries Mertens moved to Italy and became a Napoli icon, and is their all-time leading scorer with 148 goals. No small feat at a club that once had Diego Maradona on its books.

At 5ft 7in, he was never the most imposing figure in an attacking line, but he more than made up for it with intelligent movement, technical brilliance and an impressive goal catalogue. He was equally important in a Belgium shirt, representing his country over 100 times, appearing at multiple World Cups and European Championships.

Michel Preud'homme is one of the finest goalkeepers Belgium has ever produced. Commanding in the box and blessed with sharp reflexes, he was a dominant presence for both Standard Liege and Mechelen, but a match-fixing scandal in the early 1980s cost him six months of his career.

After spending the early portion of his international career behind Jean-Marie Pfaff, Preud'homme would go on to be a regular starter for the next seven years. His crowning international moment came at the 1994 World Cup, where his performances were so impressive that he was given the tournament's Golden Glove award and voted as the world's best goalkeeper by The International Federation of Football History & Statistics that same year.

Mousa Dembele rarely courted the spotlight, but those who played alongside him or against him knew exactly what they were dealing with. The midfielder possessed a rare combination of power, balance and technical ability that made him almost impossible to dispossess, and at his peak many regarded him as one of the most naturally gifted players in Europe.

His time in the Premier League with Fulham and Tottenham showcased those qualities, and he was a valued presence for Belgium across several major tournaments. He likely deserved more recognition than he got, but that's rather fitting for a player who never asked for it.

Long before Belgium's golden generation emerged, Jan Ceulemans was setting the standard for those who would follow. The powerful attacking midfielder earned more than 90 caps for his country, captained the side through one of their most successful periods and was central to the run that took them to the semi-finals of the 1986 World Cup, knocking out the Soviet Union and Spain.

At club level, he near-enough spent his entire career at Club Brugge, winning multiple league titles and becoming one of the most celebrated Belgian players ever.

A four-time Ballon d'Or nominee, Enzo Scifo's lesser-known career was one of the kickstarters to the rich vein of talent seen emanating from Belgium ever since his prominence in the 1980s. Enjoying spells with the likes of Inter and AS Monaco across his 18-year career, it was home club RSC Anderlecht wherein he enjoyed the majority of his success.

Debuting for the team as a 17-year-old in 1983, Scifo made over 100 appearances for the side across his four-year spell, marking his name out as one of the hottest young players in Europe after helping the side to three straight league titles.

Further respectable spells with Inter, Monaco, Auxerre and Torino followed, with Scifo enjoying a decent goal record across his career. Having made his debut for Belgium aged just 18, he went on to make 84 appearances for his country, scoring 18 goals. An under-appreciated and lesser-known player with a remarkable career path and depth of talent.

The game of football has seen a wide variety of players over the years, but who have been the most skilful people to ever grace the beautiful game?

Having burst onto the scene as a 19-year-old for Dutch side Ajax, Toby Alderweireld might just be one of the most underrated centre-backs to have played the game. Having made over 100 showings for the Dutch giants, a debut for his country and subsequent move to Atlético Madrid followed for Alderweireld. After struggling to break into the Atleti first team, he was loaned to Premier League side Southampton, where his impressive season took him to Tottenham on a permanent deal.

Alderweireld would go on to become ever-present in the Spurs team, and although he may not have picked up any trophies in his time there, he played a big part alongside compatriot Jan Vertonghen in reaching the 2019 Champions League final, where they were defeated cruelly by Liverpool. Alderweireld and Vertonghen's partnership transcended club level, with the pair making well over 100 appearances each for the Red Devils in a golden age for Belgian centre-backs, with a certain Vincent Kompany in the offing as well.

The Belgian title race was absolutely crazy - and won in incredible circumstances by Alderweireld's strike

The goalkeeper of the tournament in Belgium's semi-final run in the 1986 World Cup, Belgian Bayern icon Pfaff was one of the most unique goalkeepers to grace the game.

Though not the tallest goalkeeper around, standing at 5'11, Pfaff was still an incredibly confident, commanding goalkeeper who was renowned for his incredible shot-stopping ability and composure with the ball at his feet.

El Simpatico's 300+ appearance-laden time across his ten-year spell at home club Beveren eventually earned a call from Bayern Munich, where Pfaff would go on to play a further 156 games in between the sticks for the Bavarian giants, earning himself the right to call himself one of Belgium's best ever goalkeepers, and one of the best in the world in his prime.

Voted the best Belgian footballer of the 20th century, Paul Van Himst's career may not have been a particularly mainstream one, but his time at Anderlecht will forever be the stuff of legend, for them. Spending nearly his entire career with the Belgian giants between 1959 and 1975, Van Himst was an incredibly prolific and efficient goalscorer, recording double-digit seasons for ten campaigns in a row, as well as becoming the clubs highest appearance maker with 457 showings for Anderlecht.

He was renowned in Belgium for his pace and creativity, being just as effective in creating goals as he was at putting them away. His loyalty to his beloved Anderlecht may have prevented his career from hitting the mainstream, but Van Himst likely doesn't care as he became one of the most legendary players in Anderlecht's history.

We've ranked the best 11 Spanish-born players in the history of football, taking into account several factors such as trophies won and longevity.

Nearly everything that can be said in regards to long-term partner Alderweireld applies to Jan Vertonghen too. He holds the record as Belgium's most-capped player with 157 and shared the pitch with his teammate on over 350 occasions for club and country. A 2012 signing from Ajax, Vertonghen spent almost a decade with Tottenham in the Premier League, being another vital piece to the puzzle that came inches away from a remarkable Champions League success.

Vertonghen's calmness on the ball and proficiency going forward outed him in his prime as one of the better ball-playing defenders in the world, and his aforementioned partnership with Alderweireld was formidable, though it may not have brought home any trophies.

#1276. Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

Scientists are engineering bacteria that can provide nitrogen, an essential ingredient for plant growth, to wheat crops. Credit: Shakeel Ahmed/Anadolu Agency/Getty

The world’s farms depend on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers to increase crop yields, but the production and use of these chemicals generates billions of tonnes of greenhouse-gas emissions every year. Now, scientists are making progress on a greener alternative: bioengineered bacteria.

This approach takes a cue from natural bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form and provide it to certain plants. Scientists are engineering genetic features into bacteria with the aim of enabling them to fix nitrogen for important food crops, such as maize (corn) and wheat, that don’t have such natural microbial partners.

In a comment published on 10 November in Nature Biotechnology1, researchers suggest that bioengineered bacteria could eventually replace up to half of synthetic fertilizers. The bacteria deliver nitrogen more efficiently to roots than synthetic fertilizers do, which could reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and nitrogen pollution of waterways. But this would require a slew of advances, from getting different microbial species to work together to more-rigorous field trials.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster cropSome of these ‘biofertilizers’ have been augmented with genes and genetic snippets from viruses or distantly related bacteria. This means that the engineered microbes are classified as transgenic — altered to include DNA from other species. The bacteria are now being trialled on small plots of maize on farms in the Midwestern United States. The bacteria, developed by Switch Bioworks in San Carlos, California, are the first example of a transgenic biofertilizer approved for testing on fields in the country.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster crop

In September, Switch Bioworks received approval from the Brazilian regulatory agency, the National Technical Commission on Biosafety (CNTBio), to test its strains there. This is the first time that a transgenic bacterium of any kind has been approved for field tests in Brazil, says molecular biologist Mario Murakami, who is the president of CTNBio in Campinas.

Companies that have focused on editing bacterial genes rather than producing transgenic microbes are further along. Pivot Bio in Minneapolis, Minnesota, has applied its gene-edited biofertilizers to tens of millions of hectares of US farmland over the past decade, says the company’s chief technology officer Travis Frey. Some of Pivot Bio’s products have also been tested in Canada, Argentina, Kenya and Brazil.

Most plants can’t use the form of nitrogen that is present in the air. Some crops, including soya beans and peanuts, host colonies of bacteria that can convert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form. The plant takes up that nitrogen and, in return, provides carbon that fuels bacterial growth. But most staple crops lack these microbial partners, leading farmers to rely on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. These chemical fertilizers account for 5% of global greenhouse-gas emissions, and drive damaging nutrient pollution in waterways.

For decades, researchers have tried to get bacteria to fix nitrogen for staple crops. Until recently, the approach was to collect wild strains of nitrogen-fixing bacteria from soil and apply them to seeds or spray them onto plants. “It doesn’t work,” says Jean-Michel Ané, a bioengineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, who is working on microbial fertilizers. The wild microbes fail to thrive when applied to crops that don’t provide them with carbon.

#1275. Pagliuca analyses Belgium’s ‘deserved’ victory over Italy and advises Donnarumma

Former Italy goalkeeper Gianluca Pagliuca has delivered his verdict after Sunday’s 4-1 Nations League defeat against Belgium, feels that it is only natural that the Azzurri encounter a few difficulties during a rebuild phase and has explained where Gianluigi Donnarumma went wrong with his error against France on Thursday night.

Italy’s Nations League campaign came to a premature end after a 4-1 defeat away against Belgium in Brussels on Sunday evening. The Azzurri had started the night in first place in their group, but were overtaken by both their opponents on the night and by France, whom they had beaten 3-1 earlier in the week.

Italy had started brightly against Belgium, taking the lead through the in-form Pio Esposito within the first 11 minutes of the game.

Pagliuca, speaking to Radio Anch’io Sport on Monday morning, said that he thought that Italy were going to pick up where they had left off against France.

“At first I thought it was going to be a continuation of the performance from the France game, but then Belgium’s comeback began,” said the former Azzurri goalkeeper. “We suffered a lot in the second half as well. Belgium deserved it, they are more ready than us at the moment.”

Pagliuca feels that it is only normal that Italy aren’t quite up to the level just yet at this stage of Mancini’s rebuild: “I think it’s normal for a national team that is still being rebuilt to not have players at the same level of a team like France.”

He feels that Italy struggled defensively against Belgium, but, again, that this is only normal.

“We suffered against Belgium’s fast attackers. Calafiori and Bastoni, who were perfect against France, suffered yesterday as well. However, I don’t think there’s a big defensive problem. The game is a lot quicker now and more planned in attack, which means you are going to suffer a bit more defensively, but that is the same for everyone.”

Mancini’s inclusion of several youngsters over the last few weeks has gone down positively among supporters and pundits. Only three players of Italy’s starting XI on Sunday night were born before the year 2000 and five of them were aged 22 or under.

“There are lots of good young players, there’s not just one in particular,” said Pagliuca. “I think the coach, who wants to aim for the EUROs and World Cup, needs a period to test a few things out. I think it’s right to call up players even if they are not starters at club level.

“Mancini is experimenting. He will also call up some of the more experienced players for the qualifying matches. For now, he wants to test young players and see what they’re made of. The Nations League does have value, but the important thing is to qualify for the EUROs and World Cup.”

Pagliuca was asked for his thoughts on Donnarumma’s recent performances and the error that he made that led to France’s only goal in Thursday’s 3-1 win in San Siro.

“Sometimes, goalkeepers want to overdo it,” he explained. “Gigio made a mistake against France on Thursday because he was overdoing it. A goalkeeper has to do the simple things correctly. But, he made up for it by making great saves, yesterday as well.”

Lastly, on Pio Esposito, Pagliuca added: “He has also played a lot of games and is improving with every appearance. He’s cool in front of goal and is having a great season.

“I think Cristian Chivu will stick to playing with two strikers for now, but maybe we’ll start to see all three of them at some point in most games. Inter are the clear favourites for the Scudetto and I think they will win the league.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1274. Crystal Palace Reach Agreement With Thomas Frank To Become New Manager

Thomas Frank has an agreement in place to become the new Crystal Palace manager, GIVEMESPORT understands.

Frank has been the frontrunner to take over at Selhurst Park ever since Pierre Sage was sacked on November 12, with the Eagles bottom of the Premier League table.

However, while no quick appointment was made, it appears that the former Brentford and Tottenham boss is now set to take over in south London, with the international break still in full flow.

Talks over the Dane's backroom staff are also at the final stages, with an appointment expected to be made this week.

Frank will arrive at Selhurst Park and get to work with his new side ahead of the return of the Premier League this weekend. The Eagles return to action with a game against Coventry City away.

The 53-year-old has been out of work since leaving Tottenham in February. He was sacked after a 2-1 defeat to Newcastle United that left Spurs in 16th position and looking over their shoulders at the relegation zone.

Following a dismal interim spell of Igor Tudor, Tottenham eventually turned to Roberto De Zerbi to get them out of trouble, with safety only secured on the final day of the season.

Frank had a shocking 26.9% win percentage in the Premier League with Spurs, with that improved to 34.2% in all competitions, although that gave him the worst record of any permanent Spurs manager.

Prior to his spell in north London, Frank had made a name for himself with Brentford, guiding the club to promotion from the Championship in 2020/21, having just missed out on promotion the year before, and turned them into an established Premier League club.

Palace chairman Steve Parish will now be hoping the Dane can work his magic and guide the Eagles away from the relegation zone.

Speaking about his exit from Spurs in the summer, Frank said: "Leaving Tottenham has given me the chance to step back and reflect on my journey so far. Football management is a profession that demands complete commitment every single day, and periods like this are a rare opportunity to assess, learn and gain a fresh perspective.

"From the outside, it may have looked like a time of many challenges at Tottenham when results were not what we wanted. From within, however, it becomes clear why the club is so special - full of talented people who work tirelessly every day. I have no doubt Tottenham has a bright future.

"Football remains a huge part of who I am, and I have chosen to use this time productively. Over the coming months, besides spending time with family and friends, I will continue studying, observing and learning from other leaders both within sport and beyond it.

"There have been conversations and opportunities since leaving Spurs, but I have decided not to rush into the next role. For me, this summer is not the right time to go back into management.

"When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication."

It seems that the time is now right for Frank and Palace is the right club. Time will tell if that is the right call.

He also starred for Chelsea early into his career, but now lives a completely different life.

#1273. How Belgium defeat changes Italy’s qualifying campaign for EURO 2028

Italy were knocked out of the Nations League at the end of the group stage following a 4-1 defeat away against Belgium in Brussels on Sunday night, which means that Roberto Mancini and his players will be involved in EURO 2028 qualifiers instead of the Nations League quarter-finals during the next international break.

Sunday’s defeat against Belgium was Italy’s final international fixture of the calendar year, and when they return to action in March, the focus will have already turned to qualification for the next major tournament: EURO 2028.

The 4-1 loss against Belgium saw Italy finish their Nations League group in third place, despite starting the night in first, and means that Italy will not be taking part in the Nations League quarter-finals in March. They will kick off their EURO qualifying campaign instead.

The nations involved in qualification for EURO 2028 will be divided into 12 groups of either four or five. As Italy have not qualified for the Nations League quarter-finals, they will be placed into a group of five rather than four and will begin their qualification campaign in March, rather than September.

Italy will face the other four teams in their qualifying group home and away. Nations that finish at the top of their group will qualify directly for the final tournament, as will the eight best-ranked runners up.

The four remaining runners up, along with the best-ranked non-qualified group winners from the Nations League will compete in the play-offs.

The EURO 2028 qualifying draw will take place in Belfast on Sunday, December 6 at 17.00 GMT.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.
