#1272. USMNT Next Manager Odds: Pep Guardiola, Thierry Henry & Candidates to Replace Mauricio Pochettino

With Mauricio Pochettino on his way to the Premier League to take over Manchester United, the United States Men's National Team needs a new head coach. Pochettino was one of the biggest appointments in USMNT history, with the former Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea coach presiding over the team's fortunes from September 2024 until November 2026, steering them to the Round of 16 at the 2026 World Cup.

The Argentine followed in the footsteps of figures such as Gregg Berhalter, Bruce Arena, Jurgen Klinsmann and Bob Bradley, among others, and departs the scene having failed to deliver silverware, despite a win percentage of 61% during his tenure. Expectations are high among U.S. soccer fans, with many understandably excited by a crop of players which features talent such as Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams and Malik Tillman, as well as exciting prospects like Cavan Sullivan.

So, who will step into the role being vacated by Pochettino? There are plenty of major names being linked with the job, including a number of European coaching luminaries as well as home-grown talent who have proven track records in MLS, one of the top 30 leagues in world football. Here, GIVEMESPORT takes a look at the favorites to be appointed next USMNT manager.

Including Landon Donovan, Clint Dempsey, and Christian Pulisic, the best USMNT players of all time have been ranked.

Antonio Conte is currently without a job after leaving Napoli following the conclusion of the 2025/26 season and is rated a 50/1 outsider for the role currently. The former Chelsea, Inter Milan, Juventus and Tottenham boss guided Napoli to the Serie A title in 2024/25 and has an impressive CV, featuring a Premier League title with Chelsea.

Highly regarded young English coach Eddie Howe is similarly rated to Conte in terms of his chances of being appointed the next USMNT manager. Howe was recently relieved of his duties as manager of Premier League team Newcastle United and has been touted as a potential future England boss.

It might be a point of contention among their neighbors to the north, but Jesse Marsch is in the mix at 30/1 to be the next USMNT manager. Marsch, who has managed clubs in Europe, has been Canada men's national team head coach since May 2024 and led them to a round-of-16 finish in the 2026 World Cup.

Didier Deschamps won the World Cup with France both as a player and a manager, so his pedigree means that he would be a major coup for the USMNT. However, the former Marseille and Juventus legend only recently stood down from his role as France manager after 14 years at the helm and may take some time to decide on his next move. Still, he is rated 30/1 to be the next USMNT manager.

One of the most successful England managers in history, Gareth Southgate is considered a 25/1 bet to be the next USMNT manager. Southgate was recently replaced as Three Lions boss by Thomas Tuchel, but he brought the curtain down on his tenure having transformed England into a force to be reckoned with. They were beaten finalists in the 2020 and 2024 European Championships and a perennial contender for World Cups under him.

Former Germany and Bayern Munich boss Julian Nagelsmann is widely considered to be one of the best young coaches in the world and he would represent an intriguing prospect for the USMNT. Despite failing to deliver success for Germany, Nagelsmann is a progressive coach who has been able to imprint his philosophy on a variety of groups. At 25/1, however, he remains an outside bet.

Roberto Martinez won the Nations League with Portugal in 2024/25 and came third in the 2018 World Cup with Belgium. The Spanish coach's grounding came in English football, where he led Wigan Athletic to an unlikely FA Cup triumph in 2013, when they defeated Manchester City in the final. Martinez's recent association with international football means he is well used to the terrain.

From Mikel Arteta to Xabi Alonso, football is home to some of the most exciting young managers.

Interestingly, one of Martinez's assistant coaches, Thierry Henry, is deemed as likely to get the role as him at 14/1. Henry worked as Belgium assistant manager on two different occasions, as well as managing the France Under-21 and Olympic teams, guiding the latter to a silver medal in 2024. The Arsenal icon, ranked ninth among the greatest strikers in football history, has strong associations with North American soccer, too, having played for the New York Red Bulls and managed Montreal Impact.

San Diego boss Mikey Varas has already sat in the big seat for the USMNT, albeit in an interim role, manging two games in 2024 prior to the appointment of Pochettino. He has a strong feel for what is required at that level, having previously served as assistant to Gregg Berhalter and knows the players well from his time as United States Under-20 manager, during which period he won the CONCACAF U-20 Championship.

Pellegrino Matarazzo is rated 6/1 to be the next USMNT boss and the New Jersey native would be a fascinating appointment given his recent success with Real Sociedad. Interestingly, Matarazzo is close to the thinking of another candidate, Julian Nagelsmann, with the pair working together at Hoffenheim.

Mauricio Pochettino saw the 1980 US Olympic Hockey team as suitable underdog story to motivate the USMNT. But are the parallels real?

Nashville SC head coach BJ Callaghan is considered the strong favorite to get the USMNT job after Pochettino's departure and, like Varas, he has previously served in the role, having been a successful interim boss in 2023. Under Callaghan, the Americans won the CONCACAF Nations League and he took his magic touch to Nashville as they won the US Open Cup in 2025 and the MLS Supporters' Shield in 2026.

Steve Cherundolo is not far behind Callaghan in the odds reckoning at 4/1 and he is already in the ecosystem considering he is the manager of the U.S. U-23 team. Cherundolo was a fantastic servant to his country as a player and cut his teeth in management with Los Angeles FC, winning the 2022 MLS Cup and the 2024 US Open Cup.

By far the biggest name in the mix for the next USMNT head coach is Pep Guardiola, who is currently available for work following his departure from Manchester City. One of the greatest managers in history, Guardiola has won practically every title there is to win in European club football and would be something of a dream candidate for U.S. Soccer as they seek to embiggen the sport in the country and, eventually, compete for world glory.

#1271. Thomas Tuchel's 'best night' as England manager: Three Lions boss hails heroes after Spain victory - but hits out at Elliot Anderson decision made by referee he previously labelled a 'one out of 10'

Published: 18:10 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 19:58 EST, 15 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel hailed the 'best performance of my time as manager' after England beat world champions Spain in a crazy, brilliant see-sawing drama of a Nations League tie.

England played the best football of Tuchel's two-year reign as coach to end Spain's world record 43-match unbeaten run.

England raced into a 3-0 lead with a penalty from Harry Kane, and further goals from Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

But they played the last half an hour of the game with ten men after Elliot Anderson was sent off for pulling back Lamine Yamal.

Spain got two goals back to set up a nerve-wracking finish but goalkeeper James Trafford, in the team ahead of Jordan Pickford, pulled off a miracle double save in the dying minutes to seal the win.

'What a performance we put out there for 60 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up,' Tuchel said after the game. 'Thirty minutes against Spain with ten men feels like three hours.

Thomas Tuchel said England's display in the win over Spain was the best in his time as boss

'It was a statement victory. It was on the highest level football-wise. It is a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.

'It is the best performance of my time and they are unbeaten for 43 matches and that was a complete performance in that environment. To impose our identity on them was a real achievement.

'Declan Rice said he knew we were going to win and I could feel the true belief. This was the moment we wanted to prove ourselves. You need to rely on your teammates. That is why I am very proud of the win.'

Tuchel also questioned the decision to give Anderson a straight red, made by a referee he once labelled a 'one out of 10'.

The Man City midfielder was sent off because Clement Turpin adjudged him not to have been making an attempt to play the ball when he fouled Yamal.

'The red card and the penalty is always a big decision and I needed to understand why it was a double punishment but... OK,' Tuchel told ITV Sport.

'From then it was a long 30 minutes but I don't want to focus on that because there were so, so many positives.'

If United really intend to make big strides under the Argentine manager, they need to make another big investment in their defence in 2027, and Hall should be their number-one left-back target.

Newcastle may see Hall as a player worth around £100m now, having sold Tonali for a similar fee to Tottenham, but that shouldn't dissuade the Red Devils' hierarchy moving for a player who can be their left-back for many years.

#1269. When will Italy discover EURO 2028 qualifying opponents?

After missing out on a spot in the Nations League quarter-finals, Italy’s next match will be the first of their EURO 2028 qualifying campaign during the March international break: Here is everything you need to know about the upcoming draw and qualifying process.

Italy will begin their EURO 2028 qualifying campaign during the next international break, which officially kicks off on March 22, 2027.

The Azzurri will learn their EURO 2028 qualifying opponents when the draw takes place in Belfast on Sunday, December 6.

As Italy finished within the top three of the top tier of Nations League groups, they will be among the seeded nations in the EURO 2028 qualifying draw. Joining the Azzurri in the top pot will be France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Spain, England, Portugal, Denmark, Norway and Croatia.

There will be 12 qualifying groups in total and given that Italy’s EURO qualifying is now set to get underway in March, they will be placed into a group of five teams rather than four.

Each nation that qualifies at the top of their group, along with the eight-best runners up, will qualify directly for the final tournament.

The four remaining runners up along with the best non-qualified group winners from the 2026-27 Nations League, will be involved in the qualification play-offs for EURO 2028, which will take place in March, 2028.

The number of nations competing in the play-offs depends on the number of host nations that qualify. Between two to four additional spots will be up for grabs in the play-offs, depending on how many of the host nations – England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic or Ireland – qualify directly for the final tournament.

#1268. Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Anna Napolitano is a freelance journalist in London.

The number of men with high citation counts exceeds that of women.Credit: FotografiaBasica/iStock via Getty

Women are more frequently mentioned in the acknowledgements section of papers than credited as co-authors, especially for research and analytical work, a study has found. But status seems to trump gender.

An analysis of more than 20,000 authors and 60,000 acknowledged contributors on papers published in seven PLOS journals between 2016 and 2021 highlighted persistent disparities between women and men in who gets authorship over an acknowledgement.

The study, published in Scientometrics1, also found that highly cited researchers — used by the authors as a proxy for higher status — were more likely to receive authorship over acknowledgement than were their less-cited collaborators, irrespective of gender. When a highly cited woman collaborated with a less-cited man, for example, the woman was more likely to be credited as an author.

Authorship is one of the most important metrics in research evaluation, grant reviews and promotion decisions, whereas acknowledgements aren’t typically factored in. The difference between getting authorship credit versus an acknowledgement can make or break a researcher’s career. One famous example is chemist Rosalind Franklin, a key contributor to the discovery of the DNA double helix. Franklin was mentioned in the acknowledgements section of the 1953 paper describing the finding, which went on to win the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, rather than being named a co-author with James Watson and Francis Crick.

The Scientometrics study highlights the importance of status in determining who gets credit, and the uphill battle that many women in research have to face — especially in their early and mid-careers. The number of highly cited men exceeded that of women, suggesting that even if women benefit from high status once they have attained it, fewer women attain higher status in the first place.

“We realized that the issue is double. One linked with gender bias, but another surprisingly due to hierarchy bias,” says Yukie Sano, a computational scientist at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, who co-authored the paper.

The impact of a researcher’s status and gender on academic credit is well-documented, but Sano and her co-authors point to the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT) — a standardized system describing specific roles that individual scientists often take on during research — as a game-changer by providing high-quality data to track this metric across journals and disciplines.

Sano and her colleagues used CRediT data from open-access PLOS journals (which implemented the system in 2016) to track the contributions of authors and devised a separate system to track contributions in the acknowledgements section. Author gender was determined using Gender API, an artificial-intelligence-powered service that infers a person’s gender on the basis of their name.

The team found that men were generally more likely than women to receive authorship credit — particularly in investigation roles (performing the experiments) and analysis roles (analysing or synthesizing the study data). Around 70% of men were credited as authors, compared with about 65% of women.

The size of the gender gap varied between disciplines, but was particularly evident in medicine, biology and computer science, whereas environmental science showed little evidence of a gender difference in authorship versus acknowledgement rates.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7

Arsenal are expected to make a move or two in the January transfer window, as they look to bolster Mikel Arteta's attacking options ahead of the second half of the season.

The Gunners have enjoyed an impressive start to the new campaign, winning nine of their first ten Premier League matches, whilst conceding just five goals in the process. However, Arteta's side have only scored 15 goals, and thus, there is a recognition from the Premier League champions' coaching staff and hierarchy that they need more offensive firepower to get them over the line later in the season.

Antonio Nusa has been heavily linked with a switch to North London, with Arsenal reportedly weighing up a potential move for the Norwegian. Nusa has scored six goals and provided eight assists in 15 appearances already this season for RB Leipzig, so the German club are unlikely to sanction his departure mid-way through the campaign for a bargain.

The Spaniard finds himself behind the likes of Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Mikel Merino in the pecking order at the Emirates, sparking speculation that he could be on his way out in January.

The jigsaw pieces fit, while the finances also make sense. Zubimendi is doing very little with his performances to quieten the noise around a potential exit, and the convenience around the potential deal makes it too difficult for Arsenal to ignore this winter.

James is a Senior Editor for GIVEMESPORT with over eight years of experience in the industry. After graduating from the University of Southampton in 2016 with a degree in history, he joined the company as an Academy member in July 2017 and, after a short time working as a freelancer, was given a full-time role in February 2018.  He primarily covers the biggest stories in the football world but is also comfortable reporting on a variety of other sports including darts, golf, Formula 1, tennis, boxing and athletics. USA are aiming high as they search for a replacement for Pochettino. According to GiveMeSport sources, Pep Guardiola is on their radar, and they want him to be their manager.

Guardiola, considered one of the greatest managers in football history, is currently a free agent after leaving Manchester City in the summer.

It remains to be seen whether USA are able to land Guardiola, but many think that he would be an incredible coup should he put pen-to-paper.

USMNT legends Tim Howard and Landon Donovan don't share that opinion, though. Speaking on 'Unfiltered Soccer with Landon Donovan & Tim Howard', the pair explained why they thought the USA shouldn't go for Guardiola. Howard said:

"Pep Guardiola. And by the way, I think the next time I see Pep Guardiola, he might smack me and I'm okay with that. He's absolutely not the right manager for this team, for the length of time that it's going to take to get through to the next World Cup.

Their comments haven't gone down well among USMNT fans.

Inter coach Cristian Chivu won the Panchina d’Oro award in Coverciano for the best Serie A coach in the 2025-26 season.

The prizes for the best coaches in Italian football for the 2025-26 campaign were awarded today in Coverciano, with Football Italia in attendance.

Chivu beat Roma’s Gian Piero Gasperini (third) and Cesc Fabregas (second) to win the “Panchina d’Oro” for the first time.

Chivu was awarded after winning the domestic double—the Scudetto and Coppa Italia—in his first full season as a Serie A coach. Inter hired him in the summer of 2025 to replace Simone Inzaghi.

Coaches in each category determined the winners with their votes. The votes for Serie C, B and A took place in the morning in Coverciano.

“Thanks to you all for this award,” Chivu said.

“It’s always special to receive an award given by colleagues. I thank the technical sector, the coaches, my club, the players, and the staff. The players are those who turn our ideas into results. Last but not least, I want to thank my family, who always support me when I win, but mostly when I lose.”

Among the winners were Massimiliano Alvini of Frosinone as Best Serie B coach and Francesco Tomei of Ascoli as Best Serie C coach.

Below are all the winners at the Panchina d’Oro in Coverciano

Futsal Men Serie A: Diego Rios (L84 Torino)

Special Panchina d’Oro: Francesco Farioli (Porto FC) and Daniele Franceschini (Italy U17)

#1262. Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dyani Lewis is a freelance journalist in Melbourne, Australia.

In August 1987, a scandal erupted over work on the world’s highest mountain range. John Talent, a palaeontologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, announced he had found numerous anomalies in research charting the geology of the Himalayas. All of the problems were in papers by Vishwa Jit Gupta, one of India’s most celebrated palaeontologists at the time.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Gupta was outraged. But further investigations over the following seven years revealed the scale and brazenness of his fraud. Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn’t exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections that Gupta had visited. More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils Gupta claimed he had collected from specific Himalayan geological formations, but instead hailed from North America and Morocco.

“It destroyed the image of Indian science,” says retired geologist Ghulam Bhat, who completed his PhD on Himalayan geology in the same year that the allegations of fraud emerged.

Gupta died in 2022, and many geologists know to steer clear of his work. But awareness of the problem is fading, and none of Gupta’s papers have been retracted. When Nature contacted Bhat, who is now editor-in-chief of the Journal of the Geological Society of India (JGSI), he was unaware that Gupta’s papers were not marked as retracted. That’s despite the JGSI’s 1991 evaluation of 19 of Gupta’s papers that it published1, which concluded that “the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation”.

Much of Gupta’s work is inaccessible, having been published in now-defunct periodicals or in volumes that, although digitized online, have not been indexed in reference bibliometric databases such as Scopus, Web of Science and Dimensions. Despite this, Gupta’s falsehoods are now being propagated outside specialist circles, as his old journal articles are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results. When someone searches for geological landmarks in the Himalayas, such as the Tandi Limestone, Google’s AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta’s discredited papers.

Bhat now plans to rectify the digital record and says that all other journals that have published Gupta’s work should do the same. “If this problem is left as it is, unattended, it will pollute all of the geological literature in future,” he says. Gupta also published papers in Nature in the 1960s; Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, didn’t confirm that the journal would re-examine them. But he added that in general, when investigations of old papers are hampered by limited available information, an editorial expression of concern “is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues”. (Nature’s news team is editorially independent of its publisher, Springer Nature.)

The Himalayas case raises a wider issue: how to deal with fraudulent, unethical or even merely incorrect research from decades ago, especially in an era in which much old work is digitized and AI systems can pick up studies that might previously have been neglected.

There are many skeletons in science’s closet, but publishers can be reluctant to judge science of the past by today’s standards, and can find it more difficult to issue retractions when authors are dead, original records cannot be consulted or journals are no longer in print.

And as publishers struggle to deal with the fallout from rising research fraud and AI slop, finite resources can also mean that many old papers with known flaws are left as they are.

Gráinne McNamara, a council member of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in Eastleigh, UK, which advises journals on best practice, says that journals are increasingly contacting COPE to ask for advice about dealing with concerns on very old papers.

“Everybody is looking for what’s the best, most responsible way to handle these,” she says.

The widespread use of retractions as a mechanism for maintaining integrity in the scientific record is a relatively recent phenomenon. The JGSI evaluation report about Gupta served as a warning notice to the community at the time, but didn’t use the word retraction. It also pre-dates the modern standardization of retraction processes, which happened in the 2000s. Now, a journal should issue a retraction notice, and leave the original paper intact, but with a modified title and a stamp or watermark indicating that it has been retracted. The information should then feed through to bibliographic databases.

In the early 2000s, only around 30 retraction notices were published each year, and COPE first developed guidelines to standardize the retraction process in 2004. The number — and rate — of retractions has exploded since then, with more than 10,000 recorded in 2023 alone.

Digitization of old records, combined with a wider propensity to retract flawed work, has seen journals reaching farther back in time to retract studies — and this has led to some startlingly long gaps between when an article was published and when it was formally retracted. Retraction Watch, an initiative that curates a database of more than 70,000 retractions and expressions of concern (a notice that highlights potential issues with a publication), has reported that the longest gap is 80 years. That’s for a prank case report published in 1923 in the Dutch medical journal Nederlands Tijdschrift voor Geneeskunde.

It described a man who died from “piss cough”, an affliction that caused him to cough up liquid smelling of urine. In 2003, an editor at the journal happened to look up the case, which he thought was widely known to be a hoax. Realizing it had never been retracted and that others did not know it was fake, he sought confirmation of the hoax, and found it in the autobiography of a retired University of Amsterdam physician, who had helped to cook up the nonsense case when he was a medical student. Accompanying commentary on the journal’s website said that a retraction was appropriate now that the older literature had become accessible through digitization.

According to Nature’s analysis of Retraction Watch data — which capture a subset of total retractions — the number of old papers that are being retracted is rising. Overall, some 358 retraction notices and 120 expressions of concern have been issued for papers or book chapters that were more than 20 years old at the time of the editorial action (see ‘Retracting the past’). This is still a rare phenomenon: since 2015, the oldest retractions represent some 0.7% of the total number, up from 0.2% before 2010. But around 3% of expressions of concern have occurred for works older than 20 years. That illustrates how publishers might choose to issue expressions of concern for older papers, rather than retract, because it can be harder to investigate historical records.

In 2005, biochemist Barry Milborrow sought to retract five of his own papers, published between 1980 and 1982, on biochemical pathways that bacteria, algae and plants use to make pigments, because later work had disproved their findings. The Biochemical Journal, which published Milborrow’s self-retraction listing the five articles2, retracted both articles it had published. Another journal issued a correction, but no notice was issued by the publisher of the remaining two papers. Ian Swift, Milborrow’s co-author and PhD student at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, at the time, says he only found out about the retractions many years later, after Milborrow had passed away.

According to COPE guidance, journal editors can retract articles if they no longer have confidence in the results and conclusions reported in them. By that rubric, many older papers could, in theory, be retracted, but, being rarely cited, are usually left alone.

Even when invalid papers are still being cited, retraction might not follow. In 1985, for instance, geneticist Svante Pääbo reported that he had cloned DNA from an Egyptian mummy3. The seminal work marked the birth of palaeogenomics, a field that earned Pääbo a Nobel prize in 2022. But the mummy DNA was actually contamination from a modern handler, as Pääbo, now at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, has openly acknowledged. “What is problematic is if false conclusions lead other scientists and the community as a whole astray,” he told Nature when asked for this article. “I don’t think anyone is currently misled by the mummy paper,” he says, which is why he argues that the work should stand, adding that to correct very old papers with errors “would create more confusion than clarity”.

Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways

Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways

In practice, old papers tend to be considered for retraction only if they have widespread integrity issues that journal editors feel shouldn’t be allowed to stand unmarked. A major trigger for mass retractions of older work is when investigations of an individual’s research cast doubt over their entire body of work. For instance, a 2019 investigation by King’s College London into the work of psychologist Hans Eysenck and his German collaborator Ronald Grossarth-Maticek has led to papers dating back to the 1940s being flagged — albeit many with expressions of concern rather than retractions.

Eysenck died in 1997 as one of the most celebrated psychologists of the twentieth century. But in 2019, psychiatrist Anthony Pelosi, who had critiqued Eysenck’s work to no effect in the 1990s, published a renewed analysis of the studies4. An accompanying editorial called on King’s College London — where Eysenck worked from 1955 until 1983 — to conduct a formal investigation. The investigation report, also published in 2019, concluded that 24 articles by Eysenck and Maticek published between 1988 and 2000 were ‘unsafe’ and recommended they be retracted.

Those recommendations weren’t followed entirely. Only 16 of the 24 papers have been retracted, and another 4 have expressions of concern. Four remain unflagged. After sustained criticism over the narrow scope of the 2019 investigation, King’s College London published a statement in October 2025 saying that other publications based on the data set used in the 24 papers it examined are also likely to be ‘unsafe’ and should be flagged by journal editors — although it did not list affected publications.

So far, 94 of Eysenck’s hundreds of papers have been either retracted or tagged with an expression of concern, the oldest of which was published in 1943 (see ‘Longest gaps’).

Such inconsistencies in how publishers deal with research-integrity issues are common and don’t relate only to very old papers, says Andrew Grey, an endocrinologist and research-integrity specialist at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. He alerted publishers to concerns over large numbers of articles by Yoshihiro Sato, a Japanese bone-health researcher who fabricated data in dozens of clinical trials, and has reported seeing some journals respond with retractions or expressions of concern, whereas others take no action5.

One famous scandal of the past — the 1980s discrediting of work by John Darsee, a US biologist — has led to just 17 retractions. Although news reports at the time stated that more than 80 of Darsee’s papers had been retracted, this refers to editorial notes and warnings that, in parallel with the Gupta case, don’t appear in modern records as retractions.

Another trigger for retracting old work is when it attracts renewed attention, particularly in medical fields.

Each year, Marcel van der Heyden, a physiologist at the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands, asks his final-year students to write a review article about a poison or toxin. In 2025, he chose caesium salts, and his students uncovered 20 case reports of people ingesting the toxic chemical6. Often, the individuals deliberately consumed the compound as an alternative treatment for cancer. Although the US Food and Drug Administration cautioned against its use in 2018, the deadly ‘therapy’ is still promoted in books and online by some wellness centres.

The treatment traces back to two papers published in 1984 in Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. One of the papers was written by Austrian-born Hellfried Sartori, who had been prosecuted in Maryland in 1982 for fraud relating to using the unproven cancer treatment. That case ended in a mistrial. Sartori subsequently had his medical licence revoked in several US states in the 1980s and was sentenced to prison in Virginia in 1999 for practising medicine without a licence. And in 2010, an inquest into the deaths of five people in Australia found that he had been treating patients remotely from Thailand. Many more of his patients had also died under his treatment, the court heard.

The other paper promoting caesium therapy was by Wisconsin-based Aubrey Keith Brewer. Brewer died in 1986, but his namesake Brewer International Science Library continues to distribute information on caesium and other alternative therapies with a disclaimer that the protocols are “for information purposes only”, and that people should consult their physician if unwell. Nature contacted the website but received no response.

Van der Heyden contacted Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior in August 2025, suggesting an expression of concern could be warranted. “Without the original data, it’s hard to tell whether there is a mistake made, or whether it’s on purpose,” he says. But the research-integrity team at the journal’s publisher, Elsevier, decided in January this year to remove the two papers, soon after Van der Heyden informed them that his review had been accepted for publication and that his university was poised to issue a press release about it. The papers were deleted entirely this April, as Retraction Watch reported.

The move to scrub a paper, rather than merely retract and leave it in place, can be taken if the contents could present a serious health risk to the public, according to COPE guidelines.

#1261. Grief-stricken Tenerife stars return to action for first time since death of Jesus de Miguel, 30, after fatal on-field collision with goalkeeper: Tributes paid and match paused in 9th minute on emotional day

Published: 14:11 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 21:21 EST, 15 November 2026

Tenerife have returned to action for the first time since Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel was tragically killed in a collision during a game with FC Andorra earlier this month.

Goalkeeper Jesus Owono came flying out of his goal and wiped out De Miguel with a high challenge, which resulted in the striker being admitted to intensive care, where he later died.

Thirteen days on from the incident, Tenerife played their first game since the player's death as they took on AD Ceuta CF in LaLiga Hypermotion action – with the game filled with tributes to the star.

Players gave a floral tribute as they arrived for the match, and gathered outside gate nine of the Heliodoro Rodríguez Lopez Stadium – the shirt number he wore.

Grief-stricken Tenerife stars, meanwhile, took to the field carrying a bouquet of flowers, and placed it at the scene of the incident.

Both sets of players and fans then observed a minute's silence in memory of De Miguel before the game kicked off.

🕊️❤️ THE NINTH MINUTE BELONGED TO JESÚS DE MIGUEL! 🥹🏟️ Football took a back seat during Tenerife's first match following his passing.👏 In the ninth minute, the stadium came together in a heartfelt tribute to honor his memory.💔 Some losses are felt far beyond the pitch.… pic.twitter.com/mqPy4aE9Q3

After scoring 12 goals on loan at Oxford United last season, Tottenham opted to cash in on Lankshear over the summer, garnering upwards of £20 million for the young England striker.

Just a few months later, a return to the Premier League could be on the cards for the former Spurs man. An extraordinarily prolific start to the new campaign has seen Lankshear become the most-wanted talent in the Championship right now, with clubs queuing up to sign the number nine in January.

Lankshear's Statistics 2026/27 (Championship Only)

While left-back has been mooted as the priority position for United, it appears they could first move for a brand new centre-forward.

#1259. Official: Atalanta hand new contract extension to Bernasconi on 23rd birthday

Lorenzo Bernasconi is celebrating his 23rd birthday with a new Atalanta contract, the club has confirmed.

Bernasconi, who turns 23 on Monday, has put pen to paper on a new and improved contract with Atalanta, the club confirmed in a statement at the start of the week. La Dea have not formally disclosed the length of Bernasconi’s new deal, but it is understood to be a long-term contract given that his previous deal already ran until the summer of 2030.

“Having joined the Nerazzurri before turning 18, Lorenzo progressed through the youth ranks and gained valuable experience with the U23s before making the step up to the First Team,” read a statement on the club website.

“Since then, he has steadily earned an increasingly prominent role through humility, dedication and hard work, setting an example with his attitude both on and off the pitch.

“The Percassi and Pagliuca families, the sporting management and everyone at the Club wish Lorenzo every success, both individually and collectively, as he continues his journey in the Nerazzurri shirt.”

The contract extension comes shortly after Bernasconi’s 50th competitive appearance for Atalanta, which came in their 1-0 win away against Monza in their last match before the November international break.

A new contract could help Atalanta fend off interest from Juventus, who had been linked with a January move for the left-sided defender last month. The Old Lady are actively seeking a new left-back heading into the January window.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1258. Longest Unbeaten Runs in International Football History

Going unbeaten in international football, where every side is measured by the FIFA World Ranking, is harder than it may first appear. In club football, managers and head coaches see their players almost every day, and so have the opportunity to embed their tactics and style of play into their players. National team managers, however, can go months between international breaks without overseeing a single game or training session. That's what makes a long run without defeat one of the sport's rarest achievements.

The longest runs belong to some of the greatest sides the game has seen. Several of them have won major tournaments along the way, and one turned a World Cup final into a record-breaking night. Some ended in famous upsets, and some came to a stop in games few people remember.

Here's a look at the top five longest unbeaten runs in men's international football history.

GIVEMESPORT takes a look at the greatest footballers to ever play at the World Cup.

Spain's golden generation started their 35-game unbeaten streak in February 2007, when Andrés Iniesta, one of the greatest midfielders in history, scored his first goal for the Spanish national team during a 1-0 win over England at Old Trafford. In a run initially started by head coach Luis Aragonés, La Roja entered the 2008 European Championship having failed to win only twice in their previous 16 games, with draws against Iceland and Finland.

After topping their group, Spain needed penalties to edge past Italy in the quarter-finals, before dismantling Russia 3-0 in the semis. Fernando Torres' 33rd minute strike made the difference in the final against Germany as the Spanish won their first major trophy in 44 years and their second Euros title. With the likes of Carles Puyol, Xavi and David Villa at his disposal, new boss Vicente del Bosque maintained the run after taking over the national team following the tournament. Eventually, it was the USA who put an end to Spain's unbeaten run, with a 2-0 victory in the 2009 Confederations Cup semi-final, with goals from Jozy Altidore and Clint Dempsey.

Brazil share the fourth longest unbeaten run, having also lasted 35 games without defeat between 1993 and 1996. Rivaldo scored the only goal in a friendly against Mexico in December 1993 to start the run under coach Carlos Alberto Parreira. The Brazil national team entered the 1994 World Cup in the USA in good form, having not lost any of their last six games, including an 8-2 thrashing of Honduras just two weeks before the tournament.

Despite drawing their final group stage game against Sweden, Canarinho topped their group and dumped the host nation from the tournament in the Round of 16. Victories over the Netherlands and Sweden in the knockouts set Brazil up for a World Cup final against Italy. With the teams stuck at 0-0 after extra time, the game was decided by penalties, with Italy's Roberto Baggio missing the decisive spot kick to gift the title to the South-American nation.

Mario Zagallo took over the reins as coach of the national team, and carried the unbeaten streak through the 1995 Copa América. Although his side did lose the final to hosts Uruguay, that was only through penalties, meaning they were still unbeaten after extra time. Ironically, the nation whom the run started against also ended the run, with Mexico winning the Gold Cup final 2-0 in January 1996.

A look at some of the most impressive runs without losing in the Premier League

The first game of Argentina's 36-game unbeaten run would likely have been one that they didn't want to play. Having lost 2-0 to Brazil in the 2019 Copa América semi-finals, Argentina faced Chile for the third-place trophy, in what many view as a glorified friendly. However, it was only up from here, as they beat Chile 2-1 and started their unbeaten run.

Three years later, the run was still going strong as Argentina started their 2021 Copa América campaign. After topping their five-team group, Argentina dumped Ecuador and Colombia from the competition to set up a rematch of their 2019 semi-final against Brazil. Ángel Di María's first-half strike was enough to secure their first title in 28 years, and Lionel Messi, one of the greatest football players of all time, lifted his first senior international trophy.

Argentina's special run lasted right up until the first fixture of the next major tournament, having beaten Italy 3-0 in the 2022 Finalissima at Wembley, before falling to a shock 2-1 defeat to Saudi Arabia in their first game of the 2022 FIFA World Cup. And whilst the end of such an impressive run would've been disappointing, the Argentina national side turned it around and won the tournament.

Found an error? Send it info@www.givemesport.com so it can be corrected.

Having failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup, a 1-0 defeat to Portugal in September 2018 seemed an unlikely place for the Italian national team to turn their fortunes around, with the former European giants seemingly at rock bottom. And whilst their 1-1 draw with Ukraine that October didn't seem to be much of an improvement, it kickstarted what would be the second-longest unbeaten run in men's international football history.

Roberto Mancini managed to harness the experience of the likes of Giorgio Chiellini and Leonardo Bonucci ahead of the Euro 2020 competition and got the Italian national team in good form. After topping their group, they defeated Austria, Belgium and Spain on their way to a Wembley final against England, which they won on penalties.

Eventually, the run came to an end, with a 2-1 defeat to Spain in the Nations League semi-final in October 2021, in what was the Azzurri's first competitive home defeat since 1999.

Just days after a 1-0 friendly loss against Colombia, Spain's record-breaking run began with a 3-3 draw against Brazil in March 2024. That summer, Luis de la Fuente's side put in a special performance at the 2024 European Championship. The Spanish national team won all seven of their games, including 2–1 wins over Germany and France on their way to a final against England, which they also won 2-1.

Similar results followed in the 2025 Nations League, as the Spaniards reached the final, and faced Portugal. Whilst they did lose that final, it was via penalties. Therefore, they were still unbeaten after extra time. Their 2026 World Cup campaign started disappointingly, with a goalless draw against Cape Verde. They then beat the likes of Portugal, Belgium and France on their way to what would be a record-breaking World Cup final against Argentina.

With the match goalless after 90 minutes, it was substitute Ferran Torres who broke the deadlock in the 104th minute. Spain managed to hold on, won their second World Cup, and broke Italy's record to make it 38-games unbeaten.

Spain continued their unbeaten run after the World Cup, but it came to a juddering halt in November 2026 when England defeated them 3-2 in Madrid. The Spanish media described the loss to Thomas Tuchel's men as "the biggest set-back of the De La Fuente era", noting that England were "steely and composed" victors.

Longest Unbeaten Runs in International Football History

#1257. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Sandro Tonali was exceptional in midfield and teenage talent Luca Williams-Barnett also sparkled off the bench. “Tonali was unbelievable,” De Zerbi said. “We played with two players more: Tonali was double.”

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

“Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

“Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”

A special player because of the character and he has unique characteristics.

“For James Maddison or the players who are coming from a long injury, they have to work more than the other players, but he has already four or five weeks he is working very hard and consistently.”

While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. We started this pre-season with a long project and we have to stay calm and clear in the head to work to build something better than when we came here,” he said. “One win or one defeat more, nothing will change. We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Mauricio Pochettino's United States farewell tour continued on Sunday night with a pitstop at an NFL showdown.

Before his return to England, the 54-year-old is enjoying his swansong with the US. In between overseeing his final games in charge of the national team, Pochettino was spotted soaking in the action of the other variety of football.

The former Tottenham Hotspur boss attended the primetime NFL showdown between the Cincinnati Bengals and Pittsburgh Steelers at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio on Sunday night.

The head coach, sporting his blue USSF coat, was captured standing on the sidelines with members of his staff ahead of the Sunday Night Football matchup.

USMNT and future Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is at the Bengals-Steelers game 😭🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/B7Irn0YLnd

Mauricio Pochettino's United States farewell tour continued at the NFL on Sunday night

The new Manchester United boss attended the Cincinnati Bengals' game at Paycor Stadium

He was greeted by kicker Evan McPherson, long snapper William Wagner and punter Ryan Rehkow - members of the Bengals' special teams - on the turf before kickoff.

The game, which will take place around a mile north of the Bengals' Paycor Stadium, will mark Pochettino's final match in charge of the US national team.

Pochettino will begin his new role with Manchester United on Wednesday, immediately following Tuesday's second-leg. His first game will be against Liverpool at Anfield next Sunday.

He emotionally addressed his departure from the US setup and impending new job in a press conference on Friday.

Flanked by US Soccer Federation bosses at the team’s headquarters in Georgia, an emotional Pochettino wiped away tears as he thanked the players and staff.

‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

The Argentine was captured on the sidelines ahead of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers

‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay.

‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'

#1254. AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Melissa Hobson is a freelance marine-science journalist based in Hastings, UK.

Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is working to make AI energy use more sustainable.

Artificial intelligence is exploding in popularity, and many people have concerns about the sustainability of its energy consumption. AI models need vast amounts of electricity: according to the International Energy Agency, a typical AI data centre can consume as much energy as 100,000 households each year. Energy use by US data-centre servers more than tripled between 2014 and 2023 — reaching 4.4% of the nation’s total electricity consumption. This figure is expected to at least double by 20281.

However, AI might also hold the key to improving energy efficiency: offsetting some of the demand it creates. An article published by the World Economic Forum suggests that the use of AI tools across industries — in automating tasks or monitoring real-time energy use, for example — can reduce energy consumption by up to 60%. Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, a sustainable-development specialist and an author of the article, has been working to lower AI’s energy demands while finding ways to use the tools to reduce wider emissions.

Originally from Trinidad, Greene-Dewasmes became interested in solving energy-security issues for island states with few resources. In 2021, she completed a PhD on the green-energy transition across small island developing states at the University of York, UK, before joining the World Economic Forum in 2022. Now based in Geneva, Switzerland, Greene-Dewasmes has been the Forum’s AI and Energy Lead since 2024. Her work involves bringing together AI and energy leaders from around the world to identify shared challenges, align priorities and develop practical actions that can improve AI’s energy impact.

As well as looking at improving AI’s energy efficiency, Greene-Dewasmes and partners are exploring how models can find innovations that improve existing energy infrastructure, such as that in buildings that are already in use. Nature spoke to her about navigating the increasing energy needs of the technology and whether its benefits could outweigh this demand.

AI needs cloud networks, chips, graphics-processing units and cooling systems, all of which consume large amounts of energy. Developing and training models requires high levels of processing power to crunch the data, but AI use is much more energy intensive overall because of the scale. ChatGPT, the chatbot from technology firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, has more than 800 million users each month and receives more than 2.5 billion queries daily. As AI becomes mainstream, we need to build more energy infrastructure to keep up with the surge in demand.

But, when it comes to scaling up AI, I think the conversation is too skewed towards the energy needed to power centralized infrastructure, when there are lots of other things that will contribute to AI’s energy requirements. Large data centres will exist in only the few countries that have the money, space and resources to host them. For most of the world, AI infrastructure will be disaggregated and decentralized. For example, if one million people are using their phones more intensively because of AI, that affects the energy infrastructure.

Although more complex LLM queries are currently directed to remote data centres, some smaller tasks can be completed directly on new devices that have AI chips. As this becomes more common, what will that mean for infrastructure planning for energy? It’s much harder to measure this than the outputs from one data centre.

AI’s electricity impact is currently about 0.49% of total global electricity use — so it’s still fairly small, although it’s growing. The World Economic Forum, in collaboration with other specialists, has created a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework. It looks at how we can design AI models and infrastructure for efficiency — by optimizing chips, data-centre locations and liquid cooling, in which fluids are used for cooling owing to their high heat capacity — while using AI to bring down energy usage in high-impact sectors, such as transportation and urbanization, both by improving the efficiency of systems and coming up with solutions to global challenges.

For example, in Azerbaijan, operations that keep buildings running, including lighting, heating and cooling, account for a large proportion of the country’s carbon emissions. The Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Azerbaijan (a public legal entity) is using AI-powered solutions to improve efficiencies as part of its nationally determined contribution commitments — the country’s pledge to reduce emissions. This includes AI solutions that adjust heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) on the basis of building occupancy and use trends, and that predict the need for maintenance before faults arise. In some cases, this use of AI to hone efficiency has brought down HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%.

We’re also encouraging people to use AI wisely. We want AI to reduce energy consumption overall, rather than adding strain to systems.

The aim is to gather insights from leading voices in the AI ecosystem to generate thought leadership and encourage cross-discipline learning so people aren’t working in silos. It started off as one-on-one conversations with professionals working with AI, centred on the technology’s biggest challenges and opportunities. We convened a community of about 40 people, which has increased to around 70 in nine industries around the world and is still growing. We try to hear from lots of voices: university academics, public-sector entities and technology, AI and energy companies (including renewables and nuclear) are all involved. Together with our partners, we turn these insights into guidance and frameworks that can support the wider industry.

We’ve published two reports based on the learnings gleaned from these thought leaders. Artificial Intelligence Energy Paradox explores how to balance the challenges and opportunities of AI and energy. The Net-Positive AI Energy Framework is our North Star for clean, efficient and equitable AI. We’re now working on an AI Energy Readiness Compass: a methodology to support responsible AI energy developments and identify the causes of upcoming bottlenecks in the power grid that could be problematic for AI energy use.

One particular success from these collaborations is the willingness of hyperscalers — large organizations that operate cloud computing services and data centres — to embrace grid flexibility. At first, they were reluctant to adjust when they draw power because they wanted continuous access to reliable electricity, but they have come to see the benefits of balancing demand on the grid. As a result, they have embraced power flexibility, and 18 partners supported the launch of the AI Energy Management Alliance: a coalition of companies that promotes dynamic load-shifting (changing when energy is used to align with grid loads, the availability of green energy and the best pricing).

#1253. Domenech fires back at Italy after 4-1 Belgium defeat: ‘Confirmed what we thought’

Raymond Domenech has fired back at the Italy national team, suggesting that the Azzurri ‘confirmed what we thought of them’ with their 4-1 defeat away against Belgium in the Nations League on Sunday evening.

A largely encouraging Nations League campaign ended in disappointment for Italy, who had started the weekend at the top of their group, but finished in third and missed out on a spot in the quarter-finals after a 4-1 defeat against Belgium in Brussels on Sunday night. Pio Esposito, Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy, Jeremie Doku and Diego Moreira provided the goals.

The Italian press has responded with mixed verdicts, although many feel there is still room for optimism given the way that the Azzurri started the calendar year: From missing out on World Cup qualification to picking up 10 points from their last five matches, four of which came against the third-highest-ranked team in the world, France, and with a core of youngsters at the heart of Roberto Mancini’s project.

Old rivalries die hard, however, and former France head coach Domenech has not looked too kindly upon Italy during the November international break.

Shortly after Pio Esposito had scored to equalise in Italy’s eventual 3-1 victory over France, Domenech took to social media and posted the following message: “It’s beyond the Italians’ wildest dreams. So weak in every department, but what’s most surprising is their technical level. So many mistakes from easy passes, it’s alarming.”

Domenech was widely mocked by jubilant Azzurri supporters in the comments after full-time, pointing to the full-time score, and of course, the result of the 2006 World Cup final, which Domenech lost against Marcello Lippi’s Italy.

Domenech has since fired back, however, following Italy’s 4-1 defeat against Belgium, which ended their Nations League campaign at the group stage.

“France qualify as expected. Belgium crush the Italians, who confirmed what we thought of them,” he wrote on Sunday night.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. Chance for Aston Villa. Cash clips in a delivery from the right and Torres has a good chance from eight yards out but the Spaniard’s header goes wide.

This game is there for the taking for both sides, although Fulham have been much the better side since the break and currently look more likely to get the winner.

Changes for both sides. For Aston Villa, they bring Barkley on for Kamara.

Fulham meanwhile bring on Palacios and Tete.

Cairney has not been on the pitch long but he is already into the book for cynically bringing down Mbaye.

Cash fouls King and is punished with a yellow card. That is already Cash’s fifth yellow card of the campaign, which means he will miss their trip to Manchester United next weekend.

Fulham are carving Aston Villa open. Bobb drives down their right wing before cutting inside. As he approaches the Aston Villa penalty area, he plays it out to his left to pick out Iwobi in space. Iwobi could hit it first time but instead cuts back onto his right, which allows Cash to block the shot but it does spin behind for a corner.

Before that is taken, Cairney replaces Iwobi. The corner comes to nothing.

Fulham have not made any substitutions yet but based on the way they are playing, they really do not need to right now, unless anyone is exhausted.

You can hear the groans inside Villa Park as the home fans grow frustrated with their side’s performance since the break.

Fulham deserved that equaliser and have been the better side in this game, especially since the break. It does feel like this game is for the taking for Alvaro Arbeloa’s men heading into the final 20 minutes.

Unai Emery has unsurprisingly made a triple change as Mbaye, Buendia and Gomes come on.

The Aston Villa goalkeeper has been outstanding tonight but that is a huge error. The corner is swung in by Iwobi from the left and Suzuki should simply catch it. He backpedals towards his own line and ends up dropping it. By the time he re-gathers, the ball has crossed the line and Fulham have an equaliser that they deserve.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Another save from Suzuki and Fulham spurn yet more great chances. Bobb’s cross from the right side of the box falls right on the head of Iwobi, who should score, but his header is straight at Suzuki. Garcia then has a shot blocked that goes behind for a corner.

An important save from Leno. Maatsen’s volley from the edge of the box takes a deflection off his teammate Torres, forcing Leno into a good reflex save. Had that gone in, it may have been curtains for Fulham.

The chances are piling up for Fulham but they still have not been able to take advantage of any of them. First Bobb has a shot inside the box blocked before Charles curls off target from the edge of the box.

Fulham are really knocking on the door. Bobb and Castagne work it well down the right, with the latter crossing from the right side of the box, forcing Torres to put it behind for a corner. Bobb’s deliveyr beyond the back post is headed back across goal but Aston Villa frantically clear their lines. Aston Villa are under the pump.

You wonder if Unai Emery might turn to his bench imminently as Fulham are on top at the moment.

Fulham once more come agonisingly close to an equaliser. Castange flicks on with his head at the near post from a corner out on the left. Charles then flicks it towards goal but it hits his teammate Garcia and loops over the bar. Alvaro Arbeloa will be wondering how his side are behind in this game.

Fulham have started this half positively and have a corner out on the left. They take it short before Iwobi clips it in but the delivery is poor and easily cleared by Goretzka.

How have Fulham not scored there and got back on level terms? Robinson and Iwobi exchange a neat one-two on the left side of the box before the former sends in a dangerous cross. Suzuki does brilliantly to stick out a hand and the ball flies into the sliding Garcia, ricocheting off the forward and going wide. Suzuki has been crucial for Aston Villa tonight; without him having a good game thus far, Fulham may have scored a couple of times.

Possession: Aston Villa 47%-53% FulhamShots: 7-5Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 5-2Touches in opposition box: 15-14

It’s half time at Villa Park and Unai Emery’s side are 1-0 ahead thanks to that man Nicolas Jackson’s eighth goal of the season. But Villa needed Japan goalkeeper Zion Suzuki to be on top form yet again.

Fulham almost took the lead when Antonee Robinson broke clear and crossed for Gonzalo Garcia, his step over allowed Oscar Bobb in for what looked like his second goal in successive games.

But Suzuki pulled off another stunning fingertip save following his impressive display against Manchester City last week. Cue a chorus of ‘Zion Suzuki, the world’s No1’ from the Holte End. Wait, wasn’t that Emi Martinez’s song last season?

Villa went ahead five minutes before the break when Jackson powered his way past past two defenders to score after a superb pass from Johan Manzambi released the Senegal striker. Jackson’s fancy footwork created an opening for him to score.

Bassey is into the book late on in the half for a foul on Kamara.

The first half is then brought to an end moments later and Aston Villa lead 1-0 at the break thanks to Jackson’s goal. McGinn did miss a penalty for the hosts whilst Fulham have failed to take a few good chances.

Fulham have had some chances in the first half but have not been able to take advantage of any of them. King has the ball on the right side of the box and tries to pick out Garcia at the far post but there is just slightly too much on the cross.

King has a chance to equalise for Fulham but Suzuki is quick off his line to snuff out the danger. That is two big moments from Suzuki to prevent Fulham from scoring.

There will be four added minutes at the end of this first half.

He scored two against Manchester City a week ago and he now has one tonight. He is found in space on the left by Manzambi and drives into the Fulham penalty area. Both Affengruber and Castagne should probably deal with the danger but somehow allow Jackson to cut inside onto his right and fire into the far corner to put the home side in front.

Garcia shoots from the left edge of the box and tries to catch Suzuki out at his near post. Garcia though drags his effort into the side netting as he goes in search of his second Premier League goal.

The Premier League has just posted this on X about the Aston Villa penalty:

VAR: “That’s the hand right up and it hits it”.  AVAR: “For me, his hand is in an unnatural position above his head”.  REF: “After review, Fulham No.16 commits a handball offence with a hand high above the head. The final decision will be penalty kick”.

Fulham should take the lead. Robinson does brilliantly on the counter-attack to drive down Fulham’s left. It is a great save from Suzuku but Bobb should bury that opportunity.

Affengruber brings down Jackson just outside the Fulham penalty area out on the left and the Austrian defender is booked. He tried to plead his innocence but I am not sure he has a leg to stand on with that one.

Aston Villa take it short before McGinn clips in a cross which is headed away.

Fulham wasted a fifth minute chance and may regret it. Gonzalo Garcia crossed for Alex Iwobi who sent his shot over the bar.

Villa awarded a penalty in the 14th after a VAR review when Leon Goretzka’s header hit Sande Berge’s raised hand. No-one appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

But Villa captain John McGinn’s shot hit the crossbar and bounced out again. It was a mystery as to why he took it with Nicolas Jackson available, but Villa are the team on top here.

Fulham are currently having to do a lot of defending, especially negotiating set-pieces. Affengruber is on hand this time to head away McGinn’s corner from the right.

McGinn steps up but his effort smashes into the bar. Leno dived the wrong way but there is too much power and loft on that effort. A massive missed opportunity for Aston Villa and the most relieved man inside Villa Park right now will be Berge.

Penalty MISSED! John McGinn hits the bar 💥 https://t.co/2kBYkYA2BY

Berge is pretty close to Goretzka but there is no reason why his arm is above his head like that.

Another McGinn corner from the right is met by Goretzka. This time, the German gets his header on target but it is easily saved by his compatriot Leno.

There is a VAR check for a possible penalty. Is there a handball from Berge in there immediately after Goretzka got his head on the ball? It appears that it did strike Berge’s hand and the referee is sent to the screen. We know how this normally goes...

Alysson goes down inside the Fulham box, wanting a penalty, but he is not going to get that.

Aston Villa do have a corner though, which McGinn delivers. His corner is met by Goretzka, who cannot keep his header down and it goes off target.

That is a big early chance for Fulham which Iwobi wastes. Bobb steals possession deep inside his own half and drives forward into the Aston Villa half. He then finds Garcia to his right, who delivers a cross from the right side of the box. There is a nick off Lindelof and comes to Iwobi near the penalty spot but he blazes his effort into the stands. At the very least, Iwobi should be hitting the target.

Is that an example of the time of the game contributing to a decision? Goretzka is pulled back by Garcia, who avoids a yellow card. Had that not been inside the first few minutes of the game, it would not have been a surprise to have seen a yellow card.

After the Remembrance tribute is impeccably observed by those inside Villa Park, we are under way in the final Premier League game of the day.

With this being Aston Villa’s last home league game before Remembrance Sunday, Villa Park pauses to pay tribute to remember the fallen. Wreaths are laid in the middle of the centre circle before The Last Post is played.

As the pyrotechnics go off, both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at Villa Park. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Subs: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo
